curriculum: National Curriculum in England, Key Stage 3 (DfE, September 2013, statutory from September 2014 and still current)

termDates.note: England term dates are set by local authorities and individual schools, not centrally. These are the typical 2026/27 dates for England and should be checked against the family's own local authority.

designNotes.lessonVolume: Core subjects (maths, English, science) run 3 lessons per week for all 40 teaching weeks: 120 lessons each. Enrichment subjects (geography, history, computing) run at roughly half that volume, averaging 1.5 lessons per week (two lessons in alternate weeks): 62 lessons each.
designNotes.bigRocks: Lessons flagged bigRock:true carry the highest-yield content: the ideas that unlock the most later learning, or that are most often the source of persistent misconception. If time is short in a given week, these are the lessons to protect.
designNotes.ks2Routing: Every lesson carries a ks2Prerequisites array naming the Key Stage 2 statutory statements it assumes. Where a lesson is failing, the app should route back to the named KS2 objective before reteaching the KS3 lesson.
designNotes.knowledgeComponents: Each week carries a knowledgeComponents array of atomic, individually-testable items tagged to the lesson that introduces them, for use in a spaced-repetition system. Types are fact, procedure, concept and skill. Core subjects average 8-12 per week; enrichment subjects average 8-10 per week.
designNotes.assessment: Each half term ends with a consolidation and assessment week combining interleaved retrieval practice, a summative assessment tagged to knowledge components, and an error-analysis and gap-repair lesson. Assessment items should be mapped back to knowledge components so that failures reset the spacing interval on the specific component rather than the whole topic.
designNotes.sequencingRationale: Within each subject, content is sequenced so that prerequisites always precede the lessons that depend on them. In maths, algebraic notation precedes equations, which precede graphs and proof. In science, working scientifically and the particle model precede every later practical and explanation. In English, sentence-level grammar and analytical paragraph writing precede the whole-text essays. Retrieval in later terms deliberately samples earlier terms to force spacing.

sourceNotes: VERIFIED against primary sources during preparation of this document: the statutory programmes of study on gov.uk for Key Stage 3 mathematics, science, English, geography, history and computing (Department for Education, published September 2013, statutory from September 2014, and still the current national curriculum). All ncRef strings quote or closely paraphrase the wording of those documents, and all priorKnowledgeAssumed entries are taken from the corresponding Key Stage 1 and 2 statutory programmes of study. The 2026/27 term dates were checked against published England term-date calendars and give 40 teaching weeks; these are TYPICAL dates only, because in England term dates are set by local authorities and individual schools rather than centrally, so the family should confirm against their own local authority. The Year 7 split of three-year KS3 content was checked against the White Rose Maths KS3 Year 7 scheme, the Oak National Academy Year 7 maths and science unit sequences, and several published school Year 7 curriculum maps for English and science; the KS3 programmes of study themselves are written for the whole key stage without year-by-year division, so this split is a well-evidenced convention rather than a statutory requirement, and a school following a different order is equally compliant. NOT VERIFIED and drawn from general subject knowledge: the specific pedagogical content of individual lessons, including the learning objectives, the key vocabulary lists, the common misconceptions at this age, and the assessment methods. These reflect standard secondary practice in England and standard subject-specific misconception research, but they were not checked against a named published scheme of work. Named literary texts in English (for example 'The Boy at the Back of the Class' and 'A Midsummer Night's Dream') are recommendations that satisfy the statutory requirements, not statutory choices, and any text of equivalent quality may be substituted. The specific factual content within lessons (dates, formulae, definitions, scientific values) reflects standard curriculum knowledge and has not been individually re-verified against a primary reference in every case, though it has been checked for internal consistency. Reproductive biology in the science Spring 2 unit is a statutory part of the KS3 science programme of study; a home educator may wish to preview those lessons and coordinate them with any relationships education taught separately.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, key stage 3 (DfE, September 2013; statutory from September 2014). Strands: Working mathematically (develop fluency, reason mathematically, solve problems); Number; Algebra; Ratio, proportion and rates of change; Geometry and measures; Probability; Statistics.
subjects.yearShare: Key stage 3 is a three-year programme. This Year 7 scheme covers the KS3 content usually taught first: sequences and algebraic notation, place value and rounding, fractions/decimals/percentages, the four operations, introductory ratio and proportion, area and volume, directed number, constructions and angle reasoning, straight-line graphs, probability and sets, primes and proof. It follows the sequence used by the White Rose Maths KS3 scheme and the Oak National Academy Year 7 units, both of which are widely used in England.

Simultaneous equations and inequalities as regions
Quadratic graphs and factorising quadratics
Compound units in depth (density, pressure, rates) and inverse proportion
Trigonometry in right-angled triangles
Circle theorems, similarity and congruence proofs
Scatter graphs, correlation and grouped data
Tree diagrams and combined probability

knowledgeComponents.statement: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers or shapes that follows a rule.
Each entry in a sequence is called a term.
To find a term-to-term rule, calculate the difference between consecutive terms and check the difference is the same each time.
A term-to-term rule must state an operation and a number, e.g. 'add 4', not just '4'.
Given a first term and a term-to-term rule, generate a sequence by applying the rule repeatedly.
A sequence with a constant difference between terms is called an arithmetic (linear) sequence.
An ascending sequence increases; a descending sequence decreases.
A pattern of shapes can be converted to a number sequence by counting a chosen feature in each pattern.
Predicting the next term requires the rule to be verified on at least three consecutive terms.
Place value in KS2: the digit's position gives its value; 4 in 0.04 has value four hundredths.

knowledgeComponents.statement: A geometric sequence has a constant multiplier between consecutive terms.
The square numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
The triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55.
In a Fibonacci-type sequence each term is the sum of the two previous terms.
To test whether a sequence is arithmetic, check the first differences are equal.
In a sequence table, position (n) goes in the top row and term value in the bottom row.
Plotting an arithmetic sequence as (position, term) gives points that lie in a straight line.
Coordinates are written (x, y) with x measured horizontally first.
A position-to-term rule gives any term directly from its position without listing earlier terms.
To find the nth term value from a rule such as 3n + 1, substitute the position number for n.
In the rule 3n + 1, the coefficient 3 equals the common difference of the sequence.

knowledgeComponents.statement: A function machine applies operations to an input in order to produce an output.
To reverse a function machine, apply the inverse operations in the reverse order.
The inverse of add is subtract; the inverse of multiply is divide.
ab means a multiplied by b; the multiplication sign is omitted in algebra.
3y means y + y + y, that is 3 multiplied by y.
a squared means a multiplied by a; a cubed means a x a x a.
a divided by b is written as the fraction a over b.
The number in front of a variable is called the coefficient.
By convention the number is written before the letter: 3y, not y3.
To substitute, replace each letter with its value and then calculate using the order of operations.
Order of operations: brackets, indices, division and multiplication, then addition and subtraction.
With a = 5, 3a = 15 and a squared = 25.

knowledgeComponents.statement: A letter in algebra stands for a number, not for an object.
'3 less than n' is written n - 3, not 3 - n.
'n more than a number' and 'the sum of' both mean addition.
A formula is a rule connecting two or more quantities, written with an equals sign.
The subject of a formula is the variable on its own on one side of the equals sign.
To change the subject, apply the same inverse operation to both sides of the formula.
Area of a rectangle = length x width.
An expression is a collection of terms with no equals sign.
An equation contains an equals sign and is true only for particular values.
An identity is true for every value of the variable, e.g. 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6.
A term is a single number, letter, or product of numbers and letters within an expression.

knowledgeComponents.statement: The equals sign means the expressions on both sides have the same value.
An equation stays balanced if the same operation is applied to both sides.
Two expressions are equivalent if they have the same value for every value of the variable.
To solve x + 7 = 12, subtract 7 from both sides to get x = 5.
To solve 4x = 20, divide both sides by 4 to get x = 5.
A solution can be checked by substituting it back into the original equation.
To solve 3x + 4 = 19, first subtract 4, then divide by 3.
When solving, undo the operations in the reverse of the order they were applied.
To form an equation from a word problem, name the unknown with a letter and translate each phrase in order.
x = 5 and 5 = x express exactly the same solution.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Like terms contain exactly the same letters raised to the same powers.
Only like terms can be added or subtracted; 3a + 2b cannot be simplified.
The sign in front of a term belongs to that term and travels with it.
a and a squared are not like terms.
3a x 4b = 12ab: multiply the numbers, then write the letters together.
a x a = a squared, not 2a.
6a divided by 2 = 3a.
To expand a bracket, multiply the term outside by every term inside.
A negative multiplier changes the sign of every term inside the bracket.

Factorised answers can be checked by expanding them back out.
To solve an equation with the unknown on both sides, first remove the smaller x-term from both sides.
The symbol > means 'is greater than'; < means 'is less than'.
'At least 5' means greater than or equal to 5, so 5 is included.
On a number line, an open circle excludes the value and a filled circle includes it.
An inequality can be read from either end: 3 < x is the same as x > 3.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Retrieval practice is more effective when topics are mixed rather than blocked.
Showing working allows method credit even when the final answer is wrong.
An arithmetic sequence has a constant first difference; a geometric sequence has a constant ratio.
Simplify by collecting like terms; expand by multiplying over the bracket; factorise by taking out the highest common factor.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Each column to the left in our number system is worth ten times the column to its right.
Zero holds a place so that other digits keep their value.
To compare integers, compare digits from the left, starting with the highest place value.
On a number line, numbers get smaller as you move left, so -8 < -3.
The first three decimal places are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
0.5 is greater than 0.45 because 5 tenths is greater than 4 tenths.
Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left.
The symbol < means less than and points to the smaller value.

knowledgeComponents.statement: To round, look only at the digit immediately to the right of the rounding place.
A digit of 5 or more rounds the previous digit up; 4 or less leaves it unchanged.
Rounding 4.97 to one decimal place gives 5.0, because the 9 rounds up into the units.
The first significant figure is the first non-zero digit reading from the left.
To estimate a calculation, round each number to one significant figure and calculate.
The symbol for 'approximately equal to' is a wavy equals sign.
Standard form is written A x 10 to the n where A is at least 1 and less than 10.
4,500,000 in standard form is 4.5 x 10 to the 6.

In a two-way table, the row and column totals must both add to the grand total.

Bar charts for categorical data are drawn with equal gaps between bars.

Mean = sum of all values divided by how many values there are.
The median is the middle value once the data are placed in order.
The mode is the most frequent value; a data set can have more than one mode or none.
Range = largest value minus smallest value, and measures spread, not average.
An outlier can pull the mean away from the bulk of the data, making the median more representative.

Volume of any prism = area of cross-section x length.
Surface area is the total area of all faces and is measured in square units.

1 cubic centimetre holds 1 millilitre.

knowledgeComponents.statement: Fractions can only be added or subtracted when they have the same denominator.
When adding fractions with the same denominator, add the numerators and keep the denominator.
A common denominator can be found using the lowest common multiple of the denominators.
A mixed number is converted to an improper fraction by multiplying the whole number by the denominator and adding the numerator.
When the fraction part of the first mixed number is too small to subtract from, regroup one whole into fraction parts.
To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.
No common denominator is needed for multiplication.
Mixed numbers must be converted to improper fractions before multiplying.

I can divide by a fraction using the reciprocal

knowledgeComponents.statement: The reciprocal of a fraction is found by swapping its numerator and denominator.
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
1/2 divided by 1/4 = 2, because there are two quarters in a half.
Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the result larger.
Dividing a fraction by an integer multiplies the denominator by that integer.
Choosing the most convenient form (fraction, decimal or percentage) reduces both effort and error.
Two successive percentage changes are combined by multiplying the multipliers, not by adding the percentages.
A final fraction answer should always be written in its simplest form.
Fraction operations are checked by estimating with nearby simple fractions.

lessons.title: Interleaved retrieval across the year so far

knowledgeComponents.statement: Every proportional problem can be represented by a bar model, a double number line or a ratio table.
A good strategy is chosen before calculating, not discovered mid-calculation.
Persisting after a failed approach and trying a different representation is part of problem solving.
Paint coverage problems combine area, division and rounding up.

Units must be converted to a common unit before quantities are combined.
Mathematical communication requires the reader to follow the argument without asking questions.
Retrieval should be weighted towards the components most recently forgotten.

terms.name: Summer 1

Measuring a reflex angle directly instead of subtracting from 360

lessons.title: Ruler and compass constructions

knowledgeComponents.statement: An acute angle is less than 90 degrees; a right angle is exactly 90; an obtuse angle is between 90 and 180; a reflex angle is between 180 and 360.
To measure an angle, place the protractor centre on the vertex and the zero line along one arm.
A reflex angle is measured by measuring the smaller angle and subtracting from 360 degrees.
Parallel lines are marked with matching arrows; equal sides are marked with matching hatch marks.
Perpendicular lines meet at 90 degrees, shown with a small square.
A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal.
A perpendicular bisector is constructed with two arcs of equal radius from each end of the segment.
An angle bisector is constructed by drawing an arc from the vertex, then equal arcs from where it cuts each arm.
Construction arcs must be left on the diagram as evidence of the method.
Every point on a perpendicular bisector is the same distance from both ends of the segment.

lessons.title: Perpendiculars from and at a point, and simple loci
objectives: I can construct a perpendicular from a point to a line and at a point on a line
I can describe the set of points that satisfy a simple condition

misconceptions: Measuring the shortest distance to a line along a slant rather than at a right angle
Drawing a locus as a set of points rather than a continuous line

assessment.detail: Three perpendicular constructions plus two locus problems set in a garden-plan context

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: draw shapes accurately with given dimensions

lessons.title: Scale drawings, bearings and maps
objectives: I can produce and interpret a scale drawing
I can measure and use a three-figure bearing
lessons.ncRef: Geometry and measures – interpret scale drawings; Ratio and proportion – use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps
misconceptions: Writing a bearing with fewer than three figures, e.g. 45 rather than 045
Measuring a bearing from the wrong reference line

assessment.detail: Draw a scale plan of a room; measure and state five bearings on a supplied map

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known

lessons.title: Constructing and interpreting pie charts
objectives: I can calculate the sector angle for each category and draw a pie chart accurately
I can interpret a pie chart, including comparing two charts of different total size

Rounding sector angles so they no longer total 360 degrees

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs

knowledgeComponents.statement: The shortest distance from a point to a line is measured perpendicular to the line.
A locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given condition.
The locus of points a fixed distance from a point is a circle.
A scale drawing keeps all angles the same and multiplies all lengths by the same scale factor.
A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures.
North is bearing 000 or 360, east is 090, south is 180 and west is 270.
A pie chart sector angle = (frequency divided by total frequency) x 360 degrees.
Pie chart sector angles must sum to 360 degrees.
A pie chart shows proportion, so equal sectors from different totals represent different frequencies.

lessons.title: Angles at a point and on a straight line
objectives: I can use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees
I can use the fact that angles at a point sum to 360 degrees
lessons.ncRef: Geometry and measures – apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles
misconceptions: Assuming a diagram is drawn to scale and measuring instead of calculating
Using 180 where 360 is required

assessment.detail: Ten missing-angle problems, each requiring the angle fact to be named in writing

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles

lessons.title: Vertically opposite angles and angle chains
objectives: I can identify vertically opposite angles and state that they are equal

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: find missing angles using vertically opposite angles

lessons.title: Angles in parallel lines

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise parallel lines; find missing angles

knowledgeComponents.statement: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees.
Angles around a point sum to 360 degrees.
A geometric answer must name the angle fact used as its reason.
Diagrams in geometry questions are not drawn to scale and must not be measured.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
A transversal is a line that crosses two or more other lines.
Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal and form an F shape.
Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal and form a Z shape.
Co-interior angles on parallel lines sum to 180 degrees and form a C shape.
Parallel-line angle rules apply only when the lines are marked parallel.

lessons.title: Angles in a triangle and why they sum to 180
objectives: I can use the fact that angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees
I can explain, using parallel lines, why this is always true
lessons.ncRef: Geometry and measures – derive and illustrate properties of triangles using appropriate language and technologies; derive and use the sum of angles in a triangle
misconceptions: Assuming an isosceles triangle's apex is always at the top
Treating the exterior angle as equal to the adjacent interior angle

knowledgeComponents.statement: The interior angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.
The 180 degree sum can be proved by drawing a line parallel to one side and using alternate angles.
An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60 degree angles.
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and the two angles opposite them are equal.
The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
The interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360 degrees.
A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides and opposite angles equal.
A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides and diagonals that bisect at right angles.
A square is a special rectangle and also a special rhombus.
A kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides and one pair of equal opposite angles.

lessons.title: Interior angles of a polygon

knowledgeComponents.statement: The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n - 2) x 180 degrees.
One interior angle of a regular n-sided polygon is (n - 2) x 180 divided by n.
A regular hexagon has interior angles of 120 degrees.
The exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360 degrees.
One exterior angle of a regular n-sided polygon is 360 divided by n.
An interior and its adjacent exterior angle sum to 180 degrees.
Only equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons tessellate on their own, because their interior angles divide exactly into 360.
Congruent shapes are identical in size and shape; similar shapes have the same shape but different size.
A rotation is described by centre, angle and direction.
A translation is described by a column vector giving movement right and up.
An enlargement is described by centre and scale factor.
The congruence criteria for triangles are SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS.

knowledgeComponents.statement: The diameter of a circle is twice its radius.
Circumference = pi x diameter, or 2 x pi x radius.
Area of a circle = pi x radius squared.
Pi is approximately 3.14 and is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter.
A chord joins two points on a circle; a tangent touches the circle at one point.
The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
Pythagoras' theorem: a squared + b squared = c squared, where c is the hypotenuse.
To find a shorter side, subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse.

The plan view is the view from directly above the solid.

lessons.title: Interleaved retrieval: geometry and measure

Angle facts, triangle properties and parallel-line rules are combined in multi-step problems.

Partitioning splits a number into place-value parts to make a calculation easier.
Multiplying by 25 is the same as multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4.
An estimate is made before calculating so it can act as a check.

Rounding up both numbers gives an over-estimate; rounding both down gives an under-estimate.
Addition and multiplication are commutative; subtraction and division are not.
The distributive law states a(b + c) = ab + ac.

lessons.title: Coordinates and plotting straight-line graphs

A line sloping down from left to right has a negative gradient.
The y-intercept is the point where the line crosses the y-axis, where x = 0.

I can explain why more trials give a better estimate of probability
lessons.ncRef: Probability – record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0-1 probability scale
misconceptions: Believing a run of heads makes tails 'due' next
Assuming a small sample proves a die is biased

assessment.detail: Conduct 100 trials with a possibly biased spinner; tabulate, graph relative frequency against number of trials and write a conclusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: interpret data in tables and line graphs

lessons.title: Probability problem solving
objectives: I can solve multi-step probability problems
I can use a Venn diagram or two-way table to organise probability information
lessons.ncRef: Probability – enumerate sets and combinations of sets systematically; generate theoretical sample spaces
misconceptions: Adding probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive

assessment.detail: Eight multi-step problems, three set in a Venn diagram context and two in a two-way table

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: two-way tables

knowledgeComponents.statement: A sample space lists every possible outcome of an experiment.
Two dice give 36 equally likely outcomes in total.
With two dice, a total of 7 is the most likely because it occurs in six of the 36 outcomes.
Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen at once.
Relative frequency = number of successful trials divided by total number of trials.
As the number of trials increases, relative frequency tends towards the theoretical probability.
Past outcomes of a fair random event do not affect the next outcome.
Probabilities of mutually exclusive events can be added; overlapping events cannot.
Organising data in a two-way table makes combined probabilities readable directly.

lessons.title: Factors, multiples and primes
objectives: I can list all factors of a number systematically
I can identify prime numbers and explain why 1 is not prime
lessons.ncRef: Number – use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple
misconceptions: Believing 1 is prime
Thinking all odd numbers are prime
Confusing factors with multiples

assessment.detail: List factors of twelve numbers in pairs; identify primes below 100 from a Sieve of Eratosthenes

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify multiples and factors, know prime numbers up to 19, establish whether a number up to 100 is prime

lessons.title: Prime factorisation, HCF and LCM
objectives: I can write a number as a product of its prime factors
I can find the HCF and LCM of two numbers using prime factorisation
lessons.ncRef: Number – use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation theorem
misconceptions: Stopping the factor tree before reaching primes
Mixing up HCF and LCM
Taking the highest power for HCF instead of the lowest

assessment.detail: Six factor trees; eight HCF and LCM problems including two in context such as bus timetables

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: common factors, common multiples, prime factors

lessons.title: Types of number and number classification
objectives: I can classify a number as integer, rational, prime, square, triangular or cube
I can describe the number sets we use and how they nest inside one another
lessons.ncRef: Number – appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, real and rational numbers
misconceptions: Thinking there is a largest number
Believing every decimal is rational

assessment.detail: Classify 20 numbers into a nested set diagram and justify four of the placements

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: number types and place value

knowledgeComponents.statement: A factor divides exactly into a number; a multiple is the result of multiplying by an integer.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
1 is not prime because it has only one factor.
2 is the only even prime number.
Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation.
To find the HCF from prime factors, multiply the common primes taken to the lowest power.
To find the LCM from prime factors, multiply every prime taken to its highest power.
An integer is a whole number, positive, negative or zero.
A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers.
The set of integers is infinite: there is no largest integer.

lessons.title: Conjecture, counter-example and proof
objectives: I can test a conjecture with examples and disprove it with a counter-example
I can explain the difference between showing and proving
lessons.ncRef: Working mathematically – reason mathematically by making and testing conjectures and by beginning to develop an argument, justification or proof using mathematical language
misconceptions: Believing that several examples constitute a proof
Thinking one counter-example is not enough to disprove

assessment.detail: Judge eight conjectures: prove, disprove with a counter-example, or state that more evidence is needed

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: reason mathematically about number properties

lessons.title: Algebraic proof with odd, even and consecutive numbers
objectives: I can represent an odd number, an even number and consecutive numbers algebraically
I can use algebra to prove a general number statement
lessons.ncRef: Working mathematically – begin to develop an argument, justification or proof using mathematical language; Algebra – simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions
misconceptions: Using n and n + 1 as two general even numbers
Verifying with numbers and calling that an algebraic proof

assessment.detail: Six proofs, e.g. 'the sum of three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3', assessed on generality and clarity

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: express missing number problems algebraically; number properties

lessons.title: Summer 2 assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding of number sense, graphs, probability and number theory
lessons.ncRef: Working mathematically – develop fluency, reason mathematically and solve problems
misconceptions: Neglecting the reasoning and proof questions because they carry no obvious method

assessment.detail: 55-minute paper on weeks 34–39 with cumulative items from the whole year

knowledgeComponents.statement: A conjecture is a statement believed to be true but not yet proved.
One counter-example is enough to disprove a general statement.
No number of examples can prove a general statement.
Any even number can be written as 2n where n is an integer.
Any odd number can be written as 2n + 1.
Three consecutive integers can be written n, n + 1, n + 2.
The sum n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1), so it is always a multiple of 3.
An algebraic proof must use a general representation, not particular numbers.
A proof ends with a statement of what has been shown.

weeks.unit: Year review and transition to Year 8

lessons.title: Whole-year interleaved retrieval
objectives: I can retrieve and apply content from every unit of Year 7
lessons.ncRef: Working mathematically – develop fluency and make connections across mathematical topics
misconceptions: Assuming forgotten content is lost rather than needing re-spacing

assessment.detail: 60 items sampled across all 39 weeks; results reset the spacing interval on every weak knowledge component

lessons.title: Year 7 extended investigation
objectives: I can carry out an extended mathematical investigation and communicate the result
lessons.ncRef: Working mathematically – model situations mathematically and express the results using a range of formal mathematical representations
misconceptions: Presenting results without explaining the method

assessment.detail: Two-lesson investigation with a written report: pose the question, gather data, represent it, generalise and justify

lessons.title: Looking ahead: what Year 8 builds on
objectives: I can name the Year 7 topics that Year 8 will extend
I can set targets for my own next steps
lessons.ncRef: Working mathematically – consolidate mathematical capability and prepare to extend it
misconceptions: Treating the end of the year as the end of a topic

assessment.detail: Map each Year 7 unit to its Year 8 successor (ratio to proportion and rates, equations to simultaneous equations, area to circles and prisms) and record three personal targets

knowledgeComponents.statement: Algebraic manipulation underpins equations, formulae, sequences and proof alike.
Proportional reasoning connects fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and scale.
Geometric reasoning always names a fact as a reason.
Statistics summarises data; probability predicts it.
An investigation report states the question, method, findings and justification.
Year 8 extends Year 7 ratio into direct and inverse proportion and compound units.
Year 8 extends linear equations into simultaneous equations and inequalities.
Spacing intervals lengthen only after a component has been recalled successfully.

subjects.name: English
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: English programmes of study, key stage 3 (DfE, September 2013; statutory from September 2014). Strands: Reading (develop an appreciation and love of reading; understand increasingly challenging texts; read critically); Writing (write accurately, fluently, effectively and at length; plan, draft, edit and proof-read); Grammar and vocabulary; Spoken English. Statutory requirements include two Shakespeare plays across KS3, seminal world literature, works from the English literary heritage both pre-1914 and contemporary, poetry since 1789, and the spelling and grammar of English appendices 1 and 2 to the KS1 and KS2 programmes.
subjects.yearShare: Year 7 covers the first Shakespeare play of the required two, one whole modern novel, pre-1914 non-fiction and prose, poetry since 1789 including the Romantics, and the full range of writing purposes. The second Shakespeare play, a pre-1914 novel and further world literature fall in Years 8 and 9.
deferredToY8Y9: The second required Shakespeare play
A whole pre-1914 novel (e.g. Dickens or Stevenson)
Seminal world literature in translation as a whole text
Extended comparative literature essays
19th-century non-fiction in depth
priorKnowledgeAssumed: Y6: read for pleasure across a wide range of genres, forms and authors; recommend books with reasons
Y6: draw inferences such as inferring characters' feelings, thoughts and motives, and justify inferences with evidence
Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions in and across a wide range of writing
Y6: discuss and evaluate how authors use language, including figurative language, considering the impact on the reader
Y6: identify how language, structure and presentation contribute to meaning; distinguish fact from opinion
Y6: summarise main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph; retrieve, record and present information from non-fiction
Y6: plan, draft, evaluate and edit writing; select appropriate grammar and vocabulary; describe settings, characters and atmosphere
Y6: use a wide range of devices to build cohesion within and across paragraphs; ensure consistent and correct use of tense

Y6 English appendix 2: subject and object; active and passive voice; relative clauses; modal verbs; subjunctive; cohesive devices; semi-colon, colon and dash; brackets, dashes and commas for parenthesis; punctuation of speech; apostrophes
Y5-Y6 English appendix 1: the statutory spelling word list; prefixes, suffixes, homophones, morphology and etymology
Y6: perform and read aloud their own compositions and poems learned by heart, using appropriate intonation, volume and movement
Y6: participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play, improvisations and debates

terms.name: Autumn 1
terms.focus: Origins: myths, legends and the storyteller's craft. Narrative reading and writing, with a KS2 grammar and spelling consolidation strand running through every week.
coreTexts: Greek myth retellings (Theseus and the Minotaur, Icarus, Persephone, Pandora)
Extracts from Beowulf in translation (Seamus Heaney or Michael Morpurgo retelling)
Arthurian legend: the sword in the stone and Gawain and the Green Knight (retelling)
A selection of creation myths from world cultures

weeks.unit: What is a story? Origins and the oral tradition

lessons.title: Where stories come from: myth, legend and the oral tradition
objectives: I can explain the difference between a myth, a legend and a folk tale
I can identify features of a story told aloud
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of fiction and non-fiction, including whole books, short stories, poems and plays with a wide coverage of genres, historical periods, forms and authors
misconceptions: Using 'myth' to mean simply 'something untrue'
Assuming every old story has a single author

assessment.type: baseline discussion and short written response
assessment.detail: Explain in one paragraph how myth, legend and folk tale differ, with an example of each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions across a wide range of writing
Y6: participate in discussion about books

lessons.title: Baseline reading and writing assessment
objectives: I can show my current reading comprehension and writing accuracy
I can identify the areas I most need to strengthen
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write accurately, fluently, effectively and at length for pleasure and information; Reading – understand increasingly challenging texts
misconceptions: Reading a baseline result as a verdict rather than a starting point

assessment.detail: Unseen prose extract with six comprehension questions (retrieval, inference, language) plus a 30-minute descriptive writing task; marked against a KS3 reading and writing rubric and mapped to KS2 objectives for routing back

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: draw inferences and justify with evidence
Y6: write for a range of purposes with grammatical accuracy

lessons.title: Sentence foundations: clauses and sentence types
objectives: I can identify a main clause and a subordinate clause
I can write simple, compound and complex sentences accurately
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – extend and apply the grammatical knowledge set out in English appendix 2 to the key stage 1 and 2 programmes of study to analyse more challenging texts
misconceptions: Calling a long sentence 'complex' because of its length rather than its structure
Using a comma to join two main clauses (the comma splice)

assessment.detail: Twelve identification items, then write one paragraph using each sentence type at least once

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: use of subordinate clauses; relative clauses; subject and object

knowledgeComponents.statement: A myth explains origins or natural phenomena and usually involves gods.
A legend is rooted in a real person or event but has been embellished over time.
Oral stories use repetition, formulaic phrases and pattern-of-three structures as memory aids.
An archetype is a recurring character type such as the hero, the mentor or the trickster.
A clause contains a verb; a main clause makes sense on its own.
A subordinate clause depends on a main clause and cannot stand alone.
A compound sentence joins two main clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
Two main clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; that error is a comma splice.
Inference means working out what a text implies but does not state.

lessons.title: Theseus and the Minotaur: plot, character and structure
objectives: I can summarise a myth accurately and in sequence
I can identify the stages of a hero's journey in a narrative
lessons.ncRef: Reading – understand increasingly challenging texts through knowing the purpose, audience for and context of the writing; study setting, plot and characterisation, and the effects of these
misconceptions: Retelling every detail instead of summarising the significant events
Confusing summary with analysis

assessment.detail: Write a 120-word summary sequencing the plot, then label the five stages of the hero's journey

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: summarise the main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph
Y6: identify how structure contributes to meaning

lessons.title: Writing to describe: setting the labyrinth
objectives: I can use precise nouns and verbs to create atmosphere
I can appeal to more than one of the five senses in description
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences, including well-structured formal expository and narrative essays; select and use appropriate vocabulary and grammar
misconceptions: Adding adjectives to weak nouns rather than choosing a stronger noun
Describing everything rather than selecting significant detail

assessment.detail: 250-word description of the labyrinth, assessed on vocabulary precision, sensory range and sentence variety

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: describe settings, characters and atmosphere; select vocabulary and grammatical structures for effect

lessons.title: Word class and precision vocabulary
objectives: I can identify the main word classes accurately
I can choose a more precise word using a thesaurus critically
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – extend and apply the grammatical knowledge set out in English appendix 2; consolidate and build on knowledge of vocabulary
misconceptions: Assuming a word has only one word class regardless of use
Choosing the longest synonym rather than the most accurate

assessment.detail: Label word classes in a supplied paragraph, then upgrade six weak word choices with justification

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: word classes and their functions; synonyms and antonyms

knowledgeComponents.statement: The protagonist is the central character; the antagonist opposes them.
A summary states the significant events in order, without minor detail or opinion.
The hero's journey typically moves from call, to trial, to ordeal, to reward, to return.
The climax is the point of highest tension; the resolution follows it.
A precise concrete noun does more descriptive work than an adjective attached to a vague noun.
Sensory description appeals to sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.
Atmosphere is the feeling a setting creates in the reader.
A noun names; a verb states action or being; an adjective modifies a noun; an adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
A word's class is determined by how it functions in the sentence, so 'run' can be a noun or a verb.
Connotation is the association a word carries beyond its literal meaning.

lessons.title: Icarus and Pandora: theme, warning and consequence
objectives: I can identify the theme of a myth
I can support a point about theme with a short embedded quotation
lessons.ncRef: Reading – identify and discuss themes and conventions; draw on knowledge of purpose and context; read critically by knowing how language presents meaning
misconceptions: Confusing theme with plot
Quoting a whole sentence when a phrase would be sharper

assessment.detail: One What-How-Why paragraph on a theme in Icarus, using two embedded quotations

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions
Y6: retrieve, record and present information; support inference with evidence

lessons.title: Writing an analytical paragraph: What, How, Why
objectives: I can structure an analytical paragraph with a point, evidence and explanation
I can zoom in on a single word and explain its effect
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays; support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail; apply growing knowledge of vocabulary and grammar
misconceptions: Retelling the story instead of analysing the writer's choices
Ending a paragraph at the quotation with no explanation

assessment.detail: Deconstruct a model paragraph, then write two independent paragraphs assessed against a paragraph rubric

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use organisational and presentational devices; write with a clear structure

lessons.title: Punctuation for accuracy: commas, apostrophes and speech
objectives: I can punctuate direct speech correctly
I can use apostrophes for omission and possession without error
lessons.ncRef: Writing – pay attention to accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling; Grammar and vocabulary – apply the grammatical knowledge in English appendix 2
misconceptions: Using an apostrophe for a plural (the greengrocer's apostrophe)
Confusing its and it's
Starting a new speaker's words on the same line

assessment.detail: Correct a passage containing 20 deliberate punctuation errors; then punctuate an unpunctuated dialogue

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: punctuation of speech; apostrophes for possession and contraction; commas for clarity

knowledgeComponents.statement: A theme is an idea a text explores, such as ambition or greed; a plot is what happens.
Hubris is excessive pride that leads a character to destruction.
An embedded quotation is woven into your own sentence and is kept as short as possible.
An analytical paragraph moves from point, to evidence, to explanation of effect.
A topic sentence states the point the paragraph will prove.
Tentative verbs such as 'suggests', 'implies' and 'conveys' show interpretation rather than assertion.
Direct speech is enclosed in inverted commas and a new speaker begins on a new line.
A comma, question mark or exclamation mark goes inside the closing inverted comma before a reporting clause.
'Its' shows possession; 'it's' is the contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'.
An apostrophe is never used to make a word plural.

lessons.title: Beowulf and Grendel: reading a pre-1914 heroic text
objectives: I can read and make sense of a challenging older text
I can explain how Grendel is presented as monstrous
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of fiction, including in particular whole books and works from the English literary heritage, both pre-1914 and contemporary; understand increasingly challenging texts
misconceptions: Giving up on an older text rather than reading for gist first
Assuming difficult vocabulary means the whole passage is inaccessible

assessment.detail: Annotate an extract for language that presents Grendel as monstrous; answer four inference questions

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: read books structured in different ways; check the meaning of words in context

lessons.title: Writing with Anglo-Saxon craft: kennings and alliteration
objectives: I can write kennings that compress meaning into two words
I can use alliteration deliberately for effect rather than decoration
lessons.ncRef: Writing – draw on knowledge of literary and rhetorical devices from their reading and listening to enhance the impact of their writing
misconceptions: Using alliteration so densely that meaning is lost
Treating a kenning as any two-word phrase

assessment.detail: Write ten kennings and a 12-line alliterative description of a monster in the Anglo-Saxon style

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use a range of devices to build cohesion; select vocabulary for effect

lessons.title: The history of English: where our words come from
objectives: I can explain that English has absorbed words from many languages
I can identify Old English, Latin, Norse and French roots in modern words
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – consolidate and build on knowledge of vocabulary; understand the differences between Standard English and other varieties
misconceptions: Believing English has always looked the way it does now
Thinking Latinate words are always 'better' than Anglo-Saxon ones

assessment.detail: Trace the etymology of ten common words using a dictionary; write a short paragraph on why English has so many synonyms

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use dictionaries to check word meanings; understand word families and roots

knowledgeComponents.statement: Beowulf is an Old English epic poem, the earliest long poem in English, composed around the 8th to 11th century.
An epic is a long narrative poem about a hero performing great deeds.
Reading for gist first, then rereading for detail, makes a difficult text manageable.
A kenning is a compressed two-word metaphor such as 'whale-road' for the sea.
Alliteration is the repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words.
Old English verse used alliteration rather than rhyme to bind each line.
English is a Germanic language with a large Latin, Norse and French vocabulary layered on top.
Etymology is the study of the origin and history of words.
Norman French entered English after 1066, which is why we have 'cow' (Old English) and 'beef' (French).
Anglo-Saxon words tend to be short and concrete; Latinate words tend to be longer and more formal.

lessons.title: King Arthur: legend, chivalry and the code of the knight
objectives: I can explain what chivalry meant and how it shapes the Arthurian legends
I can compare how two versions of the same legend differ
lessons.ncRef: Reading – make an informed personal response, recognising that others may respond differently; make inferences and refer to evidence; compare texts
misconceptions: Assuming there is one authoritative version of the Arthur story
Reading chivalry as identical to modern politeness

assessment.detail: Compare two retellings of the sword in the stone; write a paragraph on how the differences change the effect

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: make comparisons within and across books; distinguish between fact and opinion

lessons.title: Narrative writing: openings that hook the reader
objectives: I can write an opening that establishes atmosphere and raises a question
I can vary sentence length to control pace
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative and narrative texts; consider how their writing reflects the audiences and purposes for which it was intended
misconceptions: Beginning with weather or waking up because it is familiar
Front-loading all the background before anything happens

assessment.detail: Write three different openings for the same story and evaluate which is strongest and why

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: describe settings and atmosphere; use a wide range of devices to build cohesion

lessons.title: Spoken English: reading aloud and performing a story
objectives: I can read aloud with expression, pace and clear diction
I can use pause and emphasis to hold an audience
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – improvising, rehearsing and performing play scripts and poetry in order to generate language and discuss language use and meaning, using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness and action
misconceptions: Reading faster when nervous
Assuming volume alone equals good delivery

assessment.detail: Perform a 90-second extract from memory or from text; assessed on clarity, pace, expression and use of pause

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: perform their own compositions using appropriate intonation, volume and movement

knowledgeComponents.statement: Chivalry was the medieval knightly code of honour, courage, courtesy and loyalty.
The Arthurian legends exist in many versions, retold and altered across a thousand years.
An adaptation changes a story for a new audience, and those changes carry meaning.
'In medias res' means beginning a story in the middle of the action.
A short sentence after a long one creates emphasis and quickens pace.
An effective opening raises a question in the reader's mind.
Exposition is the background information a reader needs, best released gradually.
Diction is clarity of pronunciation; intonation is the rise and fall of the voice.
A deliberate pause before a key word gives it weight.

lessons.title: Creation myths from around the world
objectives: I can identify patterns shared by creation myths from different cultures
I can respond to a text from a culture unfamiliar to me with respect and curiosity
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of fiction and non-fiction including seminal world literature; make comparisons across texts
misconceptions: Judging an unfamiliar culture's story against one's own beliefs
Assuming similarity means one culture copied another

assessment.detail: Compare three creation myths for shared motifs; write a paragraph explaining one shared pattern

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions across a wide range of writing

lessons.title: Writing your own myth: planning and structure
objectives: I can plan a myth with a clear structure and purpose
I can use a five-part narrative structure
lessons.ncRef: Writing – plan, draft, edit and proof-read; write imaginative and narrative texts
misconceptions: Starting to write with no plan and losing structural control
Planning in such detail that the writing has no energy

assessment.detail: Produce a one-page plan for an original creation myth, with each structural stage labelled

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify the audience and purpose for writing; note and develop initial ideas

lessons.title: Spelling patterns and strategies
objectives: I can apply spelling rules for suffixes and plurals
I can use a strategy to learn a word I keep getting wrong
lessons.ncRef: Writing – pay attention to accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling, drawing on the spelling patterns and rules set out in English appendix 1 to the key stage 1 and 2 programmes of study
misconceptions: Relying on 'sounding out' for words with irregular spelling
Assuming spellcheck removes the need to learn spellings

assessment.detail: Weekly 20-word test drawn from the Y5–Y6 statutory word list plus subject vocabulary; misspellings enter a personal error log for spaced retesting

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6 English appendix 1: statutory spelling word list; prefixes, suffixes and homophones

knowledgeComponents.statement: A creation myth explains how the world or humanity began.
A motif is a recurring image or idea across texts, such as water, darkness or a first ancestor.
Similar motifs across unrelated cultures can arise independently from shared human experience.
Freytag's five-part structure is exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
A plan fixes structure before drafting so the writer can concentrate on language.
A prefix is added to the start of a root word and changes its meaning; a suffix is added to the end.
Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things.
Words ending in a consonant plus y change the y to i before most suffixes.
Knowing a word's root and morphology often unlocks its spelling and its meaning.

lessons.title: Drafting an original myth
objectives: I can turn my plan into a full first draft
I can sustain a consistent narrative voice and tense
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative and narrative texts; plan, draft, edit and proof-read
misconceptions: Slipping between past and present tense mid-narrative
Switching narrative person without intent

assessment.detail: 600–800 word first draft of an original creation myth

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: ensure consistent and correct use of tense throughout a piece of writing

lessons.title: Editing and redrafting for impact
objectives: I can improve my writing by cutting, replacing and reordering
I can proof-read for accuracy separately from editing for effect
lessons.ncRef: Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing to improve its coherence and overall effectiveness; pay attention to accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling
misconceptions: Treating editing as only correcting spelling
Adding words to improve rather than cutting

assessment.detail: Produce a redraft plus a short commentary naming three deliberate improvements and their effect

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: propose changes to vocabulary, grammar and punctuation to enhance effects and clarify meaning; proof-read for spelling and punctuation errors

lessons.title: Standard English and register
objectives: I can explain what Standard English is and when it is expected
I can adjust register for a formal or informal audience
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – know the differences between spoken and written language, including differences associated with formal and informal registers, and between Standard English and other varieties of English; use Standard English confidently in their own writing and speech
misconceptions: Believing a regional dialect is 'incorrect' English
Confusing accent (pronunciation) with dialect (vocabulary and grammar)

assessment.detail: Rewrite the same message three times for three audiences; label the register features used in each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: recognise vocabulary and structures appropriate for formal speech and writing

knowledgeComponents.statement: Tense must remain consistent across a piece of writing unless a shift is deliberate.
First person narrates as 'I'; third person narrates as 'he', 'she' or 'they'.
An omniscient narrator knows the thoughts of every character.
Editing improves effect; proof-reading corrects accuracy; they are separate passes.
Cutting is usually a stronger edit than adding.
Cohesion is the linking of ideas within and between paragraphs.
Standard English is the variety used in formal writing and public communication; it is not more logical than other varieties, only more widely expected.
Accent is how words are pronounced; dialect is the vocabulary and grammar used.
Register is the level of formality chosen to match audience and purpose.

lessons.title: Autumn 1 reading assessment
objectives: I can analyse an unseen extract and support my points with evidence
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how language, including figurative language, vocabulary choice, grammar, text structure and organisational features, presents meaning
misconceptions: Feature-spotting devices without explaining their effect

assessment.detail: Unseen myth or legend extract with a 45-minute analytical response: how does the writer present the character?

lessons.title: Autumn 1 writing assessment: final myth
objectives: I can produce a polished piece of narrative writing
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write accurately, fluently, effectively and at length; write imaginative and narrative texts
misconceptions: Writing at length without shaping structure

assessment.detail: Final publishable version of the original myth, marked on content and organisation, and on technical accuracy

lessons.title: Feedback, retrieval and target setting
objectives: I can act on feedback to improve a specific piece of writing
I can recall the key terminology from this half term
lessons.ncRef: Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing to improve its coherence and overall effectiveness
misconceptions: Reading feedback without acting on it

assessment.detail: 25-item terminology retrieval quiz; then a directed rewrite of one paragraph in response to feedback

knowledgeComponents.statement: Naming a device without explaining its effect earns no credit in analysis.
A response to an unseen text should begin with a clear line of argument about the whole extract.
Structure in narrative writing carries as much weight as vocabulary.
Key Autumn 1 terminology: myth, legend, archetype, theme, kenning, alliteration, register, Standard English.
Feedback only improves work when it is acted on in a specific rewrite.
Analysis moves from what the writer does, to how, to why it affects the reader.
Accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar is assessed separately from content in most writing rubrics.
A personal error log turns repeated mistakes into targeted revision.

terms.name: Autumn 2
terms.focus: Whole-novel study: reading a complete modern novel for meaning, character and theme, and writing sustained analytical responses.
coreTexts: Primary novel: 'The Boy at the Back of the Class' by Onjali Q. Raúf (alternatives of equal quality: 'Skellig' by David Almond, 'The Explorer' by Katherine Rundell, 'Wonder' by R. J. Palacio)
Supporting non-fiction: short factual articles on refugee journeys for contextual reading
terms.note: The National Curriculum requires whole books, not extracts. Read the novel in full across the half term, roughly two to three chapters per week alongside the taught lessons.

lessons.title: Opening chapters: narrative voice and first impressions
objectives: I can describe the narrator's voice and how it is created
I can form a first impression of a character and support it with evidence
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read whole books; study setting, plot and characterisation and the effects of these; make inferences and refer to evidence in the text
misconceptions: Confusing the narrator with the author
Assuming a child narrator is unreliable simply because they are a child

assessment.detail: Annotate the opening two pages for voice; write 150 words on first impressions of the narrator with two quotations

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: draw inferences such as inferring characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions, and justify inferences with evidence

lessons.title: Reading journal: recording as you read
objectives: I can keep a reading journal that tracks character, theme and questions
I can select quotations worth returning to
lessons.ncRef: Reading – check their understanding to make sense of what they read; Writing – note and develop ideas
misconceptions: Copying long passages instead of selecting a short telling phrase

assessment.detail: Weekly journal entry: three quotations with a note on each, one prediction and one question; reviewed each Friday

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: retrieve, record and present information from non-fiction; participate in discussions about books

lessons.title: Grammar: subject, object and the passive voice
objectives: I can identify the subject and object of a sentence
I can change a sentence between active and passive voice and explain the effect
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – extend and apply the grammatical knowledge set out in English appendix 2 to analyse more challenging texts
misconceptions: Thinking the passive voice is always wrong
Identifying the first noun in a sentence as the subject regardless of structure

assessment.detail: Transform ten sentences between voices; then explain why a writer chose the passive in a supplied news headline

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: use of the passive to affect the presentation of information in a sentence; subject and object

knowledgeComponents.statement: The narrator is the voice telling the story; the author is the person who wrote it.
Narrative voice is created by vocabulary choice, sentence structure and what the narrator notices.
A first impression must be supported by a quotation, not asserted.
A short telling phrase is more useful in analysis than a long quotation.
A reading journal tracks character development, themes, predictions and questions.
The subject performs the verb; the object receives it.
In the passive voice the object becomes the subject, and the agent may be omitted.
The passive voice can hide responsibility, which makes it a deliberate choice in news writing.
'The window was broken' is passive; 'Sam broke the window' is active.

lessons.title: How writers build character
objectives: I can explain the methods a writer uses to present a character
I can trace how a character changes across the novel so far
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study setting, plot and characterisation, and the effects of these; read critically by knowing how language presents meaning
misconceptions: Describing what a character does instead of how they are presented
Assuming a character's stated opinion is the author's

assessment.detail: One analytical paragraph on characterisation, using the What-How-Why structure and two embedded quotations

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: infer characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions

lessons.title: Writing in role: a diary entry
objectives: I can write in a character's voice, sustaining their register and viewpoint
I can show a character's feelings without stating them directly
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative texts; select and use appropriate vocabulary and grammar for audience and purpose
misconceptions: Writing in one's own voice with the character's name attached
Stating emotion directly rather than implying it

assessment.detail: 400-word diary entry in role, assessed on consistency of voice and on implication rather than statement

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: select appropriate grammar and vocabulary, understanding how such choices can change and enhance meaning

lessons.title: Vocabulary: precision words for character and emotion
objectives: I can use precise vocabulary to describe character and feeling
I can distinguish between words with similar meanings but different connotations
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – consolidate and build on knowledge of vocabulary; use new vocabulary from their reading in their writing and speech
misconceptions: Treating synonyms as interchangeable
Using a sophisticated word without checking its exact meaning

assessment.detail: Place fifteen near-synonyms on a scale of intensity and use six of them correctly in original sentences

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use thesauruses; understand synonyms and antonyms

knowledgeComponents.statement: Characterisation is the set of methods a writer uses to build a character.
Direct characterisation tells the reader about a character; indirect characterisation shows through speech, action and reaction.
A character arc is the change a character undergoes across a narrative.
A character's view is not necessarily the author's view.
'Show, do not tell' means implying emotion through detail and action.
Writing in role requires the character's vocabulary, not the writer's.
Denotation is a word's literal meaning; connotation is its associated feeling.
A semantic field is a group of words linked by a shared area of meaning.
Near-synonyms differ in intensity: 'annoyed', 'angry' and 'furious' are not interchangeable.

lessons.title: Setting and its effect on meaning
objectives: I can explain how setting shapes mood and the reader's response
I can link setting to a theme in the novel
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study setting, plot and characterisation and the effects of these; knowing the purpose, audience for and context of the writing
misconceptions: Treating setting as background scenery with no function
Reading symbols into every detail

assessment.detail: One paragraph linking a specific setting to a theme, with textual evidence

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss how authors use language, including figurative language, considering the impact on the reader

lessons.title: Reading non-fiction context: refugee journeys
objectives: I can retrieve and summarise information from a factual article
I can distinguish fact from opinion
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of non-fiction; understand the purpose, audience for and context of writing; Writing – support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail
misconceptions: Treating an emotive article as neutral reporting
Assuming a statistic in a text is automatically reliable

assessment.detail: Retrieve five facts from two articles; identify three opinions and comment on the writer's likely purpose

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: distinguish between statements of fact and opinion; retrieve, record and present information from non-fiction

lessons.title: Grammar: cohesion across paragraphs
objectives: I can link paragraphs with a range of cohesive devices
I can vary paragraph openings to guide the reader
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – study the effectiveness and impact of the grammatical features of the texts they read; Writing – amend the structure of their writing to improve coherence
misconceptions: Using 'firstly, secondly, finally' as the only cohesive device
Starting every paragraph with the same subject

assessment.detail: Improve the cohesion of a supplied three-paragraph response and annotate each change

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: linking ideas across paragraphs using a wider range of cohesive devices

knowledgeComponents.statement: Setting can create mood, reveal character and carry thematic weight.
Juxtaposition places two contrasting things side by side to sharpen both.
A symbol is an object that stands for an idea beyond itself.
A fact can be verified; an opinion is a judgement.
Bias is a slant towards one view, shown through selection of detail and word choice.
A refugee is a person forced to leave their country to escape war, persecution or disaster.
Cohesive devices include adverbials, pronoun reference, repetition and conjunctions.
A topic sentence at the start of a paragraph signals its content to the reader.
Varying paragraph openings prevents monotony and clarifies the line of argument.

lessons.title: Tracing a theme across the whole novel
objectives: I can identify a theme and trace how it develops from beginning to end
I can select evidence from different parts of the book
lessons.ncRef: Reading – identify and discuss themes and conventions in and across a wide range of writing; read whole books
misconceptions: Selecting all evidence from one chapter
Confusing a topic (friendship) with a theme (friendship can outweigh fear)

assessment.detail: Complete a theme tracker with five quotations from across the novel and a sentence of analysis for each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions across a wide range of writing

lessons.title: Planning a multi-paragraph essay
objectives: I can plan an essay with a clear line of argument
I can order my paragraphs so the argument builds
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays; plan and draft; support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail
misconceptions: Planning a list of points with no argument connecting them
Saving the strongest point for a conclusion that never gets written

assessment.detail: Produce an essay plan: thesis statement, three topic sentences, evidence for each, and a conclusion in one sentence

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use organisational and presentational devices to structure text

lessons.title: Spoken English: seminar discussion about the novel
objectives: I can contribute to a discussion and build on what others say
I can disagree politely and support my view with evidence
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – participating in formal debates and structured discussions, summarising and/or building on what has been said; speak confidently and effectively
misconceptions: Treating discussion as taking turns to state prepared views
Equating disagreement with rudeness

assessment.detail: 20-minute seminar on a set question; assessed on contribution, building on others, use of textual evidence and summarising

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play and debates; use spoken language to explore ideas

knowledgeComponents.statement: A theme is an idea a text argues about, not just a topic it mentions.
Whole-text analysis draws evidence from the beginning, middle and end.
A motif is a recurring image that supports a theme.
A thesis statement is the single argument the whole essay proves.
Each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence that advances the thesis.
An essay conclusion restates the argument in the light of the evidence, adding no new evidence.
Building on a contribution means naming the speaker's point before adding to it.
Polite disagreement concedes what is right in the other view before challenging it.
A discussion contribution is stronger when anchored to a specific moment in the text.

lessons.title: Figurative language and its effects
objectives: I can identify simile, metaphor and personification
I can explain the effect of an image rather than only naming the device
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how language, including figurative language, vocabulary choice, grammar, text structure and organisational features, presents meaning
misconceptions: Naming the device and stopping there
Calling every comparison a metaphor

assessment.detail: Analyse three images from the novel: identify, explain the comparison, and explain what the reader is made to feel

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss and evaluate how authors use language, including figurative language, considering the impact on the reader

lessons.title: Structural features and how a writer controls the reader
objectives: I can comment on how a text is structured
I can explain how a shift in focus affects the reader
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how text structure and organisational features present meaning; study the effects of plot and structure
misconceptions: Treating 'structure' as paragraph count
Describing what happens rather than how it is ordered

assessment.detail: Map the structure of one chapter: openings, shifts, ending, and explain one deliberate structural choice

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how language, structure and presentation contribute to meaning

lessons.title: Punctuation for effect: colons, semi-colons and dashes
objectives: I can use a colon and a semi-colon correctly
I can use a dash or brackets for parenthesis
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – extend and apply grammatical knowledge from English appendix 2; Writing – pay attention to accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling
misconceptions: Using a semi-colon where a comma is required
Using a colon to introduce anything rather than an explanation or a list

assessment.detail: Fifteen punctuation choices, then write a paragraph using a colon, a semi-colon and a parenthesis accurately

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: use of the semi-colon, colon and dash to mark the boundary between independent clauses; use of brackets, dashes or commas for parenthesis

knowledgeComponents.statement: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing is another.
Personification gives human qualities to something non-human.
Analysing an image means explaining what the comparison makes the reader picture or feel.
An extended metaphor is developed across several lines or a whole passage.
Structure covers what the writer puts first, what shifts, and what is withheld.
Foreshadowing plants a hint of a later event.
A colon introduces an explanation, a list or an example that follows from the clause before it.
A semi-colon joins two closely related independent clauses.
Parenthesis is extra information marked off by a pair of commas, dashes or brackets.

lessons.title: Writing the novel essay: introduction and first body paragraph
objectives: I can write an introduction that states a clear argument
I can write a body paragraph that proves part of that argument
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write well-structured formal expository and narrative essays; apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar and text structure
misconceptions: Opening with a plot summary
Repeating the question as an introduction

assessment.detail: Write an introduction and one body paragraph under timed conditions; peer and self assessment against the rubric

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: write for a range of purposes with a clear structure

lessons.title: Completing the essay and writing a conclusion
objectives: I can sustain an argument across several paragraphs
I can write a conclusion that answers the question
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write accurately, fluently, effectively and at length; amend the structure of their writing to improve coherence
misconceptions: Introducing a new argument in the conclusion
Losing sight of the question by the third paragraph

assessment.detail: Complete a four-paragraph essay of around 600 words on a set question about the novel

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use a wide range of devices to build cohesion within and across paragraphs

lessons.title: Independent reading and reading for pleasure
objectives: I can choose a book independently and explain my choice
I can talk about what I am reading with reasons
lessons.ncRef: Reading – develop an appreciation and love of reading; choosing and reading books independently for challenge, interest and enjoyment; re-reading books encountered earlier
misconceptions: Choosing only books already known to be easy
Abandoning a book at the first difficulty

assessment.detail: Two-minute spoken recommendation of an independently chosen book, with reasons and one read-aloud extract

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: read for pleasure; recommend books to their peers, giving reasons for their choices

knowledgeComponents.statement: An essay introduction states the argument, not the plot.
Each body paragraph proves one part of the overall argument.
A link sentence at the end of a paragraph returns to the question.
A conclusion offers a judgement based on the evidence already presented.
Coherence means the reader can follow the argument from first sentence to last.
Volume of reading is the strongest single predictor of vocabulary growth.
A book recommendation gives the genre, a hook and a reason, without spoiling the ending.
Re-reading a text reveals patterns invisible on a first reading.

lessons.title: Autumn 2 reading assessment: the whole novel
objectives: I can write a sustained analytical essay about a whole text
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read whole books; read critically; make comparisons within a text; Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays
misconceptions: Writing about only the part of the novel most recently read

assessment.detail: 60-minute essay: how does the writer present [character or theme] across the novel? Marked against a KS3 reading rubric

lessons.title: Autumn 2 writing assessment: transactional writing
objectives: I can write for a real audience and purpose with an appropriate register
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences, including letters; select and use appropriate vocabulary and grammar
misconceptions: Using an informal register in a formal letter
Ignoring the conventions of the form

assessment.detail: Formal letter linked thematically to the novel, marked on content and organisation and on technical accuracy

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: write for a range of purposes and audiences; select the appropriate form

lessons.title: Feedback, retrieval and half-term review
objectives: I can act on my essay feedback
I can recall the terminology and grammar of this half term
lessons.ncRef: Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing to improve coherence and overall effectiveness
misconceptions: Rewriting the whole essay rather than targeting the identified weakness

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz covering weeks 1–14; a directed rewrite of the weakest paragraph

knowledgeComponents.statement: A whole-text essay draws on the beginning, development and ending of the novel.
A formal letter uses Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully, and Dear Mr Smith with Yours sincerely.
Register must match audience and purpose throughout, not only in the opening.
