Key Autumn 2 terminology: narrative voice, characterisation, motif, cohesion, passive voice, semi-colon, thesis.
Directed improvement targets one identified weakness rather than rewriting everything.
Analysis of a whole novel is stronger when it explains why an author sequenced events as they did.
A response that names devices but does not answer the question cannot reach the higher bands.
Technical accuracy is assessed on spelling, punctuation, grammar and sentence variety.

terms.name: Spring 1
terms.focus: Non-fiction, rhetoric and argument: reading viewpoint writing across time and writing to persuade, argue and inform.
coreTexts: Victorian non-fiction and social reporting: extracts from Henry Mayhew's 'London Labour and the London Poor'; a Charles Dickens journalism extract; a Lord Shaftesbury factory speech
Modern viewpoint writing and speeches: Malala Yousafzai's UN address (2013); a Greta Thunberg speech; a David Attenborough address on the natural world
Contemporary opinion columns and news reports on a shared topic, for comparison

weeks.unit: Reading non-fiction: purpose, audience and viewpoint

lessons.title: Purpose, audience and form in non-fiction
objectives: I can identify the purpose, audience and form of a non-fiction text
I can explain how a writer's purpose shapes their choices
lessons.ncRef: Reading – understand increasingly challenging texts through knowing the purpose, audience for and context of the writing and drawing on this knowledge to support comprehension
misconceptions: Assuming a text has only one purpose
Confusing form (article, speech, letter) with purpose

assessment.detail: Identify purpose, audience and form for six short texts and justify each with one textual feature

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify the audience for and purpose of writing; distinguish fact from opinion

lessons.title: Victorian London: reading Mayhew and Dickens
objectives: I can read and understand a pre-1914 non-fiction text
I can explain how a Victorian writer conveys the conditions he describes
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of non-fiction, including works from the English literary heritage, both pre-1914 and contemporary; understand increasingly challenging texts
misconceptions: Assuming archaic vocabulary makes the whole text unreadable
Reading Victorian social reporting as fiction

assessment.detail: Annotate a Mayhew extract for how the subject's own words are used; answer four inference questions

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: read books structured in different ways; check meaning of unfamiliar words in context

lessons.title: Grammar: modal verbs, conditionals and degrees of certainty
objectives: I can use modal verbs to express degrees of certainty and obligation
I can analyse how a writer uses modality to shape a reader's response
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – extend and apply the grammatical knowledge set out in English appendix 2; study the effectiveness and impact of grammatical features of the texts they read
misconceptions: Treating 'must' and 'might' as interchangeable
Missing that modality is a persuasive choice

assessment.detail: Grade ten modal verbs on a certainty scale; analyse the modality of two sentences from a Victorian reform speech

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: use of modal verbs or adverbs to indicate degrees of possibility

knowledgeComponents.statement: The four common non-fiction purposes are to inform, persuade, argue and advise.
Form is the type of text; purpose is what it is trying to do.
A text can have more than one purpose at once.
Henry Mayhew recorded the words of London's poor in 'London Labour and the London Poor', published from 1851.
Victorian social reporting used first-hand testimony to argue for reform.
A workhouse was an institution where the destitute were housed in return for labour.
Modal verbs include can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would and must.
'Must' expresses high obligation; 'might' expresses low possibility.
A writer's choice of modality controls how certain their claim sounds.

lessons.title: Ethos, pathos and logos
objectives: I can identify appeals to character, emotion and reason in a speech
I can explain which appeal a speaker relies on most and why
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how language, including figurative language, vocabulary choice, grammar, text structure and organisational features, presents meaning
misconceptions: Labelling every emotional sentence as pathos without explaining its function
Assuming logos means only statistics

assessment.detail: Annotate Malala's UN speech for ethos, pathos and logos; write a paragraph on the dominant appeal

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how language contributes to meaning; distinguish fact from opinion

lessons.title: Rhetorical devices and their effects
objectives: I can identify anaphora, tricolon, rhetorical question, direct address and antithesis
I can explain the effect of a device on a listening audience
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how language presents meaning; understanding how the work of dramatists and other writers is communicated effectively
misconceptions: Listing devices without linking them to the speaker's purpose
Confusing anaphora with any repetition

assessment.detail: Identify six devices in a supplied speech and write one sentence on the effect of each on the audience

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss and evaluate how authors use language, considering the impact on the reader

lessons.title: Comparing two viewpoints on the same issue
objectives: I can compare how two writers present the same subject differently
I can use comparative connectives to structure a comparison
lessons.ncRef: Reading – make comparisons within and across texts; Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays
misconceptions: Writing about text A then text B with no comparison
Comparing the topics rather than the writers' methods

assessment.detail: Two-paragraph comparison of a Victorian and a modern text on child welfare, using integrated comparison

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: make comparisons within and across books

knowledgeComponents.statement: Rhetoric is the art of persuasive speaking and writing.
Ethos appeals to the speaker's credibility and character.
Pathos appeals to the audience's emotions.
Logos appeals to reason, evidence and logic.
Anaphora is the repetition of the same words at the start of successive clauses.
A tricolon is a group of three, which sounds complete and memorable.
Antithesis places contrasting ideas in parallel structures.
A rhetorical question invites agreement rather than an answer.
Integrated comparison discusses both texts within the same paragraph.
Comparative connectives include 'whereas', 'similarly', 'in contrast' and 'by comparison'.

lessons.title: Building an argument: claim, evidence, counter-argument
objectives: I can construct an argument with a clear claim and supporting evidence
I can acknowledge and answer a counter-argument
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences, including arguments; support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail
misconceptions: Ignoring the opposing view entirely
Stating the counter-argument without rebutting it

assessment.detail: Plan an argument with three claims, evidence for each, and one counter-argument with rebuttal; write the rebuttal paragraph in full

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: write for a range of purposes; support opinions with reasons

lessons.title: Writing a persuasive speech
objectives: I can write a speech that uses rhetorical devices purposefully
I can shape a speech for the ear rather than the eye
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences, including notes and polished scripts for talks and presentations; draw on knowledge of literary and rhetorical devices from their reading
misconceptions: Writing an essay and calling it a speech
Overloading with devices so the argument disappears

assessment.detail: 500-word persuasive speech on an issue of the pupil's choice, assessed on argument, rhetoric and adaptation to a listening audience

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: select the appropriate form and use other similar writing as models; use devices for effect

lessons.title: Sentence variety and rhetorical impact
objectives: I can vary sentence structure deliberately for rhetorical effect
I can use a minor sentence or a very short sentence for emphasis
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – study the effectiveness and impact of the grammatical features of the texts they read; drawing on new vocabulary and grammatical constructions from their reading and listening
misconceptions: Using sentence fragments accidentally rather than deliberately
Believing longer sentences are always more sophisticated

assessment.detail: Rewrite a flat paragraph three ways using different sentence patterns; annotate the effect of each version

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: use of a wide range of sentence structures for effect

knowledgeComponents.statement: An argument has a claim, evidence and reasoning that connects them.
A counter-argument states the opposing view fairly before it is answered.
A rebuttal explains why the opposing view is weaker, not simply that it is wrong.
Addressing a counter-argument makes a case more persuasive, not less.
A speech ends with a call to action telling the audience what to do.
Writing for the ear favours shorter clauses, repetition and clear signposting.
A minor sentence lacks a main verb and is used deliberately for emphasis.
Varying sentence length controls pace and directs emphasis.
Sentence variety is a deliberate craft choice, not accidental variation.

lessons.title: Writing an informative article
objectives: I can write a clear, well-organised article for a real audience
I can use headings, subheadings and paragraphing to aid the reader
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences; apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar and text structure
misconceptions: Confusing an informative article with a persuasive one
Adding headings that do not summarise the section

assessment.detail: 500-word informative article with headline, standfirst and subheadings on a researched topic

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use organisational and presentational devices to structure text and guide the reader

lessons.title: Research, sourcing and avoiding plagiarism
objectives: I can find and evaluate sources for a piece of writing
I can put information into my own words and acknowledge my sources
lessons.ncRef: Writing – draw on their reading, support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail; Reading – read a wide range of non-fiction
misconceptions: Treating the first search result as authoritative
Changing a few words and calling it a paraphrase

assessment.detail: Gather four sources on one topic, rank them for reliability with reasons, and paraphrase one passage correctly

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: retrieve, record and present information from non-fiction; distinguish fact from opinion

lessons.title: Spoken English: delivering a formal presentation
objectives: I can deliver a prepared presentation clearly to an audience
I can respond to questions about my presentation
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – giving short speeches and presentations, expressing their own ideas and keeping to the point; speak confidently and effectively, using Standard English
misconceptions: Reading a script word for word
Preparing content but not rehearsing delivery

assessment.detail: Three-minute presentation from cue cards with two minutes of questions; assessed on clarity, structure, delivery and response to questions

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: give well-structured descriptions, explanations and narratives; participate in presentations

knowledgeComponents.statement: An informative article prioritises clarity and accuracy over opinion.
The lead paragraph of an article answers who, what, where and when.
A subheading summarises the section that follows it.
A reliable source names its author, its date and its evidence.
A primary source is first-hand; a secondary source comments on primary material.
Paraphrasing means restating an idea fully in your own sentence structure and words.
Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own.
Cue cards carry prompts, not full sentences, so delivery stays natural.
Eye contact and pacing matter as much to a listener as the content.

lessons.title: How language creates power
objectives: I can explain how word choice can include or exclude a reader
I can identify emotive and loaded language in a text
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how vocabulary choice and grammar present meaning; Grammar and vocabulary – understand the differences between Standard English and other varieties
misconceptions: Assuming emotive language is dishonest by definition
Missing that jargon can exclude as effectively as insult

assessment.detail: Analyse two headlines on the same story for framing; rewrite one to reverse its slant

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss how authors use language, considering the impact on the reader; distinguish fact from opinion

lessons.title: Reading and writing about a live issue
objectives: I can synthesise information from more than one source
I can write a balanced response that reaches a judgement
lessons.ncRef: Reading – make comparisons across texts; Writing – support ideas and arguments with necessary factual detail; write well-structured formal essays
misconceptions: Presenting both sides but never reaching a judgement
Synthesis reduced to summarising each source in turn

assessment.detail: 400-word balanced response drawing on three sources, ending with a justified judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: retrieve and present information from non-fiction; make comparisons across texts

lessons.title: Vocabulary: academic and subject-specific words
objectives: I can use tier-two academic vocabulary accurately in my writing
I can work out an unfamiliar word from its root and context
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – consolidate and build on knowledge of vocabulary; use new vocabulary from their reading and listening in their own writing and speech
misconceptions: Using an impressive word slightly wrongly
Relying on context alone when the root would give the meaning

assessment.detail: Twenty academic words defined and used correctly in sentences; five unfamiliar words decoded from roots

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use knowledge of morphology and etymology in spelling and understanding of words

knowledgeComponents.statement: Emotive language is chosen to provoke a feeling in the reader.
A euphemism substitutes a mild expression for a harsh one.
Framing is the choice of what to foreground and what to leave out.
Jargon is specialist vocabulary that can exclude non-specialist readers.
Synthesis combines information from several sources into a single argument.
A balanced response weighs evidence and still reaches a conclusion.
Tier-two vocabulary is the general academic vocabulary that appears across subjects.
Knowing that 'bene' means good and 'mal' means bad unlocks many English words.
A new word is secure only when it can be used correctly in an original sentence.

lessons.title: Spring 1 reading assessment: unseen non-fiction
objectives: I can analyse and compare unseen non-fiction texts
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically; make comparisons across texts; understand purpose, audience and context
misconceptions: Comparing content rather than the writers' methods

assessment.detail: Two unseen texts on one topic, one pre-1914 and one modern; 55-minute paper with a language question and a comparison question

lessons.title: Spring 1 writing assessment: viewpoint writing
objectives: I can write a persuasive or argumentative text with a clear viewpoint
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences including arguments and speeches; draw on rhetorical devices from their reading
misconceptions: Beginning to write before deciding on a line of argument

assessment.detail: 45-minute viewpoint writing task with a stated form, audience and purpose

lessons.title: Feedback, retrieval and debate preparation
objectives: I can act on feedback from both assessments
I can prepare a case for a formal debate
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – participating in formal debates and structured discussions; Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing
misconceptions: Preparing only one's own case and not anticipating the other side

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz on rhetorical and grammatical terminology; produce a debate case with three arguments and two anticipated rebuttals

knowledgeComponents.statement: Comparison of non-fiction texts focuses on how each writer conveys their viewpoint.
An unseen text should be read twice: once for meaning, once for method.
Viewpoint writing must match its stated form, audience and purpose throughout.
A debate motion is a statement that the proposition supports and the opposition attacks.
Anticipating the opposing case is part of preparing your own.
Key Spring 1 terminology: ethos, pathos, logos, anaphora, tricolon, antithesis, modality, synthesis.
Analysis of non-fiction must always name the writer's purpose.
Planning for two minutes before a timed writing task improves structure measurably.

terms.name: Spring 2
terms.focus: Poetry across time: reading and writing poetry, including the Romantics and contemporary voices, meeting the statutory requirement for poetry since 1789.
coreTexts: Romantic poetry (post-1789): William Blake 'The Tyger' and 'London'; William Wordsworth 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge' and an extract from 'The Prelude'
Narrative and ballad poetry: Alfred Noyes 'The Highwayman'; a traditional ballad
War and protest poetry: Wilfred Owen 'Dulce et Decorum Est' (context handled sensitively for age)
Contemporary voices: poems by Benjamin Zephaniah, Grace Nichols, Imtiaz Dharker and John Agard
Form study: sonnet, haiku, free verse

lessons.title: Reading a poem: form, structure and voice
objectives: I can describe the form and structure of a poem accurately
I can identify the speaker of a poem and distinguish them from the poet
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of poetry, including poetry since 1789; understanding how the work of poets is communicated effectively through form and structure
misconceptions: Assuming the speaker is always the poet
Calling any group of lines a verse when 'stanza' is meant

assessment.detail: Annotate two poems for stanza pattern, line length, enjambment and speaker; write two sentences on the effect of the form

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: prepare poems to read aloud; discuss and evaluate how authors use language; identify how structure contributes to meaning

lessons.title: Rhythm, rhyme and sound
objectives: I can identify a rhyme scheme and describe a poem's rhythm
I can explain how sound devices create meaning
lessons.ncRef: Reading – understand how language, including figurative language, and the conventions of poetry present meaning
misconceptions: Saying a poem 'flows' without describing what creates the effect
Assuming a poem without rhyme has no structure

assessment.detail: Mark the rhyme scheme of four poems; identify and explain three sound devices

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: learn a wider range of poetry by heart; discuss how authors use language including figurative language

lessons.title: Writing about poetry: the analytical paragraph
objectives: I can write a paragraph analysing a poem's language and form
I can link a technical feature to its effect on the reader
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays; discuss reading with precise and confident use of linguistic and literary terminology
misconceptions: Describing what the poem is about instead of analysing how it works
Making a claim about a device without quoting it

assessment.detail: Two paragraphs on 'The Tyger', one on language and one on form, using precise terminology

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss and evaluate how authors use language; provide reasoned justifications for views

knowledgeComponents.statement: A stanza is a group of lines in a poem, separated by a space.
The speaker is the voice in the poem and is not necessarily the poet.
Enjambment is when a sentence runs over the end of a line without punctuation.
A caesura is a pause within a line, usually marked by punctuation.
A rhyme scheme is labelled with letters, e.g. ABAB or AABB.
Metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line.
Sibilance is the repetition of s and sh sounds; assonance repeats vowel sounds.
Free verse has no regular metre or rhyme but still has deliberate structure.
Poetry analysis links a named technique to a specific effect on the reader.

lessons.title: Blake's London and Songs of Experience
objectives: I can explain what the Romantic movement was and when it began
I can analyse how Blake presents the city in 'London'
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of poetry including poetry since 1789; understand the context of the writing and draw on this to support comprehension
misconceptions: Reading 'Romantic' as meaning about love
Treating context as biography rather than as an aid to meaning

assessment.detail: Annotated reading of 'London' with a paragraph on how Blake presents suffering, referring to the Industrial Revolution context

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss understanding and explore the meaning of words in context; identify themes

lessons.title: Wordsworth and the natural world
objectives: I can compare how two Romantic poets present their subject
I can use context to deepen, not replace, analysis
lessons.ncRef: Reading – make comparisons across texts; understand the purpose, audience for and context of the writing
misconceptions: Writing about the historical period instead of the poem
Confusing a Petrarchan and a Shakespearean sonnet structure

assessment.detail: One integrated comparative paragraph on Blake and Wordsworth's treatment of the city or of nature

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: make comparisons within and across books; discuss figurative language

lessons.title: Learning poetry by heart and performing it
objectives: I can learn a poem by heart and recite it with understanding
I can use pace, pause and emphasis to convey meaning
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – improvising, rehearsing and performing poetry in order to generate language and discuss language use and meaning, using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness and action
misconceptions: Reciting at a rush to get through it
Adding dramatic gestures that fight the poem's meaning

assessment.detail: Recite a 12–16 line poem from memory; assessed on accuracy, clarity, pace and interpretation

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: learn a wider range of poetry by heart; prepare poems to read aloud and perform, showing understanding through intonation, tone and volume

knowledgeComponents.statement: Romanticism was a late-18th and early-19th century movement valuing nature, emotion, imagination and the individual.
'Romantic' in this literary sense does not mean 'to do with love'.
William Blake published 'Songs of Innocence and of Experience' in 1794.
The Industrial Revolution transformed British cities and is the backdrop to Blake's 'London'.
A refrain is a repeated line or phrase in a poem.
A sonnet has 14 lines; a Petrarchan sonnet divides into an octave and a sestet.
The volta is the turn in a sonnet where the argument or mood shifts.
Context should be used to explain a choice in the poem, never as a substitute for analysis.
Reciting from memory frees the voice to interpret rather than decode.

lessons.title: The ballad: storytelling in verse
objectives: I can identify the features of a ballad
I can explain how a narrative poem builds tension
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of poetry; study setting, plot and characterisation and the effects of these; understand the conventions of poetry
misconceptions: Retelling the plot rather than analysing how tension is made
Assuming all narrative poems are ballads

assessment.detail: Analyse how tension builds across 'The Highwayman', citing three structural or language choices

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how structure and presentation contribute to meaning; summarise main ideas

lessons.title: Writing narrative poetry
objectives: I can write a narrative poem with a controlled form
I can use a refrain and a consistent rhythm
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative texts including poetry; draw on knowledge of literary devices from their reading to enhance the impact of their writing
misconceptions: Forcing a rhyme at the cost of sense
Writing prose broken into short lines and calling it a poem

assessment.detail: Write a 4–6 stanza narrative poem with a chosen form; annotate three deliberate craft choices

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: write poetry; select vocabulary and grammatical structures for effect

lessons.title: Grammar: word order, inversion and poetic licence
objectives: I can identify unusual word order in poetry and explain its effect
I can recognise where a poet breaks a grammatical convention deliberately
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – study the effectiveness and impact of the grammatical features of the texts they read; extend and apply grammatical knowledge from English appendix 2
misconceptions: Assuming odd word order is an error
Believing poets ignore grammar entirely

assessment.detail: Identify inversion or unusual syntax in six poetic lines and rewrite each in ordinary order, commenting on what is lost

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: sentence structures; fronted adverbials; subject-verb agreement

knowledgeComponents.statement: A ballad is a narrative poem, often in quatrains, with a strong rhythm and a refrain.
A quatrain is a four-line stanza.
Tension in a narrative poem is built by pace, withheld information and repetition.
Ballads grew out of the oral tradition and were meant to be sung or recited.
Meaning must never be sacrificed to force a rhyme.
A refrain gives a poem structure and can gain new meaning each time it returns.
Inversion reverses normal word order, usually to place emphasis or preserve metre.
Syntax is the arrangement of words in a sentence.
A poet's departure from convention is a choice with an effect, not an error.

lessons.title: Poems of identity and belonging
objectives: I can analyse how a contemporary poet presents identity
I can respond personally to a poem and support my response
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of poetry including contemporary work and seminal world literature; make an informed personal response, recognising that others may respond differently to the same text
misconceptions: Treating non-standard spelling in a poem as an error rather than a representation of voice
Assuming a personal response needs no evidence

assessment.detail: One analytical paragraph and one personal response paragraph on a chosen contemporary poem

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: provide reasoned justifications for views; discuss and evaluate how authors use language

lessons.title: Writing free verse: your own voice
objectives: I can write free verse where line breaks carry meaning
I can use an extended image across a poem
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative texts including poetry; apply growing knowledge of vocabulary, grammar and text structure
misconceptions: Breaking lines at random
Using abstract nouns where a concrete image would be stronger

assessment.detail: Write a free-verse poem of 12–20 lines plus a 100-word commentary on three deliberate choices

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: write poetry; select vocabulary and grammatical structures for effect

lessons.title: Comparing poems: building a comparison
objectives: I can compare two poems on a shared theme
I can structure a comparison around methods rather than around texts
lessons.ncRef: Reading – make comparisons within and across texts; Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays
misconceptions: Writing all about poem A, then all about poem B
Comparing only what the poems say and not how

assessment.detail: Plan and write two integrated comparative paragraphs on two poems about identity or nature

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: make comparisons within and across books

knowledgeComponents.statement: Contemporary poets often write in non-standard forms of English to represent a real voice.
Code-switching is moving between varieties of a language depending on context.
A personal response is valid only when anchored to what is in the text.
In free verse, a line break controls emphasis and pause in place of punctuation.
Concrete images are more affecting than abstract statements of feeling.
An extended metaphor sustained across a poem gives it unity.
A comparison is organised by point of comparison, not by text.
A strong comparison identifies both similarity and difference in method.
Different readers can reach different valid readings of the same poem if both are evidenced.

lessons.title: Spring 2 reading assessment: unseen poetry comparison
objectives: I can analyse and compare two unseen poems
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of poetry; read critically; make comparisons across texts
misconceptions: Spending all the time on the first poem

assessment.detail: 55-minute paper: analyse one unseen poem, then compare it with a second on a shared theme

lessons.title: Publishing a personal anthology
objectives: I can select and present my own poems with a rationale
I can proof-read a final publishable text
lessons.ncRef: Writing – plan, draft, edit and proof-read; write imaginative texts; consider how their writing reflects the audiences and purposes for which it was intended
misconceptions: Including everything written rather than selecting the best
Skipping proof-reading on creative work

assessment.detail: A five-poem anthology with title, contents, a 150-word introduction explaining the selection, and error-free presentation

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: proof-read for spelling and punctuation errors; perform their own compositions

lessons.title: Poetry performance evening and feedback
objectives: I can perform poetry to an audience
I can give and receive constructive feedback
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – improvising, rehearsing and performing poetry, using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness and action
misconceptions: Giving feedback that is only praise or only criticism

assessment.detail: Perform two poems, one own and one studied; give structured feedback to another performer using a what-went-well and even-better-if frame

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: perform their own compositions using appropriate intonation, volume and movement

knowledgeComponents.statement: In an unseen poetry comparison, time must be divided so both poems receive analysis.
An unseen poem should first be read for what happens, then for how it is made.
An anthology is a selected collection, and the selection itself is an editorial choice.
Publishable work is proof-read separately for spelling, punctuation and layout.
Constructive feedback names a strength and one specific improvement.
Key Spring 2 terminology: stanza, enjambment, caesura, volta, sonnet, ballad, free verse, refrain, sibilance.
Poetry since 1789 is a statutory requirement of the KS3 English curriculum.
A performance interprets a poem; two performances of the same poem can differ legitimately.

terms.name: Summer 1
terms.focus: Shakespeare: a whole-play study of 'A Midsummer Night's Dream', covering context, language, character, theme and performance.
coreTexts: 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' by William Shakespeare, read in full (an edited school text is acceptable, but the whole play must be covered)
Supporting context: a short account of the Elizabethan theatre and the Globe
At least one filmed production for comparison of staging choices
terms.note: The National Curriculum requires two Shakespeare plays across Key Stage 3. This is the first; the second falls in Year 8 or Year 9.

lessons.title: Shakespeare, the Globe and the Elizabethan audience
objectives: I can describe the conditions of the Elizabethan theatre
I can explain how those conditions shaped how the plays were written
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read two Shakespeare plays across key stage 3; understand the purpose, audience for and context of the writing and draw on this knowledge to support comprehension
misconceptions: Imagining Elizabethan theatre with modern lighting, sets and seating
Assuming plays were written to be read rather than performed

assessment.detail: Fifteen context questions, then a paragraph on how the open-air stage affected Shakespeare's use of language to set a scene

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: read books structured in different ways including plays; understand the purpose of a text

lessons.title: Reading Shakespeare's language
objectives: I can work out the meaning of a Shakespearean line using context and word order
I can read blank verse without being stopped by unfamiliar words
lessons.ncRef: Reading – understand increasingly challenging texts through learning new vocabulary, relating it explicitly to known vocabulary and understanding it with the help of context and dictionaries; making inferences
misconceptions: Stopping at every unfamiliar word instead of reading for the sense of the line
Assuming all Shakespeare is in verse

assessment.detail: Paraphrase ten lines into modern English; identify which are verse and which are prose

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: check that the book makes sense, discussing understanding and exploring the meaning of words in context

lessons.title: The play begins: Act 1 and the world of the play
objectives: I can summarise the situation established in Act 1
I can explain the conflict that sets the plot in motion
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study setting, plot and characterisation and the effects of these; read whole plays
misconceptions: Reading the parental conflict through purely modern eyes without the Elizabethan legal context
Assuming a comedy means only that it is funny

assessment.detail: Summarise Act 1 in eight bullet points; explain the central conflict in one paragraph

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: summarise main ideas; identify how structure contributes to meaning

knowledgeComponents.statement: William Shakespeare lived from 1564 to 1616 and wrote around 38 plays.
The Globe was an open-air playhouse with a thrust stage, standing groundlings and no artificial lighting.
With no scenery, setting had to be established through the language of the play.
All parts in Elizabethan theatre were performed by male actors.
Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter: ten syllables in an unstressed-stressed pattern.
Shakespeare often gives verse to noble characters and prose to comic or lower-status ones.
'Thou' and 'thee' were informal or intimate; 'you' was formal or plural.
'A Midsummer Night's Dream' opens in Athens with Egeus demanding that Hermia marry Demetrius.
A Shakespearean comedy is defined by its structure ending in reconciliation and marriage, not only by humour.

lessons.title: The lovers: Hermia, Lysander, Helena and Demetrius
objectives: I can distinguish the four lovers and their relationships
I can analyse how Shakespeare presents Helena's situation
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study setting, plot and characterisation and the effects of these; make inferences and refer to evidence in the text
misconceptions: Muddling the two pairs of lovers
Reading Helena's speeches as simply comic without noticing her distress

assessment.detail: Draw a relationship map of the four lovers across the play; write one analytical paragraph on Helena in Act 1 Scene 1

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: infer characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions and justify with evidence

lessons.title: Soliloquy and dramatic technique
objectives: I can explain what a soliloquy is and why a dramatist uses one
I can analyse a soliloquy for what it reveals
lessons.ncRef: Reading – understanding how the work of dramatists is communicated effectively through dramatic techniques and performance; read critically
misconceptions: Confusing a soliloquy with a monologue spoken to others
Missing that the audience is being given privileged information

assessment.detail: Annotate Helena's soliloquy at the end of Act 1 Scene 1; write a paragraph on what it reveals and how the audience is positioned

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how language, structure and presentation contribute to meaning

lessons.title: Performing a scene
objectives: I can perform a short scene showing understanding of character
I can make and justify a staging choice
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – improvising, rehearsing and performing play scripts, using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness and action; understanding how a play's meaning can be altered by staging
misconceptions: Performing lines without deciding what the character wants
Ignoring stage directions

assessment.detail: Perform a 20-line exchange; explain in writing one staging decision and its effect on meaning

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: participate in role play and performances; use spoken language to explore ideas

knowledgeComponents.statement: Hermia loves Lysander; Demetrius loves Hermia; Helena loves Demetrius.
Unrequited love is love that is not returned.
A foil is a character whose contrast highlights the qualities of another.
A soliloquy is a speech delivered alone on stage, revealing a character's private thoughts.
An aside is a short remark to the audience that other characters do not hear.
Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something a character does not.
A performance choice is a decision about what a character wants in a scene.
Staging changes meaning, so the same script can support very different productions.
Blocking is the planned movement and position of actors on stage.

weeks.unit: The wood and the fairy world

lessons.title: Oberon, Titania and the quarrel
objectives: I can explain the conflict in the fairy world and its consequences
I can analyse Titania's speech about the disordered seasons
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study setting, plot and characterisation; read critically by knowing how figurative language and vocabulary choice present meaning
misconceptions: Reading the fairies as harmless children's characters
Missing that the fairy quarrel disrupts the human world

assessment.detail: Analyse Titania's 'forgeries of jealousy' speech: three quotations on disorder in nature, with explanation

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: discuss and evaluate how authors use language including figurative language

lessons.title: Puck, mischief and the comic engine of the plot
objectives: I can explain how Puck's errors drive the plot
I can analyse how comedy is created through confusion
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study plot and characterisation and the effects of these; understand the conventions of drama
misconceptions: Blaming Puck's mistake on carelessness rather than seeing its plot function
Treating comedy as unstructured

assessment.detail: Track the four complications caused in the wood and explain how each raises comic tension

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how structure contributes to meaning; summarise events

lessons.title: Setting as more than place: the wood and the court
objectives: I can explain the contrast between the court and the wood
I can link setting to the play's themes
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study setting and the effects of it; identify and discuss themes
misconceptions: Treating the wood as scenery rather than as a symbolic space
Assuming setting has no thematic function in drama

assessment.detail: One paragraph on how the contrast between court and wood supports a theme of the play

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions

knowledgeComponents.statement: Oberon and Titania are king and queen of the fairies and quarrel over a changeling boy.
Titania describes disordered seasons and failed harvests as a consequence of their quarrel.
In Elizabethan thinking, disorder among rulers was believed to disturb the natural world.
Puck, also called Robin Goodfellow, applies the love juice to the wrong Athenian.
Comic confusion is engineered by the playwright, not accidental.
A complication is an event that makes the situation harder to resolve.
The court represents law and order; the wood represents freedom and transformation.
The wood is a 'green world' where characters change and then return altered.
Juxtaposing two settings allows a play to test its ideas in both.

lessons.title: Bottom and the mechanicals: class, comedy and the play within a play
objectives: I can explain the function of the mechanicals in the play
I can analyse how Shakespeare creates humour through Bottom
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study characterisation and the effects of it; understand how dramatists communicate through dramatic techniques
misconceptions: Seeing the mechanicals as an unrelated subplot
Missing that their errors are deliberately written by Shakespeare

assessment.detail: One paragraph on how Bottom's language creates comedy, with two quotations

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how language contributes to meaning; discuss authors' use of language

lessons.title: Transformation: Bottom, Titania and the love juice
objectives: I can analyse the Bottom and Titania scenes
I can explain how transformation works as a theme
lessons.ncRef: Reading – identify and discuss themes and conventions; read critically
misconceptions: Reading the scene only for its slapstick
Missing the play's questions about how arbitrary desire can be

assessment.detail: Write a paragraph on what the Bottom and Titania scenes suggest about love, with textual evidence

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes; make inferences

lessons.title: Writing about a scene: the extract-to-whole-text response
objectives: I can analyse an extract in detail and then widen to the whole play
I can move between close reading and overview
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays; Reading – read whole plays and make comparisons within a text
misconceptions: Staying entirely in the extract
Abandoning the extract and writing only general plot

assessment.detail: Write two paragraphs on a set extract, each followed by a sentence connecting to the wider play

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: retrieve and record information; write with a clear structure

knowledgeComponents.statement: The mechanicals are Athenian workmen rehearsing 'Pyramus and Thisbe' for the duke's wedding.
A malapropism is the comic misuse of a word for one that sounds similar.
A play within a play draws attention to theatre itself, which is called metatheatre.
Bathos is a comic drop from the elevated to the ordinary.
Puck transforms Bottom's head into that of an ass and Titania, enchanted, falls in love with him.
The love juice makes desire look arbitrary, which is one of the play's central ideas.
An extract-based response analyses the extract closely and then connects it to the whole text.
Zooming out means showing how the extract fits the play's overall development.

lessons.title: Acts 4 and 5: resolution and return
objectives: I can explain how the play resolves its conflicts
I can evaluate whether the ending is fully satisfying
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read whole plays; study plot and structure and the effects of these; make an informed personal response
misconceptions: Assuming a comic ending means every problem is solved
Overlooking Demetrius remaining under the spell

assessment.detail: Write a paragraph evaluating how satisfying the resolution is, using evidence from Act 4 and Act 5

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: provide reasoned justifications for their views; summarise

lessons.title: Themes: love, order, illusion and dreams
objectives: I can trace a theme across the whole play
I can select evidence from all five acts
lessons.ncRef: Reading – identify and discuss themes and conventions in and across a wide range of writing; read whole plays
misconceptions: Treating a theme as a single moment rather than a developed idea
Selecting all evidence from one act

assessment.detail: Complete a theme tracker with five quotations, one from each act, and analysis of each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions

lessons.title: Comparing productions: staging changes meaning
objectives: I can compare two productions of the same scene
I can explain how a directorial choice changes the audience's response
lessons.ncRef: Reading – understanding how the work of dramatists is communicated effectively through performance and how alternative staging allows for different interpretations of a play
misconceptions: Judging a production as wrong for departing from one's own reading
Describing what happens rather than analysing the effect

assessment.detail: Compare two filmed versions of one scene; explain in two paragraphs how each staging shapes the audience's response

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: make comparisons; discuss and evaluate how meaning is presented

knowledgeComponents.statement: The play ends with three marriages and Puck's closing address to the audience.
Demetrius's love for Helena remains under the influence of the flower at the end of the play.
A denouement is the final unravelling of the plot's complications.
An ambiguous ending invites more than one valid interpretation.
Key themes of the play include love's irrationality, order and disorder, and dream versus reality.
A theme is traced by finding how an idea is developed from the first act to the last.
A director's choices of casting, design and cutting create an interpretation of the text.
The same script supports many legitimate productions, because a play is completed in performance.

lessons.title: Planning a Shakespeare essay
objectives: I can plan an essay on a character or theme across the play
I can select quotations that will support my argument
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays; plan and draft; support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail
misconceptions: Selecting quotations before deciding on an argument
Planning a plot summary rather than an argument

assessment.detail: Produce a plan with a thesis, three topic sentences and two quotations for each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use organisational and presentational devices to structure text

lessons.title: Writing with literary terminology and precision
objectives: I can use literary terminology accurately in an essay
I can write about a play using the correct conventions
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – discuss reading, writing and spoken language with precise and confident use of linguistic and literary terminology
misconceptions: Writing about a play in the past tense
Calling a play a book or a novel

assessment.detail: Correct twelve terminology and convention errors in a supplied essay, then write one paragraph applying the conventions

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use appropriate terminology when discussing texts

lessons.title: Redrafting: raising the level of an analytical paragraph
objectives: I can redraft a paragraph to deepen the analysis
I can add an alternative interpretation
lessons.ncRef: Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing to improve its coherence and overall effectiveness; Reading – make an informed personal response, recognising that others may respond differently
misconceptions: Adding length rather than depth
Offering an alternative reading with no textual support

assessment.detail: Redraft one paragraph to add a word-level analysis and one alternative interpretation; annotate both additions

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: propose changes to vocabulary, grammar and punctuation to enhance effects and clarify meaning

knowledgeComponents.statement: An essay plan begins with an argument, and quotations are selected to support it.
A thesis for a Shakespeare essay makes a claim about what the dramatist is doing and why.
Plays are written about in the present tense: 'Shakespeare presents', not 'presented'.
A play is divided into acts and scenes, referenced as Act 3 Scene 2.
Shakespeare is referred to as a dramatist or playwright, not an author of a book.
Deeper analysis zooms in on a single word and considers its connotations.
An alternative interpretation is signalled with phrases such as 'this could also suggest'.
Any alternative reading must still be supported by the same quotation.

lessons.title: Summer 1 reading assessment: the Shakespeare essay
objectives: I can write a sustained essay on the whole play
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read whole plays; read critically; Writing – write well-structured formal expository essays
misconceptions: Writing all about the extract and nothing about the play

assessment.detail: 60-minute essay from an extract, widening to the whole play; marked against a KS3 literature rubric

lessons.title: Performance assessment: a rehearsed scene
objectives: I can rehearse and perform a scene showing understanding of character and meaning
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – improvising, rehearsing and performing play scripts in order to generate language and discuss language use and meaning, using role, intonation, tone, volume, mood, silence, stillness and action
misconceptions: Learning lines without deciding on meaning

assessment.detail: Perform a rehearsed scene of 30–40 lines with a written director's note of three interpretative choices

lessons.title: Feedback, retrieval and reflection
objectives: I can act on essay feedback
I can recall the play's plot, characters and terminology
lessons.ncRef: Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing to improve its coherence and overall effectiveness
misconceptions: Assuming knowledge of the play will persist without revisiting

assessment.detail: 40-item retrieval quiz on plot, character, quotation and terminology; directed rewrite of one essay paragraph

knowledgeComponents.statement: An essay from an extract must analyse the extract and connect it to the rest of the play.
Quotations should be short, embedded and accurate.
A character objective is what the character is trying to achieve in the scene.
A director's note explains the reasoning behind an interpretative choice.
Key Summer 1 terminology: blank verse, iambic pentameter, soliloquy, aside, dramatic irony, malapropism, metatheatre, denouement.
The National Curriculum requires two Shakespeare plays across Key Stage 3.
Quotation recall is maintained by spaced retrieval, not by rereading.
The plot of the play runs: conflict in Athens, flight to the wood, enchantment and confusion, resolution, three weddings and the mechanicals' play.

terms.name: Summer 2
terms.focus: Gothic and mystery short fiction, descriptive and narrative writing craft, formal debate, and an independent reading project.
coreTexts: Pre-1914 Gothic and mystery short fiction: Edgar Allan Poe 'The Tell-Tale Heart'; Charles Dickens 'The Signal-Man'; an extract from Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' (1818)
Modern short stories for comparison: a Neil Gaiman or Kevin Crossley-Holland story
Independent reading: a full-length novel of the pupil's choosing

lessons.title: What is Gothic? Conventions and origins
objectives: I can identify the conventions of Gothic fiction
I can explain why the Gothic emerged when it did
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read a wide range of fiction including works from the English literary heritage, both pre-1914 and contemporary; identify and discuss themes and conventions
misconceptions: Equating Gothic with modern horror
Assuming Gothic must include a ghost

assessment.detail: Identify Gothic conventions in three short extracts; write a paragraph defining the genre with examples

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and discuss themes and conventions across a wide range of writing

lessons.title: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein: reading a pre-1914 extract
objectives: I can read and analyse a challenging pre-1914 prose extract
I can explain how the writer creates atmosphere
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read works from the English literary heritage, pre-1914; understand increasingly challenging texts; read critically
misconceptions: Believing Frankenstein is the name of the creature
Giving up on long 19th-century sentences rather than breaking them into clauses

assessment.detail: Annotate the creation scene for atmosphere; answer four inference questions and write one analytical paragraph

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: read books structured in different ways; check meaning of words in context

lessons.title: Writing to describe: creating atmosphere
objectives: I can build atmosphere through sensory detail and pathetic fallacy
I can control the pace of a description
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative and descriptive texts; draw on knowledge of literary devices from their reading to enhance the impact of their writing
misconceptions: Listing every scary thing rather than building slowly
Using pathetic fallacy so heavily it becomes comic

assessment.detail: 300-word Gothic description assessed on atmosphere, sensory range, pace control and vocabulary precision

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: describe settings, characters and atmosphere; select vocabulary for effect

knowledgeComponents.statement: Gothic fiction typically features isolation, decay, the supernatural, extreme emotion and a threatening setting.
The Gothic emerged in the late 18th century alongside Romanticism as a reaction to reason and order.
The uncanny is the unsettling feeling of something familiar made strange.
Pathetic fallacy is the use of weather or landscape to reflect emotion.
Mary Shelley published 'Frankenstein' in 1818; Victor Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature.
A long 19th-century sentence becomes readable when broken at its clause boundaries.
Atmosphere is built cumulatively; a slow build is more effective than a list of shocks.
A semantic field of decay or darkness unifies a description.
Withholding information from the reader creates tension.

lessons.title: Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart': the unreliable narrator
objectives: I can explain what an unreliable narrator is
I can analyse how Poe creates a sense of madness through voice and syntax
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how language, including figurative language, vocabulary choice, grammar and text structure present meaning; make inferences
misconceptions: Assuming a first-person narrator is always unreliable
Missing that the narrator's insistence on sanity is the evidence against it

assessment.detail: Analyse three passages for how sentence structure conveys the narrator's state of mind

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: infer characters' thoughts and motives; discuss how authors use language

lessons.title: Dickens's 'The Signal-Man': structure, suspense and the ghost story
objectives: I can analyse how structure creates suspense in a short story
I can compare two writers' approaches to fear
lessons.ncRef: Reading – study plot and structure and the effects of these; make comparisons across texts
misconceptions: Confusing suspense with surprise
Assuming a ghost story must explain itself

assessment.detail: Compare how Poe and Dickens create fear, in two integrated comparative paragraphs

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how structure contributes to meaning; make comparisons across books

lessons.title: Writing narrative: structuring a short story
objectives: I can structure a short story to build and release tension
I can write an ending that satisfies without being predictable
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative and narrative texts; consider how their writing reflects the audiences and purposes for which it was intended
misconceptions: Ending with 'it was all a dream'
Writing a story too broad in scope for its length

assessment.detail: Plan a short story with a five-part structure, then draft the opening 300 words

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: note and develop initial ideas; write narratives with a clear structure

knowledgeComponents.statement: An unreliable narrator gives an account the reader has reason to doubt.
Short, fragmented sentences and repetition can convey agitation or breakdown.
Poe's narrator insists on his sanity, which invites the reader to doubt it.
Suspense is created by the reader knowing danger is coming; surprise is created by concealment.
A frame narrative is a story told within another story.
Dickens published 'The Signal-Man' in 1866, drawing on Victorian anxiety about the railways.
Deliberate ambiguity at the end of a ghost story sustains its unease.
A short story should cover a short span of time and few characters.
A cyclical structure returns to the opening image, transformed by what has happened.

lessons.title: Drafting a Gothic short story
objectives: I can sustain a piece of narrative writing at length
I can maintain a consistent voice and atmosphere
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write accurately, fluently, effectively and at length for pleasure and information; write imaginative and narrative texts
misconceptions: Losing atmosphere once the plot takes over
Introducing too many characters

assessment.detail: 800–1000 word Gothic short story, first draft

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: write narratives, describing settings, characters and atmosphere; ensure consistent use of tense

lessons.title: Dialogue: making characters speak
objectives: I can write and punctuate dialogue accurately
I can use dialogue to reveal character and advance the plot
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write imaginative and narrative texts; pay attention to accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling; Grammar – apply the grammatical knowledge in English appendix 2
misconceptions: Writing dialogue that only exchanges information
Overusing adverbs in reporting clauses

assessment.detail: Write a 200-word dialogue exchange that reveals a conflict without stating it; punctuation marked strictly

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English appendix 2: punctuating direct speech; using dialogue to convey character and advance the action

lessons.title: Editing for impact and accuracy
objectives: I can edit my story for effect and proof-read it for accuracy
I can cut what does not earn its place
lessons.ncRef: Writing – amend the vocabulary, grammar and structure of their writing to improve its coherence and overall effectiveness; pay attention to accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling
misconceptions: Adding adjectives instead of choosing stronger nouns and verbs
Proof-reading and editing in a single pass

assessment.detail: Final story plus a commentary identifying three cuts, three upgrades and three corrections

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: propose changes to vocabulary, grammar and punctuation; proof-read for errors

knowledgeComponents.statement: A sustained piece of writing keeps its voice and atmosphere consistent from first line to last.
A short story is stronger with few characters, closely observed.
A new speaker's dialogue starts on a new line.
Subtext is what characters mean but do not say.
An action beat can replace a reporting clause and show character at the same time.
'Said' is usually the strongest reporting verb because it disappears.
Editing for effect and proof-reading for accuracy are separate passes.
Redundancy is any word that repeats meaning already present.
A precise verb usually replaces a weak verb plus adverb.

lessons.title: The structure of a formal debate
objectives: I can explain the roles and structure of a formal debate
I can construct a case with three supported arguments
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – participating in formal debates and structured discussions, summarising and building on what has been said; speak confidently and effectively
misconceptions: Confusing debate with argument
Preparing content but not a structure

assessment.detail: Prepare a full debate case: definition, three arguments with evidence, and two anticipated rebuttals

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: participate in debates; use spoken language to develop understanding through speculating, hypothesising and exploring ideas

lessons.title: Rebuttal, listening and thinking on your feet
objectives: I can listen actively and respond to an opposing argument
I can take notes during a speech and use them in reply
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – participating in formal debates and structured discussions, summarising and building on what has been said; listening and responding
misconceptions: Delivering a prepared speech regardless of what was said
Rebutting by simply contradicting

assessment.detail: Take notes on a two-minute speech and deliver a one-minute rebuttal that names and answers two specific points

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: listen and respond appropriately; build on the contributions of others

lessons.title: Formal debate assessment
objectives: I can take part in a formal debate using Standard English confidently
lessons.ncRef: Spoken English – speak confidently and effectively, using Standard English confidently in a range of formal and informal contexts, including classroom discussion; participating in formal debates
misconceptions: Raising volume in place of raising the quality of argument

assessment.detail: Full debate on a set motion; assessed on argument quality, use of evidence, rebuttal, delivery and use of Standard English

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: speak audibly and fluently with an increasing command of Standard English

knowledgeComponents.statement: A debate motion begins 'This house believes that...'.
The proposition argues for the motion; the opposition argues against it.
A point of information is a brief interruption offered to a speaker, which they may accept or decline.
The first speaker defines the terms of the motion.
Rebuttal names the opposing argument before answering it.
Clash is the direct engagement between the two sides on the same point.
Active listening means noting the structure of an argument, not just its topic.
Standard English is expected in formal spoken assessment.
A summation speech reviews the clash and explains why one side has won it.

lessons.title: End-of-year reading assessment
objectives: I can analyse an unseen fiction extract with confidence
lessons.ncRef: Reading – read critically by knowing how language, structure and organisational features present meaning; make inferences
misconceptions: Analysing language but ignoring structure

assessment.detail: 60-minute paper on an unseen Gothic or mystery extract: a language question, a structure question and an evaluation question

lessons.title: End-of-year writing assessment
objectives: I can write a polished descriptive or narrative piece under timed conditions
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write accurately, fluently, effectively and at length; write imaginative and narrative texts
misconceptions: Writing without planning under time pressure

assessment.detail: 50-minute descriptive or narrative task from a picture or opening line stimulus; marked on content and organisation and on technical accuracy

lessons.title: Grammar and vocabulary assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling
I can use terminology precisely
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – extend and apply grammatical knowledge from English appendix 2; discuss reading, writing and spoken language with precise and confident use of linguistic and literary terminology
misconceptions: Learning terminology as labels without understanding the function

assessment.detail: 50 items: word class, clause type, punctuation, spelling from the Y5–Y6 statutory list, and literary terminology

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6 English appendix 1 and 2: statutory spelling list and grammar terminology

knowledgeComponents.statement: An analysis of an unseen extract should cover language, structure and overall effect.
An evaluation question asks how far you agree with a statement about the text.
Five minutes of planning improves a timed writing task more than five extra minutes of writing.
Technical accuracy carries a substantial share of the marks in writing assessment.
Terminology is only useful when the function of the feature can be explained.
The Year 5 and 6 statutory spelling list remains assessable at Key Stage 3.
Sentence variety is assessed as part of technical accuracy, not only as style.
Reading the question twice before writing prevents the most common loss of marks in a timed paper.

lessons.title: Reading a self-chosen novel: sustained independent reading
objectives: I can read a full-length novel independently
I can keep a record of my reading and my responses
lessons.ncRef: Reading – develop an appreciation and love of reading, and read increasingly challenging material independently; choosing and reading books independently for challenge, interest and enjoyment
misconceptions: Choosing a book far below one's reading level to finish quickly
Reading without recording responses

assessment.detail: Completed reading log with weekly entries: summary, response, three quotations and one question

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: read for pleasure; read books that are structured in different ways

lessons.title: Writing a book review
objectives: I can write a review that evaluates rather than summarises
I can support my judgement with evidence
lessons.ncRef: Writing – write for a wide range of purposes and audiences; support ideas and arguments with any necessary factual detail; Reading – make an informed personal response
misconceptions: Retelling the plot instead of evaluating
Giving an opinion with no evidence

assessment.detail: 400-word book review for a specified audience, evaluating character, style and pacing with evidence, and avoiding spoilers

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: provide reasoned justifications for their views; recommend books giving reasons

lessons.title: Comparing a novel with a text studied this year
objectives: I can compare my chosen novel with a text studied in class
I can identify shared themes across different texts
lessons.ncRef: Reading – make comparisons within and across texts; identify and discuss themes and conventions in and across a wide range of writing; re-reading books encountered earlier to increase familiarity
misconceptions: Comparing plots rather than themes and methods

assessment.detail: Two comparative paragraphs linking the chosen novel with one class text on a shared theme

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: make comparisons within and across books

knowledgeComponents.statement: Reading stamina grows only by reading books longer than feel comfortable.
A reading log records response and question, not only summary.
A review evaluates: it judges quality and explains why.
A review must consider its audience and avoid revealing the ending.
Pacing is how quickly a narrative moves and how that is controlled.
Texts from different periods can share a theme while treating it very differently.
A comparison across texts is organised by shared idea, not by book.
An independently chosen book should be slightly beyond the reader's comfortable level to build stamina.

lessons.title: Whole-year retrieval and terminology review
objectives: I can recall the terminology, texts and grammar covered across Year 7
lessons.ncRef: Grammar and vocabulary – discuss reading, writing and spoken language with precise and confident use of linguistic and literary terminology
misconceptions: Assuming earlier terms have been retained without checking

assessment.detail: 60 items sampled across all 39 weeks; results reset the spacing interval on weak knowledge components

lessons.title: Creative showcase: presenting a year's writing
objectives: I can select and present my best work with a rationale
lessons.ncRef: Writing – plan, draft, edit and proof-read; consider how their writing reflects the audiences and purposes for which it was intended; Spoken English – giving short speeches and presentations
misconceptions: Selecting the longest piece rather than the best

assessment.detail: Compile a Year 7 writing portfolio of five pieces with a 200-word rationale; present one piece aloud

lessons.title: Looking ahead: reading targets for Year 8
objectives: I can set reading and writing targets for the year ahead
I can build a personal reading list
lessons.ncRef: Reading – develop an appreciation and love of reading; choosing and reading books independently for challenge, interest and enjoyment
misconceptions: Setting targets so vague they cannot be checked

assessment.detail: Write three specific targets and build a ten-book summer and Year 8 reading list across at least four genres

knowledgeComponents.statement: Year 7 English covered myth and legend, a whole novel, non-fiction and rhetoric, poetry since 1789, a Shakespeare play, and Gothic short fiction.
Analysis at every level moves from what, to how, to why.
Reading, writing and spoken English develop together; each strengthens the others.
A portfolio rationale explains why each piece was selected.
A useful target is specific, measurable and checkable.
Year 8 requires a second Shakespeare play and continued study of pre-1914 literature.
Reading widely across genres builds the vocabulary that all other work depends on.
Terminology is only worth recalling when the feature it names can be explained in a text.

subjects.name: Science (combined: biology, chemistry, physics)
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: science programmes of study, key stage 3 (DfE, September 2013; statutory from September 2014). Strands: Working scientifically (scientific attitudes; experimental skills and investigations; analysis and evaluation; measurement); Biology (structure and function of living organisms; material cycles and energy; interactions and interdependencies; genetics and evolution); Chemistry (the particulate nature of matter; atoms, elements and compounds; pure and impure substances; chemical reactions; energetics; the Periodic Table; materials; Earth and atmosphere); Physics (energy; motion and forces; waves; electricity and electromagnetism; matter; space physics).
subjects.yearShare: The KS3 science programme is written for the whole key stage without year-by-year division. This Year 7 scheme takes the topics conventionally taught first in England (as in the Activate and Exploring Science schemes and the Oak National Academy Year 7 units), balanced roughly evenly across biology, chemistry and physics: cells and organisation, skeleton and muscles, reproduction, ecosystems, particles and states, atoms and elements, mixtures and separation, acids and reactions, Earth and atmosphere, forces and motion, energy, sound, light and space.
deferredToY8Y9: Nutrition and digestion
Gas exchange systems and breathing
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
Inheritance, chromosomes, DNA, genes, variation and evolution
The Periodic Table in depth: groups 1, 7 and 0
Balanced symbol equations and quantitative chemistry
Electricity and electromagnetism, including circuits, resistance, static and magnetism
Waves in depth including the electromagnetic spectrum
Work, power and energy calculations in depth
priorKnowledgeAssumed: Y6: plan different types of scientific enquiries, recognising and controlling variables where necessary
Y6: take measurements using a range of scientific equipment with increasing accuracy and precision, taking repeat readings
Y6: record data using scientific diagrams and labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs
Y6: report and present findings including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations, and identify evidence that supports or refutes ideas
Y6: describe how living things are classified into broad groups; give reasons for classification
Y6: identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood
Y6: recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way the body functions
Y5: describe the life process of reproduction in some plants and animals; describe the changes as humans develop to old age including puberty
Y4: construct and interpret food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
Y3: identify that humans and some animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement
Y4: compare and group materials as solids, liquids or gases; observe changes of state and measure the temperature at which this happens

Y5: compare and group everyday materials by properties including hardness, solubility, transparency, conductivity and response to magnets; know that some materials dissolve to form a solution and describe how to recover a substance from a solution; decide how mixtures might be separated by filtering, sieving and evaporating
Y5: explain that some changes result in the formation of new materials and that this kind of change is not usually reversible
Y3: compare and group rocks; describe how fossils are formed; recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter

Y5: explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of gravity; identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction; recognise that levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect
Y5: describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun and of the Moon relative to the Earth; use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night
Y6: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines and use this to explain how objects are seen and why shadows have the shape of the object
Y4: identify how sounds are made and that vibrations travel through a medium to the ear; find patterns between pitch and the object, and between volume and the strength of the vibrations
Y6: associate the brightness of a lamp or volume of a buzzer with the number and voltage of cells; use recognised symbols for simple circuits

terms.name: Autumn 1
terms.focus: Working scientifically and laboratory skills; Biology: cells and organisation; the skeletal and muscular systems.

lessons.title: Safe working and the science laboratory
objectives: I can identify hazards and describe how to reduce the risk
I can read a hazard symbol and explain what it warns of
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – scientific attitudes: understand and use SI units; evaluate risks
misconceptions: Confusing hazard (the thing that can cause harm) with risk (the chance it will)
Assuming a substance is safe because it is a household chemical

assessment.detail: Complete a risk assessment for a heating practical; identify eight hazard symbols; a safety licence must be passed before independent practical work

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: work scientifically; take measurements using a range of scientific equipment

lessons.title: Using laboratory equipment and the Bunsen burner
objectives: I can name and use common laboratory apparatus
I can light and control a Bunsen burner safely
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – experimental skills and investigations: use appropriate techniques, apparatus and materials during fieldwork and laboratory work, paying attention to health and safety
misconceptions: Believing the blue flame is cooler because it is less visible
Leaving the burner on the roaring flame when not heating

assessment.detail: Demonstrate correct lighting, flame adjustment and safe heating; assessed against a skills checklist

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use test results to make predictions; take accurate measurements

lessons.title: Measuring accurately: SI units and instruments
objectives: I can select the right instrument and unit for a measurement
I can read a scale accurately and avoid parallax error
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – measurement: understand and use SI units and IUPAC chemical nomenclature; make and record observations and measurements using a range of methods
misconceptions: Reading a measuring cylinder from the top of the meniscus
Recording a measurement without its unit

assessment.detail: Ten measurements of length, mass, volume, temperature and time, marked for accuracy and correct units

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: take measurements using a range of scientific equipment with increasing accuracy and precision
Y6 maths: read scales; convert metric units

knowledgeComponents.statement: A hazard is something that could cause harm; risk is the chance that harm actually occurs.
Corrosive substances attack skin and materials; the hazard symbol shows a hand and surface being burned.
A control measure is an action taken to reduce risk, such as wearing eye protection.
A Bunsen burner with the air hole closed gives a yellow safety flame; open gives a hotter blue flame.
The blue roaring flame is the hottest flame, not the coolest.
The SI unit of length is the metre, of mass the kilogram, and of time the second.
Volume of a liquid is read at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level.
Parallax error occurs when a scale is read from an angle rather than straight on.
Every recorded measurement must include its unit.
Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius; volume in cubic centimetres or millilitres.

weeks.unit: Working scientifically: enquiry, variables and data

lessons.title: Asking scientific questions and making predictions
objectives: I can turn an observation into a testable scientific question
I can write a prediction with a scientific reason
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – experimental skills and investigations: ask questions and develop a line of enquiry based on observations of the real world, alongside prior knowledge and experience; make predictions using scientific knowledge and understanding
misconceptions: Writing a prediction that is only a guess with no reason
Confusing a hypothesis with a prediction

assessment.detail: Convert six observations into testable questions and write a reasoned prediction for each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: plan different types of scientific enquiries to answer questions; make predictions

lessons.title: Variables and fair testing
objectives: I can identify independent, dependent and control variables
I can explain why controlling variables makes a test valid
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – experimental skills and investigations: select, plan and carry out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries to test predictions, including identifying independent, dependent and control variables, where appropriate
misconceptions: Calling any variable that stays the same the 'control variable' without knowing why it must
Changing two variables at once and still calling the test fair

assessment.detail: For four described investigations, identify all three variable types and state one variable that must be controlled and why

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: plan enquiries including recognising and controlling variables where necessary

lessons.title: Recording, graphing and drawing conclusions
objectives: I can record results in a suitable table and plot an appropriate graph
I can write a conclusion that refers back to the prediction
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – analysis and evaluation: apply mathematical concepts and calculate results; present observations using appropriate methods, including tables and graphs; interpret observations and identify patterns; present reasoned explanations
misconceptions: Plotting the independent variable on the vertical axis
Joining every point rather than drawing a line of best fit
Concluding beyond what the data show

assessment.detail: Tabulate a supplied data set, plot the correct graph type, identify an anomaly and write a conclusion referring to the prediction

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: record data and results using scientific diagrams, labels, classification keys, tables, scatter graphs, bar and line graphs
Y6 maths: interpret and construct line graphs

knowledgeComponents.statement: A testable question can be answered by collecting evidence.
