A prediction states what will happen and gives a scientific reason.
The independent variable is the one deliberately changed.
The dependent variable is the one measured.
Control variables are kept the same so the test is valid.
Only one variable may be changed at a time for a test to be fair.
The independent variable is plotted on the horizontal (x) axis.
Continuous data are plotted on a line graph; discrete or categorical data on a bar chart.
An anomalous result does not fit the pattern and should be identified, not deleted silently.
Repeating measurements and taking a mean improves reliability.
A conclusion states the pattern found and whether it supports the prediction.

lessons.title: Cells are the fundamental unit of living organisms
objectives: I can state that all living things are made of cells
I can explain what makes something living
lessons.ncRef: Biology – structure and function of living organisms: cells and organisation – cells as the fundamental unit of living organisms, including how to observe, interpret and record cell structure using a light microscope
misconceptions: Thinking cells are only found in animals
Believing cells are all the same size and shape

assessment.detail: Fifteen items on the cell theory and the characteristics of living things

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: describe how living things are classified into broad groups
Y4–Y6: life processes of living things

lessons.title: Using a light microscope
objectives: I can set up and focus a light microscope
I can calculate total magnification
lessons.ncRef: Biology – cells and organisation: how to observe, interpret and record cell structure using a light microscope; Working scientifically – use appropriate techniques and apparatus
misconceptions: Focusing downwards while looking through the eyepiece and crushing the slide
Adding the lens magnifications instead of multiplying them

assessment.detail: Prepare an onion cell slide, focus at two magnifications and produce a labelled biological drawing with the magnification stated

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: use a range of scientific equipment; record findings using labelled diagrams

lessons.title: Animal and plant cells: structure and function
objectives: I can name the parts of an animal cell and a plant cell and state their functions
I can explain the differences between animal and plant cells
lessons.ncRef: Biology – cells and organisation: the functions of the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole, mitochondria and chloroplasts
misconceptions: Thinking plant cells have no cell membrane because they have a cell wall
Believing all plant cells contain chloroplasts, including root cells
Confusing the vacuole with a gap

assessment.detail: Label both cell types from memory; a five-mark question comparing plant and animal cells

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise that living things can be grouped by observable characteristics

knowledgeComponents.statement: All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
The seven life processes are movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition.
A unicellular organism is made of one cell; a multicellular organism of many.
Total magnification = eyepiece magnification x objective magnification.
Always focus by moving the objective lens away from the slide while looking through the eyepiece.
The nucleus contains DNA and controls the cell's activities.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy.
The cell wall is made of cellulose and supports the plant cell; it is found in plant cells only.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis.
The permanent vacuole contains cell sap and keeps a plant cell firm.
Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole; animal cells have none of these.

lessons.title: Specialised cells and how structure fits function
objectives: I can describe how a specialised cell is adapted to its job
I can link a cell's structure to its function
lessons.ncRef: Biology – cells and organisation: the similarities and differences between plant and animal cells; the role of diffusion in the movement of materials in and between cells
misconceptions: Thinking specialised cells have extra organelles rather than modified structure
Describing an adaptation without linking it to the function

assessment.detail: For six specialised cells, state one adaptation and explain how it helps the cell do its job

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment

I can explain what makes diffusion faster

misconceptions: Thinking diffusion requires energy from the cell
Believing particles stop moving once diffusion is complete
Describing diffusion as movement 'to where there is space'

assessment.detail: Observe diffusion of food colouring at two temperatures; explain the results using the particle model

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: dissolving and materials; Y6: particle ideas from states of matter

lessons.title: Levels of organisation: cells, tissues, organs, systems
objectives: I can order the levels of organisation in an organism
I can give an example at each level
lessons.ncRef: Biology – cells and organisation: the hierarchical organisation of multicellular organisms: from cells to tissues to organs to systems to organisms

Placing the levels in the wrong order

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: identify and name the main parts of the human circulatory system and describe the functions of the heart, blood vessels and blood

knowledgeComponents.statement: A specialised cell has a structure adapted to a particular function.
Red blood cells have no nucleus and are biconcave, giving more room and surface area for oxygen.
Root hair cells have a long extension that increases surface area for absorbing water.
Nerve cells are long with branched endings to carry electrical impulses over distance.
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a high to a low concentration.
Diffusion is a passive process and requires no energy input from the cell.
Diffusion is faster at higher temperature, with a steeper concentration gradient and with a larger surface area.
Particles continue to move randomly even after the concentrations are equal.
The order of organisation is cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
A tissue is a group of similar cells working together.
An organ is made of several tissues working together for one function.

weeks.unit: Biology: unicellular organisms and microscopy investigation

lessons.title: Unicellular organisms and their adaptations
objectives: I can describe the structure of a unicellular organism
I can explain how a unicellular organism carries out all life processes in one cell
lessons.ncRef: Biology – cells and organisation: the structural adaptations of some unicellular organisms
misconceptions: Thinking all microorganisms cause disease
Believing a single cell cannot move or feed

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: describe how living things are classified into broad groups including micro-organisms

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: plan enquiries, controlling variables; report and present findings including conclusions and explanations

lessons.title: Cells review and biological drawing
objectives: I can produce an accurate biological drawing with correct conventions
I can recall and apply all the cell knowledge from this unit
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – make and record observations and measurements using a range of methods; Biology – cells and organisation
misconceptions: Shading or sketching rather than using single clean lines
Crossing label lines or using arrowheads

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: record findings using scientific diagrams and labels

knowledgeComponents.statement: A unicellular organism carries out all seven life processes within a single cell.
Euglena has a flagellum for movement and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
Amoeba moves and feeds using pseudopods, extensions of its cytoplasm.
Bacterial cells have no nucleus; their DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm.
Most microorganisms are harmless or useful; only a minority cause disease.
A larger surface area to volume ratio gives a faster rate of diffusion.
A random error varies between repeats; a systematic error shifts every reading the same way.
An evaluation names the specific weakness in the method and a specific improvement.
Biological drawings use clear single lines, no shading, horizontal label lines and no arrowheads.
A biological drawing must state the magnification used.

lessons.title: The functions of the skeleton
objectives: I can state the four main functions of the skeleton
I can name the major bones of the human skeleton

misconceptions: Thinking bone is dead, dry material
Believing the skeleton's only job is support

assessment.detail: Label 12 bones from memory; answer six questions on the four functions

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: identify that humans and some animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement

lessons.title: Joints and how they move
objectives: I can name the main types of joint and give an example of each
I can describe the structures that make a joint work
lessons.ncRef: Biology – the skeletal and muscular systems: biomechanics – the interaction between skeleton and muscles, including the measurement of force exerted by different muscles
misconceptions: Confusing ligaments (bone to bone) with tendons (muscle to bone)
Thinking cartilage is a type of bone

assessment.detail: Match joint type to location; label a synovial joint and state the function of each structure

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: skeletons and muscles for movement

lessons.title: Bone as living tissue and making blood cells
objectives: I can explain that bone is living tissue that grows and repairs
I can describe the role of bone marrow
lessons.ncRef: Biology – the skeletal and muscular systems: the structure and functions of the human skeleton, to include making blood cells
misconceptions: Believing broken bones cannot repair themselves
Thinking blood is made in the heart

assessment.detail: Explain how bones repair; describe where and how blood cells are made; explain why calcium matters in the diet

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: the circulatory system and the function of blood

knowledgeComponents.statement: The four functions of the skeleton are support, protection, movement and making blood cells.
The cranium protects the brain and the ribcage protects the heart and lungs.
The femur is the thigh bone and the longest bone in the body.
Bone is living tissue with a blood supply that grows and repairs itself.
A hinge joint, such as the elbow or knee, allows movement in one plane.
A ball and socket joint, such as the hip or shoulder, allows movement in many directions.
Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
Cartilage cushions the ends of bones and synovial fluid lubricates the joint.
Red and white blood cells are made in the bone marrow of some bones.
Calcium and vitamin D are needed for strong bones.

lessons.title: Antagonistic muscle pairs
objectives: I can explain how muscles work in antagonistic pairs
I can describe what happens at the elbow when the arm bends and straightens
lessons.ncRef: Biology – the skeletal and muscular systems: the function of muscles and examples of antagonistic muscles
misconceptions: Saying a muscle 'pushes' rather than only pulls
Thinking one muscle both bends and straightens a joint

assessment.detail: Annotate the arm to show biceps and triceps action in both directions; six-mark explanation question

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: muscles for movement

lessons.title: Biomechanics: measuring muscle force
objectives: I can measure the force a muscle can exert
I can present and interpret force data
lessons.ncRef: Biology – the skeletal and muscular systems: biomechanics – the interaction between skeleton and muscles, including the measurement of force exerted by different muscles; Working scientifically – make and record measurements
misconceptions: Recording force in kilograms rather than newtons
Assuming a larger muscle is always stronger

assessment.detail: Measure grip strength across repeated trials; tabulate, calculate a mean and plot the results

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of forces; Y6 maths: mean; reading scales

lessons.title: Exercise, health and the musculoskeletal system
objectives: I can explain how exercise affects muscles and bones
I can evaluate a claim about exercise using evidence
lessons.ncRef: Biology – the skeletal and muscular systems; Working scientifically – scientific attitudes: evaluate risks; understand that scientific methods and theories develop as earlier explanations are modified
misconceptions: Believing muscle turns into fat when exercise stops
Assuming correlation proves cause

assessment.detail: Evaluate three claims about exercise; state what evidence would be needed to test each

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way the body functions

knowledgeComponents.statement: Muscles can only pull; they cannot push.
An antagonistic pair is two muscles that pull a joint in opposite directions.
To bend the arm, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.
To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.
Muscles are attached to bones by tendons, so contraction moves the bone.
Force is measured in newtons using a newtonmeter.
A joint acts as a lever with the joint as the fulcrum.
Regular exercise increases muscle strength and bone density.
Muscle and fat are different tissues; neither turns into the other.
A correlation between two variables does not by itself show that one causes the other.

lessons.title: Interleaved retrieval: working scientifically, cells and body systems
objectives: I can recall and apply the key knowledge from this half term
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – analysis and evaluation: interpret observations and data; Biology – cells and organisation; skeletal and muscular systems
misconceptions: Recognising a term without being able to explain it

assessment.detail: 40 mixed items across weeks 1–7, including six 'explain' questions

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding of cells, organisation and the musculoskeletal system
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically; Biology – structure and function of living organisms
misconceptions: Describing when the question asks you to explain

assessment.detail: 50-minute paper: recall, application, data analysis and one extended six-mark explanation; each item tagged to a knowledge component

lessons.title: Assessment review and command words
objectives: I can identify and correct my errors
I can respond correctly to different command words
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – present reasoned explanations, including explaining data in relation to predictions and hypotheses
misconceptions: Using the same style of answer regardless of the command word

assessment.type: error analysis plus command word drill
assessment.detail: Personalised correction sheet; rewrite six answers to match their command words

knowledgeComponents.statement: 'Describe' means say what is happening; 'explain' means say why it happens.
'Evaluate' requires strengths, weaknesses and a judgement.
'Suggest' asks you to apply known science to an unfamiliar situation.
Cells, tissues, organs and systems form a hierarchy of organisation.
Structure and function are linked at every level of biological organisation.
Any valid investigation controls all variables except the independent one.
A six-mark answer needs a logical sequence of linked scientific points, not a list.
Scientific terminology must be used precisely in written answers.

terms.name: Autumn 2
terms.focus: Chemistry: the particulate nature of matter and changes of state; atoms, elements and compounds; the Periodic Table.

lessons.title: Solids, liquids and gases: the particle model
objectives: I can describe the arrangement and movement of particles in each state
I can explain the properties of each state using the particle model
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the particulate nature of matter: the properties of the different states of matter (solid, liquid and gas) in terms of the particle model; Physics – matter: the differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density
misconceptions: Thinking particles themselves expand when heated
Believing there is air between particles in a solid
Thinking particles in a solid do not move at all

assessment.detail: Draw particle diagrams for all three states; explain three properties using particle arrangement

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: compare and group materials as solids, liquids or gases
Y5: know that some materials dissolve to form a solution

lessons.title: Changes of state and their names
objectives: I can name all six changes of state
I can explain each change using the particle model
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the particulate nature of matter: changes of state in terms of the particle model; Physics – matter: conservation of material and of mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation and dissolving
misconceptions: Using 'melting' for a solid dissolving in water
Thinking evaporation only happens at the boiling point
Believing steam is visible water vapour

assessment.detail: Name and describe six changes of state; explain three everyday examples using particles

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: observe that some materials change state when heated or cooled, and measure the temperature at which this happens
Y5: the water cycle including evaporation and condensation

lessons.title: Heating curves and energy in changes of state
objectives: I can interpret a heating or cooling curve
I can explain why temperature stays constant during a change of state
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – energetics: the change of temperature and the energy changes during changes of state; Physics – matter: energy in matter, changes with temperature
misconceptions: Believing temperature keeps rising while ice is melting
Thinking energy is not being supplied during the plateau

assessment.detail: Record a cooling curve for stearic acid or ice; plot the graph and explain the plateau

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: measure the temperature at which materials change state
Y6 maths: interpret line graphs

knowledgeComponents.statement: In a solid, particles are in a regular arrangement, touching, and vibrate about fixed positions.
In a liquid, particles are close together, randomly arranged, and can slide past each other.
In a gas, particles are far apart, randomly arranged, and move quickly in all directions.
Gases can be compressed because there is space between the particles.
Particles themselves never expand, melt or change size; only their arrangement and motion change.
Melting is solid to liquid; freezing is liquid to solid.
Evaporation and boiling are liquid to gas; condensation is gas to liquid.
Sublimation is solid directly to gas, as in solid carbon dioxide.
Evaporation can occur at any temperature; boiling occurs only at the boiling point.
Melting and boiling points are fixed for a pure substance.
During a change of state the temperature stays constant because energy is used to overcome forces of attraction between particles.
Mass is conserved in every change of state.

lessons.title: Gas pressure and the particle model
objectives: I can explain gas pressure in terms of particle collisions
I can predict what happens to pressure when volume or temperature changes
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the particulate nature of matter: the properties of the different states of matter in terms of the particle model, including gas pressure
misconceptions: Thinking gas pressure is caused by particles pushing each other
Believing a gas 'runs out' of pressure over time in a sealed container

assessment.detail: Explain three demonstrations (syringe, can crush, balloon in warm water) in terms of particle collisions

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: states of matter; Y5: properties of materials

lessons.title: Diffusion in gases and liquids; Brownian motion
objectives: I can explain diffusion using the particle model
I can describe the evidence that particles move randomly
lessons.ncRef: Physics – matter: Brownian motion in gases; diffusion in liquids and gases driven by differences in concentration; Chemistry – pure and impure substances: diffusion in terms of the particle model
misconceptions: Thinking diffusion requires stirring or air currents
Believing heavier gases cannot diffuse

assessment.detail: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride diffusion tube demonstration, or bromine diffusion; explain the result and the effect of temperature

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: dissolving; Y6: mixtures

lessons.title: Density and the particle model
objectives: I can calculate density from mass and volume
I can explain differences in density using particle spacing
lessons.ncRef: Physics – matter: the differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density; similarities and differences, including density differences, between solids, liquids and gases
misconceptions: Confusing density with mass, so 'heavy' is used for 'dense'
Thinking a large object must be denser than a small one
Believing ice is denser than water

assessment.detail: Determine the density of three regular and two irregular solids by measurement and displacement; predict which will float

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: compare and group materials by their properties including solubility
Y6 maths: volume of cuboids; division; units

knowledgeComponents.statement: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.
Reducing the volume of a gas increases pressure because collisions become more frequent.
Increasing temperature makes gas particles move faster, increasing pressure in a sealed container.
Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a high to a low concentration due to random motion.
Brownian motion is the random jiggling of visible particles caused by collisions with invisible particles.
Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids because gas particles move faster and are further apart.
Lighter gas particles diffuse faster than heavier ones at the same temperature.
Density = mass divided by volume.
Density is measured in grams per cubic centimetre or kilograms per cubic metre.
An object floats if it is less dense than the fluid it is placed in.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.
The volume of an irregular solid can be found by water displacement.

lessons.title: Atoms and the structure of the atom
objectives: I can describe the simple structure of an atom
I can name the three subatomic particles and where they are found
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – atoms, elements and compounds: a simple (Dalton) atomic model
misconceptions: Drawing the nucleus far too large relative to the atom
Thinking atoms are the smallest possible things with nothing inside

assessment.detail: Draw and label an atom; complete a table of the three subatomic particles with charge and location

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: properties and changes of materials

lessons.title: Elements and chemical symbols
objectives: I can define an element
I can write and read chemical symbols correctly
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – atoms, elements and compounds: differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
misconceptions: Writing a symbol with two capital letters, e.g. CO for cobalt
Confusing Co (cobalt) with CO (carbon monoxide)

assessment.detail: Write the symbols for 25 common elements from memory, and name 25 from their symbols

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: compare and group materials by their properties

lessons.title: The Periodic Table: an introduction
objectives: I can describe how the Periodic Table is arranged
I can use the table to find information about an element
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the Periodic Table: the principles underpinning the Mendeleev Periodic Table; the properties of metals and non-metals; the periodic table: periods and groups; atomic number
misconceptions: Reading groups as horizontal rows
Believing Mendeleev's table was arranged by atomic number rather than atomic mass

assessment.detail: Locate elements by group and period; classify twelve elements as metal or non-metal; explain why Mendeleev left gaps

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: compare and group everyday materials on the basis of their properties

knowledgeComponents.statement: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; electrons orbit in shells around it.
Protons are positive, electrons are negative and neutrons have no charge.
Almost all of an atom's volume is empty space; the nucleus is tiny by comparison.
An element is a substance made of only one type of atom.
A chemical symbol has a capital first letter and, if there is a second letter, it is lower case.
Common symbols: H hydrogen, O oxygen, C carbon, N nitrogen, Na sodium, Fe iron, Cu copper, Ca calcium, Cl chlorine, Mg magnesium.
Groups are the vertical columns of the Periodic Table; periods are the horizontal rows.
Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
Metals are on the left of the Periodic Table and non-metals on the right.
Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and left gaps for elements not yet discovered.
The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom and identifies the element.

lessons.title: Properties of metals and non-metals
objectives: I can list the typical properties of metals and non-metals
I can classify an element from its properties
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the Periodic Table: the properties of metals and non-metals; Chemistry – materials: the properties of ceramics, polymers and composites
misconceptions: Believing all metals are magnetic
Thinking mercury is not a metal because it is liquid
Assuming all non-metals are gases

assessment.detail: Test six unknown elements for conductivity, appearance and hardness; classify each and justify

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: compare and group everyday materials on the basis of their properties, including hardness, solubility, transparency, conductivity and response to magnets

lessons.title: Compounds and chemical formulae
objectives: I can explain the difference between an element and a compound
I can interpret a chemical formula
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – atoms, elements and compounds: the differences between atoms, elements and compounds; chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds
misconceptions: Reading H2O as containing two water molecules
Thinking a compound is a mixture of elements
Believing a compound keeps the properties of its elements

assessment.detail: Interpret twelve formulae: name the elements and count the atoms of each; classify twenty substances as element, compound or mixture

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: know that some changes result in the formation of new materials, and that this kind of change is not usually reversible

lessons.title: Naming compounds and word equations
objectives: I can name a simple compound from the elements it contains
I can write a word equation for a reaction
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – atoms, elements and compounds: chemical symbols and formulae for elements and compounds; chemical reactions: representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
misconceptions: Applying the -ide ending when oxygen is present as well as a third element
Writing an equation with an equals sign instead of an arrow

assessment.detail: Name fifteen compounds from their constituent elements; write eight word equations from descriptions

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: irreversible changes producing new materials

knowledgeComponents.statement: Metals are shiny, malleable, ductile, and good conductors of heat and electricity.
Non-metals are usually dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors.
Only iron, cobalt and nickel are magnetic among common metals.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity, which is an exception to the general rule.
A compound contains two or more elements chemically bonded together.
In H2O the subscript 2 means two hydrogen atoms are bonded to one oxygen atom.
A compound has different properties from the elements that make it.
A compound of two elements ends in -ide, e.g. magnesium oxide.
A compound containing oxygen plus another element ends in -ate, e.g. copper sulfate.
In a word equation, reactants are written on the left and products on the right, joined by an arrow.

weeks.unit: Chemistry: mixtures and conservation of mass

lessons.title: Mixtures compared with compounds
objectives: I can explain the difference between a mixture and a compound
I can decide whether a substance is pure or a mixture
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: the concept of a pure substance; mixtures, including dissolving
misconceptions: Using 'pure' in the everyday sense of 'natural' or 'healthy'
Thinking air is a compound
Believing a mixture cannot be separated

assessment.detail: Classify twenty substances as element, compound or mixture; explain the reasoning for five of them

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: know that some materials will dissolve in liquid to form a solution, and describe how to recover a substance from a solution

lessons.title: Conservation of mass in chemical reactions
objectives: I can state that mass is conserved in a chemical reaction
I can explain an apparent mass change
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – atoms, elements and compounds: conservation of mass changes of state and chemical reactions; chemical reactions: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
misconceptions: Thinking mass is lost when a gas escapes
Believing burning always reduces mass
Thinking atoms are created or destroyed in a reaction

assessment.detail: Weigh reactants and products for a reaction in a closed and an open container; explain both results

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: explain that some changes result in the formation of new materials

lessons.title: Physical and chemical changes
objectives: I can distinguish a physical change from a chemical change
I can give evidence that a chemical reaction has occurred
lessons.ncRef: Physics – matter: the difference between chemical and physical changes; Chemistry – chemical reactions: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
misconceptions: Assuming all irreversible changes are chemical and all reversible ones physical
Thinking dissolving is a chemical change
Believing a colour change always means a chemical reaction

assessment.detail: Observe six changes; classify each as physical or chemical and give the evidence used

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: explain that some changes result in the formation of new materials and that this kind of change is not usually reversible

knowledgeComponents.statement: A mixture contains substances that are not chemically joined and can be separated physically.
In science, a pure substance contains only one element or one compound.
Air is a mixture of gases, mainly nitrogen and oxygen.
In a solution, the solute dissolves in the solvent.
A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point; a mixture melts over a range.
Mass is always conserved in a chemical reaction because atoms are only rearranged.
An apparent loss of mass usually means a gas has escaped from an open container.
An apparent gain of mass on burning means a gas from the air has combined with the substance.
In a physical change no new substance is made and the change is usually easy to reverse.
Evidence of a chemical reaction includes a gas given off, a precipitate, a permanent colour change or a temperature change.
Dissolving is a physical change: the solute can be recovered by evaporation.

lessons.title: Investigation: what affects the rate of dissolving?
objectives: I can plan and carry out an investigation into dissolving
I can explain my results using the particle model
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – select, plan and carry out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries; Chemistry – pure and impure substances: mixtures, including dissolving
misconceptions: Thinking sugar disappears when it dissolves
Believing a solution weighs less than the solute plus solvent

assessment.detail: Plan, run and write up an investigation into temperature or surface area and dissolving rate, including a particle-model explanation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: use knowledge of solids, liquids and gases to decide how mixtures might be separated; dissolving

lessons.title: Materials: ceramics, polymers and composites
objectives: I can describe the properties of ceramics, polymers and composites
I can select a material for a purpose and justify the choice
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – materials: the properties of ceramics, polymers and composites (qualitative)
misconceptions: Thinking all plastics behave identically
Believing composites are just mixtures with no structural advantage

assessment.detail: Choose materials for four given applications and justify each choice by property

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: compare and group everyday materials on the basis of their properties; give reasons for the particular uses of everyday materials

lessons.title: How scientific models change: atomic models through history
objectives: I can describe how the model of the atom has changed over time
I can explain why scientists change a model
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – scientific attitudes: understand that scientific methods and theories develop as earlier explanations are modified to take account of new evidence and ideas, together with the importance of publishing results and peer review
misconceptions: Thinking earlier scientists were simply wrong rather than working with less evidence
Believing scientific models are facts that never change

assessment.detail: Build a timeline of four atomic models; explain for each what new evidence forced the change

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise that scientific ideas change and develop over time

knowledgeComponents.statement: Dissolving is faster at higher temperature, with smaller particles and with stirring.
A dissolved solute is still present; the particles are spread between the solvent particles.
The mass of a solution equals the mass of the solute plus the mass of the solvent.
A saturated solution can dissolve no more solute at that temperature.
Ceramics are hard, brittle, heat-resistant and are electrical insulators.
Polymers are made of long chain molecules and are usually flexible and light.
A composite combines two materials to give properties better than either alone, e.g. reinforced concrete.
A scientific model is a simplified representation used to explain and predict.
Models change when new evidence cannot be explained by the existing model.
Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus.
Peer review is the checking of scientific work by other scientists before publication.

lessons.title: Interleaved retrieval: particles, atoms and the Periodic Table
objectives: I can recall and apply the chemistry knowledge from this half term
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the particulate nature of matter; atoms, elements and compounds; the Periodic Table
misconceptions: Reciting the particle arrangements without using them to explain a property

assessment.detail: 40 mixed items across weeks 9–14, plus five biology items from Autumn 1 for spacing

lessons.title: Autumn term assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding of the autumn term biology and chemistry
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically; Biology – structure and function of living organisms; Chemistry – the particulate nature of matter and atoms, elements and compounds
misconceptions: Neglecting the working scientifically questions

assessment.detail: 60-minute cumulative paper covering weeks 1–14, including a data-analysis section and one six-mark question

lessons.title: Review, gap repair and a chemistry demonstration
objectives: I can correct my errors and name the misconception behind each
I can explain a demonstration using the particle model
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – present reasoned explanations; interpret observations and identify patterns
misconceptions: Correcting an answer without understanding why it was wrong

assessment.detail: Personalised correction sheet; write a full particle-model explanation of a demonstration such as the collapsing can

knowledgeComponents.statement: The particle model explains states, changes of state, pressure, diffusion and density.
Elements contain one type of atom; compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically joined; mixtures are not chemically joined.
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, only rearranged.
The Periodic Table is arranged so that elements with similar properties fall in the same group.
A good scientific explanation links observation to the model that accounts for it.
Correcting an error requires naming the misconception behind it.
A cumulative assessment tests retention as well as recent learning.
Data-analysis questions require reading the graph or table before answering.

terms.name: Spring 1
terms.focus: Physics: forces, their effects, balanced and unbalanced forces, pressure in fluids, and describing motion.

lessons.title: What is a force? Contact and non-contact forces
objectives: I can define a force and give its unit
I can classify forces as contact or non-contact
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: forces as pushes or pulls, arising from the interaction between 2 objects; non-contact forces: gravity forces acting at a distance on Earth and in space, forces between magnets, and forces due to static electricity
misconceptions: Thinking a moving object 'carries' a force inside it
Believing gravity requires air to act
Treating force as a substance rather than an interaction

assessment.detail: Classify sixteen forces; explain three everyday situations in terms of the interacting pair

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity; identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction

lessons.title: Measuring force and Hooke's law
objectives: I can measure force with a newtonmeter
I can describe and explain the relationship between force and extension in a spring
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: forces measured in newtons, measurements of stretch or compression as force is changed; force-extension linear relation; Hooke's law as a special case
misconceptions: Recording total length rather than extension
Assuming the relationship stays linear beyond the limit of proportionality

assessment.detail: Measure spring extension for increasing loads; plot force against extension and identify where proportionality ends

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of forces; Y6 maths: plotting graphs, gradient

lessons.title: Weight, mass and gravity
objectives: I can distinguish mass from weight
I can calculate weight from mass and gravitational field strength
lessons.ncRef: Physics – space physics: gravity force, weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g), on Earth g = 10 N/kg, different on other planets and stars
misconceptions: Using mass and weight interchangeably
Thinking mass changes on the Moon
Giving weight in kilograms

assessment.detail: Ten calculations of weight on Earth, the Moon and Mars; explain in writing why mass is unchanged

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity acting between the Earth and the falling object

knowledgeComponents.statement: A force is a push or a pull arising from an interaction between two objects.
Force is measured in newtons, symbol N.
Contact forces require the objects to be touching; non-contact forces act at a distance.
The three non-contact forces met at KS3 are gravity, magnetism and electrostatic force.
Extension is the increase in length, found by subtracting the original length from the new length.
Hooke's law states that extension is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.
Beyond the limit of proportionality a spring does not return to its original length.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and does not change with location.
Weight is the force of gravity on an object, measured in newtons, and changes with location.
Weight = mass x gravitational field strength; on Earth g is about 10 N/kg.
Gravitational field strength on the Moon is about 1.6 N/kg, roughly one sixth of Earth's.

lessons.title: Force diagrams and resultant force
objectives: I can draw a force diagram with correctly labelled arrows
I can calculate the resultant of forces acting in one line
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: using force arrows in diagrams, adding forces in one dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces
misconceptions: Drawing arrow length unrelated to force size
Adding forces that act in opposite directions
Thinking a balanced force means no force at all

assessment.detail: Draw eight force diagrams and calculate the resultant force and direction for each

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction that act between moving surfaces

lessons.title: Balanced forces: equilibrium, springs and supporting surfaces
objectives: I can explain what happens when forces are balanced
I can identify the pairs of balanced forces in a stationary object
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: balanced forces – opposing forces and equilibrium: weight held by stretched spring or supported on a compressed surface
misconceptions: Believing a table cannot exert an upward force because it is not alive
Thinking balanced forces mean an object must be stationary rather than at constant velocity

assessment.detail: Identify balanced pairs in six situations; explain how a table supports a book

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of forces including gravity

lessons.title: Unbalanced forces and their effects on motion
objectives: I can predict the effect of an unbalanced force on an object
I can explain that a force can change speed, direction or shape
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: forces being needed to cause objects to stop or start moving, or to change their speed or direction of motion (qualitative only); change depending on direction of force and its size
misconceptions: Believing a constant force is needed to keep an object moving at a steady speed
Thinking a moving object must have a forward force acting on it

assessment.detail: Predict the motion in eight scenarios from the force diagram and explain each prediction

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction

knowledgeComponents.statement: On a force diagram, arrow length shows the size of the force and arrow direction shows its direction.
Forces in the same direction are added; forces in opposite directions are subtracted.
The resultant force is the single force with the same effect as all the forces combined.
Forces are balanced when the resultant force is zero.
A surface pushes back on an object resting on it with a normal contact force.
An object with balanced forces stays still or keeps moving at a constant speed in a straight line.
An unbalanced force changes an object's speed, direction of motion, or shape.
No force is needed to keep an object moving at a steady speed if there is no friction.
A resultant force in the direction of motion speeds an object up; a resultant force against the motion slows it down.

lessons.title: Friction, drag and air resistance
objectives: I can describe friction and drag and where they act
I can explain when friction is useful and when it is a nuisance
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: forces: associated with... friction, including air resistance, and with rotation
misconceptions: Thinking friction always acts backwards relative to the ground rather than opposing relative motion
Believing friction is always a problem to be removed

assessment.detail: Investigate friction on different surfaces using a newtonmeter; tabulate, graph and conclude

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction that act between moving surfaces

lessons.title: Moments: the turning effect of a force
objectives: I can calculate the moment of a force
I can apply the principle of moments to a balanced lever
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: moment as the turning effect of a force
misconceptions: Measuring distance from the wrong point
Ignoring that distance must be perpendicular to the force
Confusing moment with force

assessment.detail: Balance a metre rule with masses; calculate moments; solve eight numerical problems

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: recognise that levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect
Y6 maths: multiplication; rearranging a formula

lessons.title: Pressure in fluids: liquids and the atmosphere
objectives: I can calculate pressure from force and area
I can explain how pressure changes with depth and with height
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: pressure in fluids: atmospheric pressure, decreases with increase of height as weight of air above decreases with height; pressure measured by ratio of force over area
misconceptions: Confusing pressure with force
Thinking pressure in a liquid acts only downwards
Believing atmospheric pressure pushes only down

assessment.detail: Ten pressure calculations; explain why a dam is thicker at the base and why ears pop on a mountain

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of forces; Y6 maths: division, area, units

knowledgeComponents.statement: Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces.
Drag is the resistance force from a fluid such as air or water.
Friction is useful for walking, gripping and braking, and unhelpful when it wastes energy as heat.
Streamlining reduces drag by allowing fluid to flow smoothly around an object.
Moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Moment is measured in newton metres (Nm).
A lever is balanced when the clockwise moment equals the anticlockwise moment.
Pressure = force divided by area.
Pressure is measured in pascals; 1 pascal is 1 newton per square metre.
Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and acts equally in all directions.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because there is less air above.
Upthrust is the upward force from a fluid; an object floats when upthrust equals weight.

lessons.title: Speed: calculating and measuring
objectives: I can calculate speed from distance and time
I can rearrange the speed equation to find distance or time
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: describing motion – speed and the quantitative relationship between average speed, distance and time (speed = distance / time)
misconceptions: Confusing average speed with instantaneous speed
Failing to convert units before calculating
Rearranging the formula incorrectly

assessment.detail: Measure walking and running speed over a measured distance; complete fifteen calculations including rearrangement

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: use simple formulae; convert units of measure; division

lessons.title: Distance-time graphs
objectives: I can plot and interpret a distance-time graph
I can find speed from the gradient of a distance-time graph
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: representing journeys on distance-time graphs
misconceptions: Reading a horizontal line as moving backwards rather than stationary
Treating the graph as a map of the route
Confusing a steeper line with a longer journey

assessment.detail: Interpret three distance-time graphs including a return journey; plot one from a description and calculate two speeds

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: interpret and construct line graphs and use these to solve problems

lessons.title: Relative motion
objectives: I can describe motion relative to a chosen observer
I can explain that whether something is moving depends on the frame of reference
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces: relative motion – trains and cars passing one another
misconceptions: Assuming there is a single absolute answer to whether something is moving
Adding relative speeds when objects travel in the same direction

assessment.detail: Solve six relative motion problems involving vehicles and passengers; explain two in full sentences

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: forces and motion; Y6 maths: addition and subtraction of measures

knowledgeComponents.statement: Speed = distance divided by time.
Speed is measured in metres per second (m/s) or kilometres per hour (km/h).
Distance = speed x time, and time = distance divided by speed.
Average speed uses total distance and total time, including any stops.
Units must match before a speed calculation: convert minutes to seconds and kilometres to metres.
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a greater speed.
A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary.
Speed is the gradient of a distance-time graph.
Whether an object is moving depends on the observer's frame of reference.
Two cars travelling in the same direction at similar speeds have a small relative speed.

lessons.title: Investigation: what affects the speed of a falling object?
objectives: I can plan and carry out an investigation into falling objects
I can explain the results using balanced and unbalanced forces
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – select, plan and carry out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries; Physics – motion and forces
misconceptions: Thinking heavier objects always fall faster in the absence of air resistance
Believing terminal velocity means the object stops

assessment.detail: Paper spinner or parachute investigation: plan, results, graph, conclusion and evaluation with a force explanation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: identify the effects of air resistance; Y6: plan enquiries and control variables

lessons.title: Simple machines: levers, pulleys and gears
objectives: I can explain how a simple machine changes the size or direction of a force
I can identify the effort, load and pivot in a machine
lessons.ncRef: Physics – energy: energy changes and transfers – simple machines give bigger force but at the expense of smaller movement (and vice versa): product of force and displacement stays the same; Physics – moments
misconceptions: Believing a machine creates extra energy
Thinking a longer lever gives a greater force with no trade-off

assessment.detail: Measure the effort needed to lift a load with and without a pulley; explain the trade-off in force and distance

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: recognise that some mechanisms, including levers, pulleys and gears, allow a smaller force to have a greater effect

lessons.title: Forces in the real world: safety and design
objectives: I can apply force ideas to a real design problem
I can explain how a safety feature reduces harm
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces; Working scientifically – scientific attitudes: evaluate risks; pay attention to objectivity
misconceptions: Thinking a safety feature removes the force rather than spreading it over time or area

assessment.detail: Explain how four safety features work in terms of force, area and time; design and justify one improvement

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: forces; Y6: report and present findings including causal relationships

knowledgeComponents.statement: A falling object speeds up until drag equals weight, at which point it falls at a constant terminal velocity.
Terminal velocity means constant speed, not zero speed.
With no air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass.
A larger surface area increases air resistance and lowers terminal velocity.
A simple machine gives a larger force in exchange for a smaller movement.
The product of force and displacement is unchanged by a simple machine.
In a lever the effort and load act about a pivot, and a longer effort arm reduces the effort needed.
A crumple zone increases the time of impact, which reduces the force experienced.
Spreading a force over a larger area reduces the pressure and so reduces damage.

lessons.title: Interleaved retrieval: forces and motion
objectives: I can recall and apply the physics knowledge from this half term
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces; Working scientifically – analysis and evaluation
misconceptions: Recalling an equation but not knowing which quantity is which

assessment.detail: 40 mixed items across weeks 16–20, plus five chemistry and five biology items for spacing

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding of forces, pressure and motion
lessons.ncRef: Physics – motion and forces; Working scientifically
misconceptions: Omitting units from calculated answers

assessment.detail: 50-minute paper with a calculation section, a graph section and one six-mark explanation; items tagged to knowledge components

lessons.title: Review, gap repair and equation practice
objectives: I can correct my errors
I can use every physics equation from this unit fluently
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – measurement: undertake basic data analysis including simple statistical techniques; apply mathematical concepts and calculate results
misconceptions: Substituting into an equation before rearranging it

assessment.detail: Timed 30-item equation drill covering weight, speed, pressure, density and moments; personalised correction sheet

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: use simple formulae; rearrange to find a missing value

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Year 7 physics equations are: weight = mass x g, speed = distance / time, pressure = force / area, density = mass / volume, moment = force x distance.
Every calculated answer needs a number and a unit.
An equation should be rearranged first, then values substituted.
Balanced forces produce no change in motion; unbalanced forces change speed, direction or shape.
Forces always come in interaction pairs between two objects.
Gradient on a distance-time graph gives speed.
Working should be shown so method marks can be awarded even when the answer is wrong.
Units must be converted to a consistent system before substituting into an equation.

terms.name: Spring 2
terms.focus: Biology: reproduction in humans and plants, interdependence in ecosystems, and health.
terms.note: The reproduction unit is a statutory part of the KS3 science programme of study and is taught factually and age-appropriately. A home educator may wish to preview these lessons and coordinate them with any relationships education being taught separately.

lessons.title: The human reproductive systems
objectives: I can name the main structures of the male and female reproductive systems
I can state the function of each structure
lessons.ncRef: Biology – structure and function of living organisms: reproduction – reproduction in humans (as an example of a mammal), including the structure and function of the male and female reproductive systems
misconceptions: Confusing the oviduct with the uterus
Thinking urine and gametes leave by the same route in females

assessment.detail: Label both systems from memory; complete a table of structures and their functions

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: describe the life process of reproduction in some plants and animals
Y5: describe the changes as humans develop to old age

lessons.title: Gametes and fertilisation
objectives: I can describe how sperm and egg cells are adapted to their function
I can explain what happens at fertilisation
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: the structure and function of the male and female reproductive systems, gametes, fertilisation
misconceptions: Thinking the egg is fertilised in the uterus rather than the oviduct
Believing many sperm enter the egg

assessment.detail: Explain three adaptations of sperm and two of the egg; describe fertilisation in a labelled sequence

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: describe the life process of reproduction in some plants and animals

lessons.title: The menstrual cycle
objectives: I can describe the main stages of the menstrual cycle
I can explain the purpose of the uterus lining
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: the menstrual cycle (without details of hormones)
misconceptions: Believing every cycle is exactly 28 days
Thinking ovulation and menstruation happen at the same time

assessment.detail: Annotate a 28-day cycle diagram with the four stages; answer six questions on timing and purpose

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: describe the changes as humans develop to old age, including puberty

knowledgeComponents.statement: The ovaries produce egg cells; the testes produce sperm cells.
The oviduct carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus and is where fertilisation occurs.
The uterus is where a fertilised egg implants and the fetus develops.
Gametes are the sex cells: the sperm and the egg.
A sperm cell has a tail for swimming, many mitochondria for energy, and an enzyme-containing head.
The egg cell is large and contains a food store for the early embryo.
Fertilisation is the fusion of the nucleus of a sperm with the nucleus of an egg.
The fertilised egg is called a zygote and it divides to form an embryo.
Menstruation is the loss of the uterus lining and marks the start of the cycle.
Ovulation is the release of an egg, typically around day 14 of a 28-day cycle.
Cycle length varies between individuals and between cycles; 28 days is only an average.

lessons.title: Gestation: the developing fetus
objectives: I can describe how a fetus develops during gestation
I can explain the role of the placenta and umbilical cord
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: gestation and birth
misconceptions: Thinking the mother's and fetus's blood mix directly
Believing the amniotic fluid provides food

assessment.detail: Label a diagram of the uterus in pregnancy; explain the exchange at the placenta using diffusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: describe the changes as humans develop to old age

lessons.title: How maternal lifestyle affects the fetus
objectives: I can explain how substances cross the placenta
I can describe the effect of smoking, alcohol and diet on a developing fetus
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: the effect of maternal lifestyle on the fetus through the placenta
misconceptions: Thinking the placenta filters out all harmful substances
Believing effects only occur late in pregnancy

assessment.detail: Interpret data on smoking and birth weight; write a six-mark explanation of how a substance reaches the fetus and its effect

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way their bodies function

lessons.title: Puberty and adolescence
objectives: I can describe the physical changes that occur during puberty
I can explain why these changes happen
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: reproduction in humans, including... the effect of maternal lifestyle; linked to the KS2 requirement to describe the changes as humans develop to old age including puberty
misconceptions: Believing puberty happens at the same age for everyone
Thinking the changes are complete within a year

assessment.detail: Classify twelve changes as male, female or both; explain the biological purpose of two of them

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: describe the changes as humans develop to old age, including the changes experienced in puberty

knowledgeComponents.statement: Human gestation lasts about 40 weeks, or nine months.
The placenta allows exchange of substances between mother and fetus without their blood mixing.
Oxygen and nutrients diffuse from mother to fetus; carbon dioxide and waste diffuse the other way.
The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta.
Amniotic fluid cushions and protects the fetus.
Nicotine, carbon monoxide, alcohol and some medicines can cross the placenta.
Carbon monoxide from smoking reduces the oxygen the fetus receives, which can lower birth weight.
Puberty is the period when the reproductive system matures and secondary sexual characteristics develop.
Puberty is triggered by hormones and occurs over several years, at different ages for different people.

lessons.title: Flower structure and pollination
objectives: I can name the parts of a flower and state their functions
I can compare insect and wind pollination
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: reproduction in plants, including flower structure, wind and insect pollination, fertilisation, seed and fruit formation and dispersal, including quantitative investigation of some dispersal mechanisms
misconceptions: Confusing pollination with fertilisation
Thinking all flowers are pollinated by insects
Believing pollen is a plant's seed

assessment.detail: Dissect a flower; produce a labelled diagram; complete a comparison table of insect and wind pollinated flowers

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: explore the part that flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal
Y5: describe the life process of reproduction in some plants

lessons.title: Fertilisation, seed and fruit formation
objectives: I can describe fertilisation in a flowering plant
I can explain how the ovary becomes a fruit and the ovule a seed
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: reproduction in plants, including fertilisation, seed and fruit formation
misconceptions: Thinking a fruit must be sweet and edible
Believing pollen travels down the style by itself without a pollen tube

assessment.detail: Order the eight stages from pollination to seed; explain which flower part becomes which part of the fruit

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: seed formation and dispersal
Y5: reproduction in plants

lessons.title: Seed dispersal: a quantitative investigation
objectives: I can describe the main methods of seed dispersal
I can investigate a dispersal mechanism quantitatively
lessons.ncRef: Biology – reproduction: seed and fruit formation and dispersal, including quantitative investigation of some dispersal mechanisms; Working scientifically – make and record measurements
misconceptions: Thinking dispersal is only about spreading, not about avoiding competition with the parent plant
Assuming a model sycamore seed behaves identically to the real one

assessment.detail: Build and test paper helicopter models of winged seeds; measure fall time against wing length, tabulate, graph and conclude

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: seed dispersal
Y6: plan enquiries, take repeat measurements and present data in graphs

knowledgeComponents.statement: The stamen is the male part of a flower and consists of the anther and filament.
The carpel is the female part and consists of the stigma, style and ovary.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma.
Insect-pollinated flowers have large bright petals, scent, nectar and sticky pollen.
Wind-pollinated flowers have small dull petals, exposed anthers, feathery stigmas and light, smooth pollen.
After pollination a pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
Fertilisation in plants is the fusion of the pollen nucleus with the ovule nucleus.
After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Seed dispersal methods include wind, animal, water and explosive mechanisms.
Dispersal reduces competition between the parent plant and its offspring for light, water and nutrients.

lessons.title: Food chains, food webs and energy transfer
objectives: I can construct a food chain and a food web
I can explain what happens to a population when one species is removed
lessons.ncRef: Biology – interactions and interdependencies: relationships in an ecosystem – the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem, including food webs and insect pollinated crops
misconceptions: Drawing arrows in the direction of eating rather than of energy transfer
Thinking removing a predator always benefits the prey population indefinitely

assessment.detail: Construct a food web from a species list; predict and justify the effect of removing two named species

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey
Y6: give reasons for classifying plants and animals

lessons.title: Pollinators, crops and the accumulation of toxic materials
objectives: I can explain why insect pollinators matter for food production
I can explain how toxic materials build up along a food chain
lessons.ncRef: Biology – interactions and interdependencies: the importance of insect pollinated crops; how organisms affect, and are affected by, their environment, including the accumulation of toxic materials
misconceptions: Thinking a toxin becomes less concentrated as it moves up the chain
Believing pollinator decline affects only wild plants

assessment.detail: Interpret bioaccumulation data across four trophic levels; explain the pattern and its consequences

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: describe how living things are classified; Y4: food chains

lessons.title: Sampling an ecosystem
objectives: I can use a quadrat to sample a habitat
I can estimate a population from sample data
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – make and record observations and measurements using a range of methods for different investigations; apply sampling techniques; Biology – interactions and interdependencies
misconceptions: Placing quadrats where the plants look interesting, introducing bias
Assuming one small sample represents the whole area

assessment.detail: Use random quadrat sampling in a garden or park; calculate mean abundance and estimate total population; evaluate the sampling method

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: record data using classification keys and tables
Y6 maths: mean, scaling up, proportion

knowledgeComponents.statement: A producer makes its own food by photosynthesis and begins every food chain.
Arrows in a food chain point in the direction that energy is transferred, from the eaten to the eater.
A food web shows the many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.
Removing one species from a food web affects many others, not only its direct predator or prey.
Decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.
Around three quarters of leading global food crops depend to some degree on animal pollination.
Toxic materials become more concentrated at each higher trophic level, a process called bioaccumulation.
A quadrat is a square frame used to sample the abundance of organisms in a set area.
Quadrats must be placed randomly to avoid bias in the sample.
A population is estimated by scaling the mean number per quadrat up to the total area.

lessons.title: Recreational drugs and their effects on the body
objectives: I can explain how recreational drugs affect behaviour, health and life processes
I can evaluate evidence about the effects of a drug
lessons.ncRef: Biology – health: the effects of recreational drugs (including substance misuse) on behaviour, health and life processes
misconceptions: Thinking only illegal substances count as drugs
Believing alcohol is a stimulant because it makes people lively

assessment.detail: Classify six drugs as stimulant or depressant; evaluate a data set on alcohol and reaction time

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way their bodies function

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding of reproduction, ecosystems and health
lessons.ncRef: Biology – structure and function of living organisms; interactions and interdependencies; health; Working scientifically
misconceptions: Using everyday rather than scientific vocabulary in written answers

assessment.detail: 50-minute paper on weeks 22–26 with cumulative items from the autumn term; one six-mark question

lessons.title: Review, gap repair and interleaved retrieval
objectives: I can correct my errors and name the misconception behind each
I can retrieve content from all three sciences so far this year
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – present reasoned explanations; evaluate data
misconceptions: Assuming autumn term content is secure without retesting

assessment.detail: Personalised correction sheet; 40-item quiz sampling biology, chemistry and physics from weeks 1–26

knowledgeComponents.statement: A drug is any substance that changes the way the body works.
A stimulant speeds up messages in the nervous system; a depressant slows them down.
Alcohol is a depressant and slows reaction times.
Nicotine is a stimulant and is addictive.
Tolerance means larger doses are needed to produce the same effect over time.
Caffeine, alcohol and medicines are all drugs, whether legal or not.
Reproduction in humans and in plants both involve the fusion of two gamete nuclei.
Diffusion explains gas exchange at the placenta, in cells and in the lungs alike.
Scientific vocabulary must replace everyday vocabulary in written answers.

terms.name: Summer 1
terms.focus: Chemistry: pure and impure substances and separation techniques; chemical reactions; acids, alkalis and neutralisation; energetics and metal reactivity.

lessons.title: Solutions, solubility and saturation
objectives: I can use the terms solute, solvent, solution and solubility correctly
I can describe how temperature affects solubility
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: mixtures, including dissolving
misconceptions: Thinking a solute disappears when it dissolves
Believing all solids become more soluble in hot water

assessment.detail: Determine the solubility of a salt at three temperatures; plot a solubility curve and interpret it

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: know that some materials will dissolve in liquid to form a solution, and describe how to recover a substance from a solution

lessons.title: Filtration and evaporation
objectives: I can separate an insoluble solid from a liquid by filtration
I can recover a dissolved solid by evaporation or crystallisation
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation
misconceptions: Thinking filtration separates a dissolved solid from its solvent
Confusing the residue with the filtrate

assessment.detail: Separate a sand, salt and water mixture; explain each step and justify the technique used

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: use knowledge of solids, liquids and gases to decide how mixtures might be separated, including through filtering, sieving and evaporating

lessons.title: Distillation: simple and fractional
objectives: I can describe how distillation separates a liquid from a solution
I can explain how fractional distillation separates two liquids
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: simple techniques for separating mixtures: distillation
misconceptions: Thinking distillation destroys the dissolved solid
Believing the collected liquid is the substance with the higher boiling point

assessment.detail: Distil salt water and, if available, an ink or ethanol-water mixture; draw and label the apparatus and explain the process

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: separating mixtures; Y4: changes of state

knowledgeComponents.statement: A solute dissolves in a solvent to make a solution.
Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in a fixed volume of solvent at a given temperature.
Most solids become more soluble in water as temperature rises, but gases become less soluble.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
The residue stays in the filter paper; the filtrate passes through.
Evaporation and crystallisation recover a dissolved solid from a solution.
Distillation separates a liquid from a solution by boiling then condensing the vapour.
Fractional distillation separates liquids with different boiling points; the liquid with the lower boiling point distils first.
A condenser cools the vapour so it turns back into liquid.

lessons.title: Chromatography
objectives: I can use chromatography to separate a mixture of coloured substances
I can interpret a chromatogram
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: simple techniques for separating mixtures: chromatography; the identification of pure substances
misconceptions: Drawing the baseline in ink rather than pencil
Starting the experiment with the baseline below the solvent level

assessment.detail: Separate ink or food colouring; interpret which pens contain which dyes and identify an unknown

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: separating mixtures; dissolving

lessons.title: Testing for purity
objectives: I can use melting point to test whether a substance is pure
I can explain how impurities change melting and boiling points
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: the concept of a pure substance; the identification of pure substances
misconceptions: Using 'pure' to mean 'natural'
Thinking an impurity always raises the melting point

assessment.detail: Given melting point data for four samples, decide which are pure and justify each decision

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: measure the temperature at which materials change state

lessons.title: Choosing and combining separation techniques
objectives: I can select the right separation technique for a mixture
I can plan a sequence of techniques to separate a complex mixture
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
misconceptions: Choosing a technique by habit rather than by the properties of the mixture

assessment.detail: Plan a full separation of a four-component mixture and justify each technique chosen

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: decide how mixtures might be separated

knowledgeComponents.statement: Chromatography separates substances by how strongly they are attracted to the paper compared with the solvent.
The baseline in chromatography must be drawn in pencil, because ink would dissolve and separate.
The solvent level must start below the baseline so the sample is not washed off.
A pure substance produces a single spot on a chromatogram.
A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point.
An impurity lowers the melting point and makes it melt over a range.
An impurity raises the boiling point of a liquid.
The separation technique is chosen from the physical properties of the components, especially solubility and boiling point.
Filtration is used first to remove any insoluble solid before other techniques are applied.

lessons.title: What happens in a chemical reaction?
objectives: I can explain a chemical reaction as the rearrangement of atoms
I can identify reactants and products in a reaction
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms; representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
misconceptions: Thinking atoms are created or destroyed
Believing a reaction can be reversed simply by cooling

assessment.detail: Model three reactions with atom models; write word equations and state what is conserved

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: explain that some changes result in the formation of new materials and that this kind of change is not usually reversible

lessons.title: Combustion and oxidation
objectives: I can describe combustion as a reaction with oxygen
I can write word equations for combustion and oxidation reactions
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
misconceptions: Thinking mass is lost during burning
Believing incomplete combustion is the same reaction as complete combustion

assessment.detail: Burn magnesium and observe the mass change; write word equations for five combustion reactions

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: irreversible changes such as burning; Y5: properties of materials

lessons.title: Thermal decomposition and displacement
objectives: I can describe thermal decomposition and give an example
I can predict the products of a displacement reaction
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions; Chemistry – materials: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series
misconceptions: Thinking decomposition needs another reactant
Predicting a displacement without checking the reactivity series

assessment.detail: Decompose copper carbonate and test the gas; predict the outcome of six displacement reactions using the reactivity series

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: reversible and irreversible changes

knowledgeComponents.statement: In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged; none are created or destroyed.
Reactants are the starting substances; products are the new substances made.
A chemical reaction makes one or more new substances and is usually hard to reverse.
Combustion is a reaction of a substance with oxygen that releases energy.
Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water.
Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide and soot because there is too little oxygen.
The fire triangle requires fuel, oxygen and heat; removing any one stops the fire.
Thermal decomposition is the breakdown of one substance into simpler ones using heat.
Metal carbonates decompose to a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
Limewater turns cloudy in the presence of carbon dioxide.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.
The reactivity series in order is potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold.

lessons.title: Acids, alkalis and the pH scale
objectives: I can use the pH scale to classify a substance
I can use indicators to test a solution
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions; the pH scale for measuring acidity and alkalinity, and indicators
misconceptions: Thinking all acids are dangerous and all alkalis are safe
Believing pH 7 means no chemicals are present
Confusing an alkali with a base

assessment.detail: Test twelve household and laboratory substances with universal indicator; record pH and classify each

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: compare and group materials by their properties; safety with materials

lessons.title: Neutralisation
objectives: I can describe a neutralisation reaction
I can explain everyday uses of neutralisation
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions; reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
misconceptions: Thinking neutralisation always gives exactly pH 7 regardless of the acid and alkali used
Believing 'salt' means only sodium chloride

assessment.detail: Neutralise dilute acid with alkali, tracking pH; graph the pH change and identify the neutral point

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: mixing materials and reversible and irreversible changes

lessons.title: Reactions of acids with metals and carbonates
objectives: I can write word equations for acid reactions
I can test for hydrogen and carbon dioxide
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen; reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
misconceptions: Naming the salt from the metal only, ignoring the acid
Confusing the tests for hydrogen and carbon dioxide

assessment.detail: React three metals and a carbonate with acid; carry out both gas tests; write six word equations

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: irreversible changes producing gases

knowledgeComponents.statement: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14; below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.
