Universal indicator turns red in strong acid, green at neutral and purple in strong alkali.
Litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
Strong alkalis are as corrosive as strong acids.
Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base or alkali.
Acid + alkali gives salt + water.
Neutralisation is used in indigestion remedies and in treating acidic soil with lime.
Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen.
Acid + metal carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint; carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy.
Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates and nitric acid makes nitrates.

lessons.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
objectives: I can classify a reaction as exothermic or endothermic
I can design a fair test to compare energy changes
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – energetics: exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative)
misconceptions: Thinking endothermic reactions feel hot
Believing exothermic reactions create energy

assessment.detail: Measure temperature change for four reactions; classify each and explain the energy transfer

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: measure temperature; Y6: plan enquiries and control variables

lessons.title: Catalysts and rates of reaction
objectives: I can explain what a catalyst does
I can identify what affects the rate of a reaction
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – chemical reactions: catalysts
misconceptions: Thinking a catalyst is used up in the reaction
Believing a catalyst changes the products

assessment.detail: Observe catalysed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide with manganese dioxide; explain the role of the catalyst and name three other rate factors

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: dissolving rate factors; Y6: control variables

lessons.title: Metals, extraction and the reactivity series in use
objectives: I can use the reactivity series to explain how a metal is extracted
I can explain the role of carbon in metal extraction
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – materials: the order of metals and carbon in the reactivity series; the use of carbon in obtaining metals from metal oxides
misconceptions: Thinking all metals are extracted the same way
Believing carbon can extract every metal

assessment.detail: Explain why gold is found native, why iron is extracted with carbon, and why aluminium requires electrolysis

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: properties and uses of materials; rocks and materials from the Earth

knowledgeComponents.statement: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings and the temperature rises.
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings and the temperature falls.
Combustion, neutralisation and most oxidation reactions are exothermic.
Thermal decomposition is endothermic because energy must be supplied.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up by it.
Rate of reaction increases with higher temperature, higher concentration, larger surface area and a catalyst.
Enzymes are biological catalysts.
An ore is a rock containing enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting.
Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by heating with carbon.
Metals more reactive than carbon, such as aluminium, must be extracted by electrolysis.
Unreactive metals such as gold are found as the metal itself in the ground.

weeks.unit: Chemistry: the Earth and the atmosphere

lessons.title: The structure of the Earth and the rock cycle
objectives: I can describe the layered structure of the Earth
I can explain how the three rock types form and change
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – Earth and atmosphere: the composition of the Earth; the structure of the Earth; the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
misconceptions: Thinking the mantle is entirely molten liquid
Believing rocks never change type
Confusing weathering with erosion

assessment.detail: Label the Earth's structure; draw the rock cycle and explain two pathways in full

ks2Prerequisites: Y3: compare and group rocks on the basis of their appearance and physical properties; describe how fossils are formed

lessons.title: The atmosphere: composition and change
objectives: I can state the composition of the atmosphere
I can explain how human activity is changing atmospheric carbon dioxide
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – Earth and atmosphere: the composition of the atmosphere; the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
misconceptions: Thinking the atmosphere is mostly oxygen
Confusing the greenhouse effect (natural and necessary) with the enhanced greenhouse effect
Confusing climate change with the ozone hole

assessment.detail: Interpret a carbon dioxide concentration graph from 1960 onwards; write a six-mark explanation of the greenhouse effect and its enhancement

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: properties of materials; Y6: interpret line graphs

lessons.title: Earth as a resource: recycling and sustainability
objectives: I can explain why the Earth's resources are finite
I can evaluate the effectiveness of recycling
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – Earth and atmosphere: the Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
misconceptions: Thinking recycling has no environmental cost
Believing all materials can be recycled indefinitely

assessment.detail: Compare the energy cost of producing aluminium from ore with recycling it; write a justified evaluation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: uses of everyday materials; Y6: report and present findings

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Earth has a thin crust, a mostly solid mantle that can flow slowly, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.
Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and crystallises.
Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are compacted and cemented over long periods.
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting.
Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion transports the broken material away.
Slow cooling gives large crystals; rapid cooling gives small crystals in igneous rock.
The atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases including argon and carbon dioxide.
Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, warming the Earth's surface.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, increasing its atmospheric concentration.
A finite resource is one that cannot be replaced on a human timescale.
Recycling aluminium uses far less energy than extracting it from its ore.

lessons.title: Interleaved retrieval: chemistry of the year
objectives: I can recall and apply all the chemistry taught this year
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – the particulate nature of matter; atoms, elements and compounds; pure and impure substances; chemical reactions; energetics; the Periodic Table; materials; Earth and atmosphere
misconceptions: Recalling a technique without knowing which mixture it suits

assessment.detail: 45 mixed chemistry items from weeks 9–32, plus five biology and five physics items for spacing

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding of separation, reactions, acids and Earth chemistry
lessons.ncRef: Chemistry – pure and impure substances; chemical reactions; energetics; Earth and atmosphere; Working scientifically
misconceptions: Writing a formula where a word equation is asked for, or vice versa

assessment.detail: 55-minute paper with a practical technique section, a word equation section and one six-mark explanation

lessons.title: Review, gap repair and a required practical audit
objectives: I can correct my errors
I can describe every practical technique met this year
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – experimental skills and investigations; analysis and evaluation
misconceptions: Remembering the result of a practical but not the method

assessment.detail: Write a full method for six practicals from memory; personalised correction sheet from the assessment

knowledgeComponents.statement: Separation technique is chosen from physical properties; reactions make new substances.
Acid + alkali gives salt + water; acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Every chemical reaction conserves mass because atoms are only rearranged.
A practical method must state apparatus, quantities, steps in order, measurements and safety.
A word equation uses names; a chemical equation uses symbols and formulae.
Reactivity determines both displacement reactions and how a metal is extracted.
Exothermic reactions release energy; endothermic reactions absorb it.
The particle model underlies dissolving, diffusion, states, pressure and separation alike.

terms.name: Summer 2
terms.focus: Physics: energy stores, transfers and costs; heating and cooling; sound; light; space physics.

lessons.title: Energy stores and pathways
objectives: I can name the main energy stores
I can describe an energy transfer between stores
lessons.ncRef: Physics – energy: changes in systems – energy as a quantity that can be quantified and calculated; comparing the starting with the final conditions of a system and describing increases and decreases in the amounts of energy associated with movements, temperatures, changes in positions in a field, in elastic distortions and in chemical compositions
misconceptions: Saying energy is 'used up' or 'lost'
Calling energy a substance that flows
Using 'types of energy' language such as 'sound energy' rather than stores and pathways

assessment.detail: Draw energy transfer diagrams for eight everyday situations, naming the store at the start and end

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: electricity and circuits; Y5: forces and mechanisms

lessons.title: Conservation and dissipation of energy
objectives: I can state the law of conservation of energy
I can explain what happens to energy that is 'wasted'
lessons.ncRef: Physics – energy: changes in systems – energy as a quantity that can be quantified and calculated; using physical processes and mechanisms, rather than energy, to explain the intermediate steps that bring about changes in systems
misconceptions: Thinking energy disappears when it is wasted
Believing a machine can be 100% efficient

assessment.detail: For six devices, identify useful and wasted energy and describe where the wasted energy goes

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines; electricity

lessons.title: Fuels, food and the cost of energy at home
objectives: I can compare the energy content of fuels and foods
I can calculate the cost of running an appliance
lessons.ncRef: Physics – energy: calculation of fuel uses and costs in the domestic context – comparing energy values of different foods (from labels, in kJ), comparing power ratings of appliances in watts, comparing amounts of energy transferred (J, kJ, kW hour), domestic fuel bills, fuel use and costs, fuels and energy resources
misconceptions: Confusing power (rate) with energy (total amount)
Thinking a kilowatt-hour is a unit of power

assessment.detail: Compare food labels in kJ; calculate the cost of running five appliances for stated times at a given unit price

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: multiplication, decimals and money; convert units

knowledgeComponents.statement: Energy stores include kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, nuclear and magnetic.
Energy is transferred between stores by mechanical working, electrical working, heating and radiation.
Energy is measured in joules.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
Wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy.
No device can transfer all of its input energy usefully.
Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts; 1 watt is 1 joule per second.
Energy transferred = power x time.
A kilowatt-hour is the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in one hour, and is the unit on an electricity bill.
Cost = energy in kilowatt-hours x price per unit.

weeks.unit: Physics: heating, cooling and energy resources

lessons.title: Conduction, convection and radiation
objectives: I can describe the three ways thermal energy is transferred
I can explain each using a particle or wave model
lessons.ncRef: Physics – energy: energy changes and transfers – heating and thermal equilibrium: temperature difference between 2 objects leading to energy transfer from the hotter to the cooler one, through contact (conduction) or radiation; such transfers tending to reduce the temperature difference
misconceptions: Thinking metals feel cold because they are colder
Believing radiation needs a medium
Confusing temperature with thermal energy

assessment.detail: Demonstrate all three transfers; write a particle-level explanation of conduction and convection

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: measure temperature; Y5: thermal conductors and insulators

lessons.title: Investigation: reducing energy transfer
objectives: I can plan and carry out an investigation into insulation
I can apply the results to reducing energy use in a home
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – select, plan and carry out the most appropriate types of scientific enquiries; Physics – energy: energy changes and transfers
misconceptions: Thinking insulation 'keeps cold out' rather than slowing energy transfer
Failing to control the starting temperature

assessment.detail: Compare insulating materials on identical containers of hot water; plot cooling curves; conclude and apply to a real home

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: thermal insulators; Y6: plan enquiries, control variables and present data in line graphs

lessons.title: Energy resources: renewable and non-renewable
objectives: I can classify energy resources as renewable or non-renewable
I can evaluate an energy resource using several criteria
lessons.ncRef: Physics – energy: fuels and energy resources
misconceptions: Thinking renewable means no environmental impact
Believing nuclear power is renewable

assessment.detail: Complete a comparison table for eight resources against reliability, emissions, cost and impact; write a justified recommendation for one location

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: report and present findings including causal relationships and explanations

knowledgeComponents.statement: Conduction transfers energy through vibrating particles colliding, mainly in solids.
Metals conduct well because free electrons transfer energy quickly.
Convection occurs in fluids: warmed fluid becomes less dense and rises.
Infrared radiation is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum.
Energy always transfers from a hotter object to a cooler one, reducing the temperature difference.
Metals feel cold because they conduct energy away from the skin quickly, not because they are colder.
Insulation slows the rate of energy transfer in both directions.
Trapped air is a good insulator because it conducts poorly and cannot form convection currents.
Non-renewable resources are coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel; renewables include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, geothermal and biomass.
Renewable resources are replenished but are often less reliable and have their own environmental costs.

lessons.title: How sound is made and how it travels
objectives: I can explain that sound is caused by vibrations
I can explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: sound waves – sound produced by vibrations of objects, in loud speakers, detected by their effects on microphone diaphragm and the ear drum; sound waves are longitudinal; sound needs a medium to travel, the speed of sound in air, in water, in solids
misconceptions: Thinking sound travels fastest in air because air is light
Believing sound can travel through space
Confusing longitudinal and transverse waves

assessment.detail: Bell jar demonstration; explain in writing why the sound fades as air is removed; compare speeds of sound in three media

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: identify how sounds are made, associating some of them with something vibrating; recognise that vibrations from sounds travel through a medium to the ear

lessons.title: Frequency, pitch, amplitude and loudness
objectives: I can link frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness
I can interpret an oscilloscope trace
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: sound waves – frequencies of sound waves, measured in hertz (Hz); echoes, reflection and absorption of sound; the auditory range of humans and animals
misconceptions: Confusing amplitude with frequency
Thinking a higher pitch means a louder sound

assessment.detail: Use a signal generator and oscilloscope; sketch traces for high and low pitch and for loud and quiet; state the human auditory range

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: find patterns between the pitch of a sound and features of the object that produced it; find patterns between volume of a sound and the strength of the vibrations

lessons.title: Echoes, absorption and uses of ultrasound
objectives: I can explain echoes and sound absorption
I can describe uses of ultrasound
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: sound waves – echoes, reflection and absorption of sound; energy and waves – pressure waves transferring energy; use for cleaning and physiotherapy by ultra-sound
misconceptions: Thinking absorbed sound is destroyed rather than transferred to the material
Believing ultrasound is a different kind of wave from audible sound

assessment.detail: Calculate a distance from an echo time using speed of sound; describe three uses of ultrasound

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: recognise that sounds get fainter as the distance from the source increases

knowledgeComponents.statement: Sound is produced by a vibrating object.
Sound waves are longitudinal: the particles vibrate along the direction the wave travels.
Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases, because the particles are closer together in solids.
The speed of sound in air is about 330 to 340 metres per second.
Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
Higher frequency gives a higher pitch; larger amplitude gives a louder sound.
The human auditory range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Ultrasound is sound above 20,000 Hz, beyond the human hearing range.
An echo is sound reflected from a hard surface; soft materials absorb sound.
Distance from an echo = (speed of sound x time) divided by 2, because the sound travels there and back.

lessons.title: Light travelling and the ray model
objectives: I can describe how light travels and how we see objects
I can use ray diagrams to explain shadows and a pinhole camera
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: light waves – the similarities and differences between light waves and waves in matter; light waves travelling through a vacuum, speed of light; the transmission of light through materials: absorption, diffuse scattering and specular reflection at a surface; use of ray model to explain imaging in mirrors, the pinhole camera
misconceptions: Thinking we see because light comes out of the eye
Believing light needs a medium like sound
Drawing rays without arrows

assessment.detail: Draw ray diagrams for seeing a luminous and a non-luminous object, for a shadow and for a pinhole camera

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines; use the idea that light travels in straight lines to explain that objects are seen because they give out or reflect light into the eye; explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them

lessons.title: Reflection and the law of reflection
objectives: I can state and use the law of reflection
I can describe the image formed in a plane mirror
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: light waves – specular reflection at a surface; use of ray model to explain imaging in mirrors
misconceptions: Measuring angles from the mirror surface rather than from the normal
Thinking a mirror image is upside down rather than laterally inverted

assessment.detail: Measure angles of incidence and reflection for five rays; tabulate and state the law; describe the image in a plane mirror using four properties

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines; explore reflection

lessons.title: Refraction and lenses
objectives: I can explain refraction using change of speed
I can describe how a convex lens focuses light
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: light waves – the transmission of light through materials; use of ray model to explain refraction and action of convex lens in focusing (qualitative)
misconceptions: Thinking light bends because it 'wants' to
Getting the direction of bending wrong when entering a denser medium
Believing refraction requires a lens

assessment.detail: Trace rays through a glass block; measure the bending; draw a ray diagram of a convex lens focusing parallel light

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: light travels in straight lines

knowledgeComponents.statement: Light travels in straight lines and can travel through a vacuum.
The speed of light in a vacuum is about 300,000,000 metres per second.
We see a non-luminous object because light from a source reflects off it into the eye.
A shadow forms where an opaque object blocks light travelling in straight lines.
Angles in optics are always measured from the normal, a line at 90 degrees to the surface.
The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
A plane mirror image is virtual, upright, the same size and laterally inverted.
Specular reflection occurs at a smooth surface; diffuse scattering occurs at a rough one.
Refraction is the change of direction of light when its speed changes on entering a new medium.
Light bends towards the normal when entering a denser medium and away from it when leaving.
A convex lens converges parallel light rays to a focal point.

lessons.title: Dispersion, the spectrum and colour
objectives: I can explain how a prism splits white light
I can explain why an object appears a particular colour
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: light waves – colours and the different frequencies of light, white light and prisms (qualitative only); differential colour effects in absorption and diffuse reflection
misconceptions: Thinking a prism adds colour to white light
Believing a red object emits red light
Thinking a filter changes light to a new colour

assessment.detail: Disperse white light with a prism; predict and test the appearance of coloured objects under coloured light and behind filters

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: light and reflection; Y3: light sources and shadows

lessons.title: Waves in water: transverse waves and superposition
objectives: I can describe a transverse wave and label its parts
I can explain reflection and superposition of water waves
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: observed waves – waves on water as undulations which travel through water with transverse motion; these waves can be reflected, and add or cancel – superposition
misconceptions: Thinking the water itself travels along with the wave
Confusing wavelength with amplitude

assessment.detail: Use a ripple tank or simulation; label a wave diagram; explain reflection and one case of superposition

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: sound as vibrations; Y6: light

lessons.title: Waves that carry energy and information
objectives: I can explain that waves transfer energy without transferring matter
I can describe how waves are used to carry information
lessons.ncRef: Physics – waves: energy and waves – pressure waves transferring energy; waves transferring information for conversion to electrical signals by microphone
misconceptions: Thinking waves carry matter from source to receiver
Believing a microphone makes sound rather than detecting it

assessment.detail: Explain the energy transfer in four wave situations; describe how a microphone and a loudspeaker each work

ks2Prerequisites: Y4: sound travels to the ear; Y6: electrical circuits

knowledgeComponents.statement: White light is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum.
A prism disperses white light because each colour refracts by a different amount.
The spectrum in order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
An object appears red because it reflects red light and absorbs the other colours.
A coloured filter transmits its own colour and absorbs the others.
In a transverse wave the oscillation is at right angles to the direction of travel.
Wavelength is the distance between two matching points on a wave; amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position.
Superposition occurs when two waves meet and their displacements add, reinforcing or cancelling.
A wave transfers energy without transferring matter.
A microphone converts sound waves into an electrical signal; a loudspeaker does the reverse.

lessons.title: The solar system and gravity in space
objectives: I can describe the structure of the solar system
I can explain orbits in terms of gravitational forces
lessons.ncRef: Physics – space physics: our Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy, other galaxies; the light year as a unit of astronomical distance; gravity force; the relationship of Earth and Moon and Earth and Sun, and the associated gravitational forces (qualitative)
misconceptions: Thinking the Sun orbits the Earth
Believing there is no gravity in space
Confusing a solar system with a galaxy

assessment.detail: Order the planets; explain why the Moon orbits the Earth; convert a light-year distance into a statement about how old the light is

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: describe the movement of the Earth and other planets relative to the Sun; describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth; describe the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies

lessons.title: Day, night and the seasons
objectives: I can explain day and night using the Earth's rotation
I can explain the seasons using the Earth's tilt
lessons.ncRef: Physics – space physics: the seasons and the Earth's tilt, day length at different times of year, in different hemispheres
misconceptions: Thinking the seasons are caused by the Earth being closer to the Sun in summer
Believing the Earth's tilt changes through the year
Confusing rotation with orbit

assessment.detail: Model the Earth's orbit and tilt with a lamp and globe; write a six-mark explanation of why summer is warmer

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky

lessons.title: Stars, galaxies and the scale of the universe
objectives: I can describe how stars, galaxies and the universe are related in scale
I can use light years to compare astronomical distances
lessons.ncRef: Physics – space physics: our Sun as a star, other stars in our galaxy, other galaxies; the light year as a unit of astronomical distance
misconceptions: Thinking a light year is a unit of time
Believing all stars in a constellation are close together

assessment.detail: Build a scale model or ordered list from Earth to the observable universe; carry out three light-year calculations

ks2Prerequisites: Y5: Earth and space; Y6 maths: standard form, large numbers

knowledgeComponents.statement: The order of the planets is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Gravity is the force that keeps planets in orbit around the Sun and the Moon in orbit around the Earth.
A more massive object has a stronger gravitational field.
The Sun is an ordinary star, one of hundreds of billions in the Milky Way galaxy.
The Earth rotates once in about 24 hours, giving day and night.
The Earth orbits the Sun once in about 365.25 days.
The Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees, and this tilt causes the seasons.
In summer the hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, giving longer days and more concentrated sunlight.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 million million kilometres.
A light year is a unit of distance, not of time.
Looking at a distant object in space means looking back in time, because the light took years to arrive.

weeks.unit: Year review and transition to Year 8

lessons.title: End-of-year assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate secure understanding across biology, chemistry and physics
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically; Biology, Chemistry and Physics – full Year 7 content
misconceptions: Revising only the most recent topic

assessment.detail: Two 45-minute papers: paper 1 biology and chemistry, paper 2 physics and working scientifically; every item tagged to a knowledge component

lessons.title: Whole-year interleaved retrieval and gap repair
objectives: I can identify and repair my remaining gaps across all three sciences
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – analysis and evaluation
misconceptions: Assuming a topic is secure because it once was

assessment.detail: 60-item quiz sampling all 39 weeks; personalised correction sheet; weak components re-queued at short spacing

lessons.title: Looking ahead: what Year 8 builds on
objectives: I can explain how Year 8 topics build on Year 7
I can name the big ideas that run through all three sciences
lessons.ncRef: Working scientifically – understand that scientific methods and theories develop as earlier explanations are modified
misconceptions: Seeing biology, chemistry and physics as unconnected

assessment.detail: Map each Year 7 unit to its Year 8 successor (cells to digestion and respiration, particles to the periodic table and reactions, forces to electricity and magnetism); identify three big ideas that span all three

knowledgeComponents.statement: The particle model, energy, forces, cells and interdependence are the big ideas running through KS3 science.
Year 8 biology extends cells into nutrition, digestion, gas exchange, photosynthesis and respiration.
Year 8 chemistry extends the Periodic Table into groups, chemical equations and the Earth's resources.
Year 8 physics extends forces into electricity, magnetism and electromagnetism.
Energy is conserved in every process studied across the three sciences.
Every scientific explanation must link an observation to a model or mechanism.
Spaced retrieval maintains knowledge; a single end-of-topic test does not.
Working scientifically skills are assessed alongside subject content in every paper.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: geography programmes of study, key stage 3 (DfE, September 2013; statutory from September 2014). Strands: Locational knowledge (extend to Africa, Russia, Asia including China and India, and the Middle East); Place knowledge (a region within Africa and a region within Asia); Human and physical geography (geological timescales and plate tectonics; rocks, weathering and soils; weather and climate including change from the Ice Age to the present; the water cycle, rivers, coasts and glaciation; population and urbanisation; international development; economic activity in the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors; the use of natural resources); Geographical skills and fieldwork (maps, atlases, globes, GIS, Ordnance Survey maps, and fieldwork in contrasting locations).
subjects.yearShare: Enrichment strand at roughly half the volume of a core subject: 1.5 lessons per week on average (two lessons in alternate weeks). Year 7 covers geographical skills and GIS, the UK, plate tectonics, rivers and the water cycle, weather, climate and biomes, the African locational and regional requirement, and population, urbanisation and resources. The Asian locational and regional requirement, coasts and glaciation are covered in Years 8 and 9.
deferredToY8Y9: Locational knowledge of Russia, Asia including China and India, and the Middle East
A regional depth study within Asia
Coasts and coastal management
Glaciation and glacial landforms
Globalisation and changing economies in depth
Ecosystems in depth including cold environments
priorKnowledgeAssumed: Y5-Y6: locate the world's countries using maps, concentrating on Europe and North and South America, and their environmental regions, key physical and human characteristics, countries and major cities

Y5-Y6: name and locate counties and cities of the United Kingdom, geographical regions and their identifying human and physical characteristics, key topographical features including hills, mountains, coasts and rivers, and land-use patterns

Y5-Y6: identify the position and significance of latitude, longitude, Equator, Northern and Southern Hemisphere, the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, Arctic and Antarctic Circle, the Prime/Greenwich Meridian and time zones

Y5-Y6: understand geographical similarities and differences through the study of human and physical geography of a region of the UK, a region in a European country, and a region in North or South America
Y5-Y6: describe and understand key aspects of physical geography including climate zones, biomes and vegetation belts, rivers, mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes, and the water cycle

Y5-Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including types of settlement and land use, economic activity including trade links, and the distribution of natural resources including energy, food, minerals and water
Y5-Y6: use maps, atlases, globes and digital/computer mapping to locate countries and describe features studied
Y5-Y6: use the eight points of a compass, four and six-figure grid references, symbols and key including Ordnance Survey maps

Y5-Y6: use fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present the human and physical features in the local area using a range of methods including sketch maps, plans and graphs, and digital technologies

terms.name: Autumn 1
terms.focus: Our world: geographical skills, maps, GIS and the geography of the UK. 12 lessons.

lessons.title: What geographers do and why it matters
objectives: I can explain what physical, human and environmental geography study
I can give an example of a geographical question
lessons.ncRef: Purpose of study – geography inspires a curiosity and fascination about the world; pupils develop knowledge about diverse places, people, resources and natural and human environments
misconceptions: Thinking geography is only about learning capital cities
Believing physical and human geography are unconnected

assessment.detail: Baseline map and place-knowledge quiz; classify twenty topics as physical, human or environmental

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of physical and human geography

lessons.title: Locating the world: continents, oceans and lines of latitude
objectives: I can name and locate the continents and oceans
I can use latitude and longitude to describe a location
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge – extend their locational knowledge and deepen their spatial awareness of the world's countries; Geographical skills – build on their knowledge of globes, maps and atlases
misconceptions: Confusing latitude (horizontal) with longitude (vertical)
Thinking Europe and Asia are separated by an ocean

assessment.detail: Label continents, oceans and the five key lines of latitude from memory; give coordinates for six locations

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: locate the world's countries; identify the position and significance of latitude, longitude, Equator, Northern and Southern Hemisphere, the Tropics, Arctic and Antarctic Circle, the Prime/Greenwich Meridian and time zones

knowledgeComponents.statement: Physical geography studies natural processes and features; human geography studies people and their activities.
Scale in geography ranges from local to regional, national and global.
The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania and South America.
The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
Lines of latitude run east to west and measure distance north or south of the Equator.
Lines of longitude run north to south and measure distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.
The Equator is at 0 degrees latitude; the Prime Meridian at 0 degrees longitude passes through Greenwich.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23.5 degrees north and the Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5 degrees south.

lessons.title: Grid references and direction
objectives: I can use four-figure and six-figure grid references
I can use the eight points of the compass and take a bearing
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – interpret Ordnance Survey maps in the classroom and in the field, including using grid references and scale
misconceptions: Reading northings before eastings
Counting the grid line to the right of a square rather than to its left

assessment.detail: Twenty grid reference questions on a 1:25000 OS extract, plus six bearings

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use the eight points of a compass, four and six-figure grid references, symbols and key (including the use of Ordnance Survey maps)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Grid references are read along the bottom first, then up: eastings before northings.
A four-figure grid reference identifies a whole grid square.
A six-figure grid reference divides each grid square into tenths to identify a precise point.
The eight compass points are north, north-east, east, south-east, south, south-west, west, north-west.
A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures.
On an OS map, north is always at the top of the sheet.
Grid lines on an OS map are one kilometre apart.
A map key explains what each symbol represents.

lessons.title: Scale, distance and area on maps
objectives: I can measure straight-line and curved distances on a map
I can convert map distance to real distance using the scale
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – interpret Ordnance Survey maps, including using grid references and scale, topographical and other thematic mapping
misconceptions: Reading 1:50000 as meaning 50000 cm on the map
Measuring a winding road as a straight line

assessment.detail: Measure eight distances, including two curved routes with string, and convert each to kilometres

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use maps, atlases and OS maps; Y6 maths: ratio and scale factors, unit conversion

lessons.title: Relief, contours and cross-sections
objectives: I can interpret contour lines to describe the shape of the land
I can draw a simple cross-section from a map
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – interpret Ordnance Survey maps, including topographical and other thematic mapping
misconceptions: Thinking widely spaced contours mean steep land
Reading contours as roads or paths

assessment.detail: Describe the relief of two map areas; draw and annotate one cross-section between named grid references

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use maps and atlases; describe key physical features

knowledgeComponents.statement: A scale of 1:25000 means 1 cm on the map represents 25000 cm, that is 250 m, on the ground.
On a 1:50000 map, 2 cm represents 1 km.
Straight-line distance is measured with a ruler; a winding route is measured with string.
Contour lines join points of equal height above sea level.
Contours close together mean steep land; contours far apart mean gentle land.
A spot height marks the exact height at a single point.
Contours forming a V pointing uphill indicate a valley, usually with a river.
Relief means the shape and height of the land surface.

lessons.title: GIS and satellite imagery
objectives: I can explain what a Geographic Information System is
I can use layers of geographical data to answer a question
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – use Geographical Information Systems (GIS) to view, analyse and interpret places and data; use aerial and satellite photographs
misconceptions: Thinking a satellite image is the same as a map
Believing GIS just displays maps rather than analysing data

assessment.detail: Use a free GIS tool to answer a question such as where flood risk overlaps with housing; produce an annotated screenshot and conclusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use maps, atlases, globes and digital or computer mapping to locate countries and describe features

knowledgeComponents.statement: A Geographic Information System stores, displays and analyses data linked to locations.
GIS data are held in layers that can be switched on and off and overlaid.
A satellite image shows what is actually there; a map is a selective, symbolic representation.
Remote sensing is collecting data about the Earth from a distance, usually from satellites or aircraft.
A choropleth map uses shading intensity to show the value of a variable across areas.
Overlaying layers reveals relationships that a single map cannot show.
GIS is used in planning, emergency response, conservation and business location decisions.
All data on a map are selected by someone, so every map involves choices.

lessons.title: The physical geography of the UK
objectives: I can locate the UK's major upland areas, rivers and coasts
I can describe the pattern of relief across the UK
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge – extend locational knowledge and deepen spatial awareness; Place knowledge – understand geographical similarities, differences and links between places
misconceptions: Confusing the UK, Great Britain and the British Isles
Thinking all of England is flat

assessment.detail: Label 20 UK physical features from memory; write a paragraph describing the north-west to south-east relief pattern

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: name and locate counties and cities of the United Kingdom, geographical regions and their identifying human and physical characteristics, key topographical features (including hills, mountains, coasts and rivers)

lessons.title: The human geography of the UK
objectives: I can locate the UK's major cities and describe the population distribution
I can explain why some areas are densely populated
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation; Locational knowledge
misconceptions: Confusing population density with total population
Assuming the largest area has the most people

assessment.detail: Interpret a UK population density map; identify three dense and three sparse areas and explain each pattern

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: name and locate counties and cities of the UK and understand how some aspects have changed over time

knowledgeComponents.statement: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Great Britain is the island containing England, Scotland and Wales; the British Isles also includes Ireland.
The UK's uplands are mainly in the north and west; the lowlands are mainly in the south and east.
Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the UK at 1,345 metres.
The River Severn is the longest river in the UK; the Thames is the longest wholly in England.
Population density is the number of people per square kilometre.
The UK's most densely populated areas are London, the West Midlands, and the north-west around Manchester and Liverpool.
A conurbation is a continuous built-up area formed by neighbouring towns merging.
Relief, climate, resources and transport links all influence where people settle.

lessons.title: Local fieldwork: collecting geographical data
objectives: I can plan and carry out a local fieldwork enquiry
I can collect data using more than one method
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – use fieldwork in contrasting locations to collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data, using multiple sources of increasingly complex information
misconceptions: Collecting data with no question in mind
Confusing primary data (collected yourself) with secondary data

assessment.detail: Local enquiry (for example an environmental quality survey or traffic count) with a stated question, a data collection sheet and a written conclusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present the human and physical features in the local area using a range of methods, including sketch maps, plans and graphs, and digital technologies

knowledgeComponents.statement: A geographical enquiry begins with a question, not with data collection.
Primary data are collected first-hand; secondary data come from an existing source.
Sampling means collecting data from part of an area to represent the whole.
An environmental quality survey scores features such as litter, noise and greenery on a fixed scale.
A risk assessment must be completed before fieldwork begins.
The enquiry process is: question, plan, collect, present, analyse, conclude, evaluate.
Data collected at only one time of day may not represent the usual pattern.
A sketch map records the layout of a place with labelled features, not to scale.

lessons.title: Presenting fieldwork data
objectives: I can choose an appropriate way to present geographical data
I can draw and interpret a located bar chart or a choropleth map
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data using multiple sources of increasingly complex information
misconceptions: Choosing a chart type from habit rather than from the data
Using too many shading categories on a choropleth

assessment.detail: Present the week 6 fieldwork data in two different ways and justify which communicates the pattern better

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: construct and interpret pie charts, line graphs and bar charts

lessons.title: Analysing and concluding from data
objectives: I can describe a pattern in geographical data
I can reach a conclusion that answers the enquiry question
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data
misconceptions: Describing the data without answering the question
Treating a correlation as proof of cause

assessment.detail: Write a full analysis and conclusion for the fieldwork enquiry, including one evaluation point about reliability

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: interpret data; Y6 science: report findings including conclusions

knowledgeComponents.statement: A located bar chart places a small bar chart at the position on a map where the data were collected.
A choropleth map uses graded shading, darker for higher values.
A proportional symbol map varies the size of a symbol with the value it represents.
A flow line map shows movement, with line thickness representing volume.
Describing a pattern means stating the general trend, then any exception, with data quoted.
An anomaly is a data point that does not fit the overall pattern.
A conclusion must directly answer the enquiry question using the evidence collected.
An evaluation considers whether the data were reliable enough to support the conclusion.

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: skills and the UK
objectives: I can apply map, GIS and enquiry skills to unseen material
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork; Locational knowledge
misconceptions: Reading grid references in the wrong order under time pressure

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: OS map skills, a GIS interpretation, UK locational knowledge and one extended explanation of a population pattern

knowledgeComponents.statement: Eastings are always read before northings.
Close contours mean steep slopes.
Map scale converts map distance to ground distance.
UK population is concentrated in the south-east and in the industrial cities of the Midlands and north.
A geographical explanation links a pattern to a physical or human cause.
GIS layers can be combined to answer questions no single map can.
Primary data are collected by the geographer; secondary data are collected by others.
Every geographical description should include named places and figures.

terms.name: Autumn 2
terms.focus: The restless Earth: plate tectonics, volcanoes and earthquakes. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: The structure of the Earth and plate tectonics
objectives: I can describe the layers of the Earth
I can explain what tectonic plates are and why they move
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – understand, through the use of detailed place-based exemplars at a variety of scales, the key processes in physical geography relating to: geological timescales and plate tectonics
misconceptions: Thinking the mantle is entirely molten
Believing plates move quickly enough to feel

assessment.detail: Label the Earth's structure; explain plate movement with an annotated convection diagram

ks2Prerequisites: Y3 science: rocks; Y5–Y6 geography: describe key physical features

lessons.title: Continental drift and the evidence for it
objectives: I can describe the evidence for continental drift
I can explain why Wegener's theory was rejected at first
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – geological timescales and plate tectonics
misconceptions: Thinking the continents were always in their present positions
Believing a theory is a guess

assessment.detail: Sort four types of evidence for continental drift and explain how each supports the theory

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 science: recognise that scientific ideas change and develop over time

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Earth has a crust, a mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.
The crust is broken into tectonic plates that float on the mantle beneath.
Plates move a few centimetres a year, driven by convection currents and slab pull in the mantle.
Oceanic crust is thinner and denser than continental crust.
Pangaea was the supercontinent that existed about 250 million years ago.
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 but could not explain the mechanism.
Evidence for drift includes the jigsaw fit of coastlines, matching fossils, matching rock types and ancient climate evidence.
Sea floor spreading, discovered in the 1960s, provided the mechanism that confirmed plate tectonics.

lessons.title: Types of plate boundary
objectives: I can describe what happens at destructive, constructive and conservative boundaries
I can locate examples of each on a world map
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – plate tectonics; Locational knowledge
misconceptions: Thinking earthquakes only occur at destructive boundaries
Believing volcanoes occur at every type of boundary

assessment.detail: Draw annotated cross-sections of three boundary types; locate and name three real examples of each

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: locate the world's countries; describe key physical features

knowledgeComponents.statement: At a destructive boundary, denser oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust.
Destructive boundaries produce ocean trenches, fold mountains, volcanoes and powerful earthquakes.
At a constructive boundary, plates move apart and magma rises to form new crust.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a constructive boundary; Iceland sits on it.
At a conservative boundary, plates slide past one another, causing earthquakes but no volcanoes.
The San Andreas Fault in California is a conservative boundary.
A collision boundary between two continental plates forms fold mountains such as the Himalayas.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific plate boundaries.

lessons.title: How volcanoes form and erupt
objectives: I can describe the structure of a volcano
I can compare composite and shield volcanoes
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – plate tectonics; rocks and rock cycle
misconceptions: Using magma and lava interchangeably
Thinking all volcanoes erupt explosively

assessment.detail: Label a volcano; complete a comparison table of composite and shield volcanoes with a named example of each

ks2Prerequisites: Y3 science: rocks and how they are formed

lessons.title: Living with volcanoes: a case study
objectives: I can explain why people live near volcanoes
I can describe the effects of a named eruption and the responses to it
lessons.ncRef: Place knowledge – understand geographical similarities, differences and links between places through the study of human and physical geography; Human and physical geography
misconceptions: Assuming people near volcanoes are simply unaware of the risk
Confusing primary and secondary effects

assessment.detail: Case study of a named eruption (for example Eyjafjallajökull 2010 or Mount St Helens 1980): classify effects and responses, and explain why people stay

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe key aspects of physical geography including volcanoes and earthquakes

knowledgeComponents.statement: Magma is molten rock below ground; lava is molten rock at the surface.
A composite volcano is steep-sided, built of alternating ash and lava, and erupts explosively.
A shield volcano is broad and gently sloping, formed from runny lava, and erupts less violently.
Thick, viscous magma traps gas and produces explosive eruptions.
A pyroclastic flow is a fast-moving cloud of hot gas and volcanic material.
Primary effects happen immediately from the eruption itself; secondary effects follow on afterwards.
People live near volcanoes for fertile soils, geothermal energy, minerals and tourism.
Volcanoes are monitored using seismometers, gas sensors and ground deformation measurements.

lessons.title: What causes an earthquake and how it is measured
objectives: I can explain how an earthquake happens
I can describe how earthquakes are measured
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – plate tectonics
misconceptions: Confusing focus and epicentre
Thinking the Richter scale is linear so 6 is twice 3

assessment.detail: Label a cross-section showing focus and epicentre; explain the magnitude scale and answer six questions on measurement

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe key physical processes including earthquakes

knowledgeComponents.statement: An earthquake is caused by a sudden release of built-up stress along a fault.
The focus is the point underground where the earthquake starts.
The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus.
Shallow-focus earthquakes usually cause more surface damage than deep-focus ones.
Earthquake magnitude is measured on a logarithmic scale, so each whole number is about 32 times more energy.
A seismometer records the ground movement caused by seismic waves.
An aftershock is a smaller earthquake following the main one along the same fault.
A tsunami can be triggered when an earthquake displaces the sea floor.

lessons.title: Comparing earthquakes in richer and poorer countries
objectives: I can compare the effects of two earthquakes of similar magnitude
I can explain why wealth affects the impact of a hazard
lessons.ncRef: Place knowledge – understand geographical similarities, differences and links between places; Human and physical geography – the use of natural resources; economic activity and development
misconceptions: Assuming a bigger magnitude always means more deaths
Thinking preparedness is only about buildings

assessment.detail: Compare two named earthquakes of similar magnitude in countries at different levels of development; explain the difference in impact

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand geographical similarities and differences through study of human and physical geography of regions

lessons.title: Reducing the risk: prediction, protection and planning
objectives: I can describe strategies for reducing earthquake risk
I can evaluate which strategy is most effective
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes, environments and the climate
misconceptions: Believing earthquakes can be reliably predicted
Thinking one strategy alone is sufficient

assessment.detail: Rank four risk reduction strategies for effectiveness and cost, and justify the ranking in writing

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: report and present findings with reasoned explanations

knowledgeComponents.statement: The impact of an earthquake depends on magnitude, depth, population density, time of day and the country's wealth.
Wealthier countries generally have stronger building codes, better emergency services and faster recovery.
Vulnerability is how exposed and how able to cope a population is.
Earthquakes cannot currently be predicted accurately in time and place.
Protection means designing buildings and infrastructure to withstand shaking.
Preparation includes drills, emergency supplies and public education.
Land use planning avoids building on the most unstable ground.
Reducing risk requires a combination of strategies rather than any single one.

lessons.title: Rock types, weathering and the rock cycle
objectives: I can identify the three rock types and explain how each forms
I can describe the processes of weathering and erosion
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – rocks, weathering and soils; geological timescales
misconceptions: Confusing weathering with erosion
Thinking the rock cycle has a fixed starting point

assessment.detail: Identify six rock samples; draw and annotate the rock cycle; explain freeze-thaw weathering step by step

ks2Prerequisites: Y3 science: compare and group rocks; describe how fossils are formed; recognise that soils are made from rocks and organic matter

knowledgeComponents.statement: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma or lava; examples are granite and basalt.
Sedimentary rocks form from compacted layers of sediment; examples are limestone and sandstone.
Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change existing rock; examples are marble and slate.
Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion moves the fragments away.
Freeze-thaw weathering occurs when water in a crack freezes, expands and widens the crack.
Chemical weathering includes acid rain dissolving limestone.
Biological weathering includes plant roots widening cracks in rock.
The rock cycle is continuous, with no beginning or end.
Soil forms from weathered rock combined with decayed organic matter.

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: the restless Earth
objectives: I can explain tectonic processes and their consequences using named examples
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – plate tectonics, rocks, weathering and soils
misconceptions: Writing a general answer without a named place

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: plate boundaries, one case study question, a rock cycle explanation and one nine-mark evaluation of hazard management

lessons.title: Review, retrieval and geographical writing
objectives: I can write a full geographical explanation using connectives
I can repair my identified gaps
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills – communicate geographical information in a variety of ways, including through maps and writing at length
misconceptions: Listing points without linking them causally

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz on weeks 1–14; rewrite one answer as a fully connected explanation chain

knowledgeComponents.statement: A geographical explanation uses a causal chain: this happens, which means, which results in.
Every case study answer must name the place, the date and specific figures.
Volcanoes occur at destructive and constructive boundaries but not at conservative ones.
Earthquakes occur at all three types of plate boundary.
Hazard impact is a function of both the physical event and human vulnerability.
The rock cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks through weathering, transport, deposition, heat and pressure.
An evaluation weighs advantages against disadvantages and reaches a judgement.
Plate tectonics explains the global distribution of volcanoes, earthquakes and fold mountains.

terms.name: Spring 1
terms.focus: Rivers and the water cycle: hydrological processes, river landforms and flooding. 9 lessons.

lessons.title: The hydrological cycle
objectives: I can describe the stages of the water cycle
I can explain how water moves between stores
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – the water cycle including weather and climate, rivers and coasts
misconceptions: Thinking the water cycle is only evaporation, condensation and rain
Believing new water is created by the cycle

assessment.detail: Draw and fully annotate the hydrological cycle showing all stores and transfers

ks2Prerequisites: Y4 science: identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle; Y5–Y6 geography: describe rivers and the water cycle

lessons.title: Drainage basins
objectives: I can label the features of a drainage basin
I can explain what happens to rainfall when it lands in a basin
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – the water cycle; rivers
misconceptions: Confusing a watershed with a river
Thinking a river's source is always a spring

assessment.type: labelled diagram and OS map task
assessment.detail: Label a drainage basin diagram; identify source, tributaries, confluence and mouth on an OS map extract

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of physical geography including rivers

knowledgeComponents.statement: The water cycle is a closed system: the total amount of water on Earth stays the same.
Evaporation turns liquid water into vapour; transpiration releases vapour from plants.
Condensation forms clouds when water vapour cools.
Infiltration is water soaking into the soil; surface run-off is water flowing over the ground.
A drainage basin is the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
The source is where a river begins; the mouth is where it enters the sea or a lake.
A confluence is where two rivers meet; a tributary is a smaller river joining a larger one.
A watershed is the ridge of high land separating two drainage basins.

lessons.title: Erosion, transport and deposition
objectives: I can name and describe the four processes of river erosion and four of transport
I can explain when a river deposits its load
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – rivers; how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes
misconceptions: Confusing abrasion (rocks scraping the bed) with attrition (rocks hitting each other)
Thinking a river erodes everywhere along its course equally

assessment.detail: Match eight processes to definitions; explain where each dominates along a river's course

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe key aspects of physical geography including rivers

knowledgeComponents.statement: Hydraulic action is the force of water forcing air into cracks in the bank and bed.
Abrasion is the river's load scraping against the bed and banks.
Attrition is rocks in the load colliding with each other and becoming smaller and rounder.
Solution is the dissolving of soluble rock such as limestone by slightly acidic water.
Traction rolls the largest particles along the bed; saltation bounces smaller ones.
Suspension carries fine particles within the water; solution carries dissolved material.
Deposition occurs when a river loses energy and can no longer carry its load.
Vertical erosion dominates in the upper course; lateral erosion and deposition dominate downstream.

lessons.title: Upper course landforms: V-shaped valleys and waterfalls
objectives: I can explain the formation of a V-shaped valley
I can explain how a waterfall and gorge form
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – rivers; how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes
misconceptions: Thinking a waterfall stays in the same place
Confusing a gorge with a V-shaped valley

assessment.detail: Write a four-stage annotated explanation of waterfall formation; identify both landforms on an OS map

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe key physical features including rivers and mountains

lessons.title: Lower course landforms: meanders, ox-bow lakes and floodplains
objectives: I can explain how a meander forms and migrates
I can explain the formation of an ox-bow lake and a floodplain
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – rivers
misconceptions: Thinking erosion happens on the inside of a meander bend
Believing floodplains are flat because they were built flat

assessment.detail: Draw a labelled meander cross-section; write a five-stage explanation of ox-bow lake formation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: physical geography including rivers

knowledgeComponents.statement: A V-shaped valley forms as vertical erosion cuts down and weathering causes the sides to slump.
A waterfall forms where a band of hard rock lies over softer rock that erodes faster.
Undercutting causes the hard rock overhang to collapse, so the waterfall retreats upstream leaving a gorge.
A plunge pool is the deep hollow eroded at the base of a waterfall.
On a meander, water flows fastest on the outside bend, causing erosion and a river cliff.
On the inside bend the water is slower, so deposition forms a slip-off slope.
An ox-bow lake forms when erosion narrows a meander neck until the river cuts through and the old bend is cut off.
A floodplain is built up by repeated deposition of alluvium during floods.
Levees are raised banks formed when the coarsest material is deposited first at the channel edge.

lessons.title: Causes of flooding and the flood hydrograph
objectives: I can explain the physical and human causes of flooding
I can interpret a flood hydrograph
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – rivers; how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes and environments
misconceptions: Thinking heavy rain alone causes flooding
Believing a short lag time means less water

assessment.detail: Interpret two contrasting flood hydrographs; explain how urbanisation changes lag time and peak discharge

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: interpret line graphs; Y5–Y6 geography: rivers

knowledgeComponents.statement: Discharge is the volume of water passing a point in a river per second, measured in cumecs.
A flood hydrograph plots rainfall and river discharge against time.
Lag time is the delay between peak rainfall and peak discharge.
A short lag time and high peak discharge make flooding more likely.
Impermeable rock, steep slopes and saturated soil all increase surface run-off.
Urbanisation creates impermeable surfaces and drains that move water to rivers quickly.
Deforestation reduces interception and increases run-off.
Flooding results from the interaction of physical conditions and human land use.

lessons.title: Hard and soft flood management
objectives: I can describe hard and soft engineering strategies
I can evaluate a flood management scheme
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes, environments and the climate; and how human activity relies on effective functioning of natural systems
misconceptions: Assuming hard engineering is always more effective
Thinking flood management can eliminate flood risk entirely

assessment.detail: Evaluate a named UK flood scheme against cost, effectiveness, environmental impact and sustainability

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe how human geography interacts with physical geography

lessons.title: River fieldwork enquiry
objectives: I can measure river characteristics safely
I can test a geographical hypothesis with data
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – use fieldwork in contrasting locations to collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data
misconceptions: Measuring depth at only one point across the channel
Collecting data without a hypothesis

assessment.detail: Measure width, depth and velocity at two or three sites (or use a supplied secondary data set); test the hypothesis that a river gets wider and faster downstream

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present features; Y6 maths: mean, graphs

knowledgeComponents.statement: Hard engineering uses built structures such as dams, embankments and flood walls.
Soft engineering works with natural processes, using afforestation, washlands and flood warnings.
Hard engineering is usually expensive, effective in the short term and can shift the problem downstream.
Soft engineering is usually cheaper and more sustainable but slower to take effect.
A cost-benefit analysis weighs the money spent against the damage avoided.
River velocity is measured with a flow meter or by timing a float over a set distance.
Depth must be measured at several equally spaced points across the channel and averaged.
A river typically becomes wider, deeper and faster downstream as discharge increases.

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: rivers
objectives: I can explain river processes and landforms and evaluate flood management
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – the water cycle and rivers; Geographical skills and fieldwork
misconceptions: Describing a landform without explaining its formation

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: labelled diagrams, a hydrograph interpretation, one landform formation explanation and one nine-mark evaluation of flood management

knowledgeComponents.statement: A landform explanation must sequence the processes that formed it over time.
Erosion dominates the upper course; deposition dominates the lower course.
The water cycle is a closed system with fixed total water but changing distribution.
Flood risk is increased by both physical basin characteristics and human land use.
A hydrograph with a steep rising limb and short lag time indicates high flood risk.
Sustainable management meets present needs without harming future capacity.
A nine-mark evaluation needs both sides of the argument and a clear judgement.
Named examples with figures raise the quality of any geographical answer.

terms.name: Spring 2
terms.focus: Weather, climate and climate change: from UK weather to global climate zones. 8 lessons.

lessons.title: The difference between weather and climate
objectives: I can distinguish weather from climate
I can measure and record the main weather elements
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – weather and climate, including the change in climate from the Ice Age to the present
misconceptions: Using a cold week as evidence against a warming climate
Confusing air pressure with wind

assessment.detail: Set up and record a week of weather observations; distinguish weather data from climate data

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y4 science: measure temperature; Y5–Y6 geography: describe and understand climate zones

lessons.title: UK weather: air masses and depressions
objectives: I can explain how air masses affect UK weather
I can describe the weather associated with a depression
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – weather and climate
misconceptions: Thinking low pressure always means rain everywhere in the UK
Reading closely spaced isobars as heavy rain rather than strong wind

assessment.detail: Interpret two synoptic charts; predict the weather for named UK locations and justify each prediction

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of physical geography including climate zones and weather

knowledgeComponents.statement: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place over hours or days; climate is the average weather over about 30 years.
An anemometer measures wind speed and a rain gauge measures precipitation.
A Stevenson screen shades a thermometer so it records air temperature accurately.
Wind direction is named for where the wind comes from, so a westerly blows from the west.
An air mass takes on the temperature and humidity of the region it forms over.
Low pressure (a depression) brings cloud, rain and wind; high pressure (an anticyclone) brings settled weather.
Isobars join points of equal air pressure; closely spaced isobars mean strong winds.
A warm front brings steady rain; a cold front brings heavy showers and a temperature drop.

lessons.title: Global climate zones and why they occur
objectives: I can locate the world's major climate zones
I can explain why temperature varies with latitude
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – weather and climate; Locational knowledge – environmental regions, including polar and hot deserts
misconceptions: Thinking the tropics are hot because they are closer to the Sun
Confusing climate zones with continents

assessment.detail: Label the world climate zones; write an explanation of why temperature decreases with latitude, using a diagram

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: identify the position and significance of latitude, the Tropics and the polar circles; describe and understand climate zones, biomes and vegetation belts

knowledgeComponents.statement: The main climate zones are tropical, arid, temperate, continental and polar.
Temperature generally decreases with distance from the Equator.
Sunlight is concentrated near the Equator and spread over a larger area near the poles because of the Earth's curvature.
Sunlight also passes through more atmosphere at high latitudes, losing more energy.
Warm air rises at the Equator, creating low pressure and heavy rainfall.
Air sinks at about 30 degrees north and south, creating high pressure and the world's hot deserts.
Altitude, distance from the sea and ocean currents also affect climate.
The North Atlantic Drift keeps the UK milder than other places at the same latitude.

lessons.title: Global biomes and their distribution
objectives: I can locate the world's major biomes
I can explain how climate determines the biome
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge – key physical characteristics including environmental regions; Human and physical geography – the water cycle, climate; interaction of physical and human processes
misconceptions: Thinking a biome is the same as a country or continent
Believing all deserts are hot and sandy

assessment.detail: Label the world's biomes; match four climate graphs to their biome and justify each match

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of physical geography including biomes and vegetation belts

lessons.title: The tropical rainforest: structure, adaptation and threats
objectives: I can describe the structure of a rainforest and how plants and animals adapt
I can explain the causes and effects of deforestation
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes, environments and the climate; and how human activity relies on effective functioning of natural systems
misconceptions: Assuming rainforest soil is fertile
Thinking deforestation has only local effects

assessment.detail: Annotate a rainforest structure diagram; write a causal chain explaining the effects of deforestation on climate and people

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: biomes and vegetation belts; Y6 science: interdependence and habitats

knowledgeComponents.statement: A biome is a large-scale ecosystem defined by its climate and vegetation.
Tropical rainforests lie near the Equator where it is hot and wet all year.
Hot deserts lie around 30 degrees north and south where air is sinking.
A climate graph shows monthly temperature as a line and precipitation as bars.
Rainforest layers from top to bottom are emergent, canopy, understorey and forest floor.
Drip tips shed heavy rain and buttress roots support tall trees in shallow soil.
Rainforest soil is thin and infertile because nutrients are held in the vegetation and cycled rapidly.
Deforestation is driven by logging, cattle ranching, farming, mining and road building.
Deforestation reduces biodiversity, increases soil erosion and releases stored carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Climate change from the Ice Age to the present
objectives: I can describe how the Earth's climate has changed over long timescales
I can explain the difference between natural and human causes
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – weather and climate, including the change in climate from the Ice Age to the present
misconceptions: Thinking climate was stable before humans
Believing natural change disproves human-caused change

assessment.detail: Interpret an ice core temperature record and a modern temperature record; explain what each shows and how the causes differ

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: climate zones; Y6 science: interpret data and evidence

lessons.title: Effects of climate change and responses
objectives: I can describe the effects of climate change on people and environments
I can compare mitigation and adaptation
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes, environments and the climate
misconceptions: Confusing mitigation (reducing causes) with adaptation (coping with effects)
Thinking climate change affects all countries equally

assessment.detail: Classify twelve responses as mitigation or adaptation; write a justified judgement on which matters more for the UK

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: report findings with reasoned explanations

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Earth has moved between glacial and interglacial periods for millions of years.
Ice cores, tree rings and pollen records provide evidence of past climate.
Natural causes of climate change include orbital changes, volcanic eruptions and solar variation.
The current rapid warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels.
Effects of climate change include sea level rise, more extreme weather, shifting ecosystems and pressure on water and food supply.
Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change; adaptation reduces its impacts.
Renewable energy, energy efficiency and afforestation are mitigation strategies.
Flood defences, drought-resistant crops and managed retreat are adaptation strategies.
The countries least responsible for emissions are often the most vulnerable to the effects.

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: weather, climate and biomes
objectives: I can explain climate processes and evaluate responses to climate change
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – weather and climate; biomes; interaction of human and physical processes
misconceptions: Confusing weather events with climate trends in an extended answer

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: climate graph interpretation, a biome question, a synoptic chart and one nine-mark evaluation on climate change responses

knowledgeComponents.statement: Climate is described over decades; weather over hours and days.
Latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and ocean currents together explain a place's climate.
Global atmospheric circulation explains the belts of rainforest and desert.
Vegetation in every biome is adapted to its climate.
Deforestation both results from and contributes to climate change.
Evidence for recent warming comes from instrumental records, ice cores and satellite data.
An evaluation of climate responses must consider cost, effectiveness, scale and who benefits.
Physical and human geography are connected: neither can be explained alone.

terms.name: Summer 1
terms.focus: Africa: a continent of contrasts, with a regional depth study, meeting the KS3 requirement to extend locational knowledge to Africa. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: The physical geography of Africa
objectives: I can locate Africa's countries, major rivers, deserts and mountains
I can describe the physical diversity of the continent
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge – extend locational knowledge and deepen spatial awareness of the world's countries using maps of the world to focus on Africa, Russia, Asia (including China and India), and the Middle East, focusing on their environmental regions, including polar and hot deserts, key physical and human characteristics, countries and major cities
misconceptions: Referring to Africa as a country
Assuming the whole continent is hot desert or jungle

assessment.detail: Label 20 African countries, five rivers, three deserts and three mountain ranges from memory

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: locate the world's countries, using maps to focus on their environmental regions, key physical and human characteristics, countries and major cities
