lessons.title: The human geography of Africa
objectives: I can locate Africa's major cities and describe its population distribution
I can describe the diversity of cultures, languages and economies
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge – key physical and human characteristics, countries and major cities; Place knowledge
misconceptions: Assuming Africa is uniformly poor
Believing African borders reflect long-standing cultural divisions

assessment.detail: Interpret a population density map of Africa; write a paragraph challenging one common stereotype using evidence

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand geographical similarities and differences through the study of human and physical geography of a region

knowledgeComponents.statement: Africa is a continent of 54 countries, not a single country.
The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert, covering much of North Africa.
The Nile is the longest river in Africa; the Congo carries the greatest volume.
The Great Rift Valley runs through East Africa where the African plate is splitting.
The Sahel is a semi-arid belt of land between the Sahara and the savanna.
Africa's biomes range from desert and Mediterranean to savanna, rainforest and mountain.
Lagos, Cairo and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities.
Africa is the fastest urbanising continent and has the youngest population.
Many African borders were drawn by European powers in the late 19th century, cutting across cultural groups.

lessons.title: Africa's climate zones and the Sahel
objectives: I can explain the pattern of climate across Africa
I can explain the causes and effects of desertification in the Sahel
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – weather and climate; how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes, environments and the climate
misconceptions: Blaming desertification entirely on climate or entirely on people
Thinking desertification means the desert physically advancing as a front

assessment.detail: Draw a causal diagram of desertification with both physical and human causes; explain two management strategies

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: climate zones, biomes and vegetation belts

knowledgeComponents.statement: Africa's climate is broadly symmetrical about the Equator: rainforest at the centre, then savanna, then desert.
Desertification is the degradation of land in dry areas into desert-like conditions.
Physical causes of desertification include reduced and less reliable rainfall and higher temperatures.
Human causes include overgrazing, over-cultivation, deforestation for fuelwood and population pressure.
Removing vegetation exposes soil, which is then eroded by wind and rain.
Desertification threatens food security for millions of people in the Sahel.
Management strategies include tree planting, stone lines, water harvesting and improved farming methods.
The Great Green Wall is an African-led project to restore degraded land across the Sahel.

lessons.title: Measuring development
objectives: I can define development and name several measures of it
I can explain why a single measure can be misleading
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – international development; economic activity in the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors
misconceptions: Equating development only with wealth
Thinking a national average describes everyone in the country

assessment.detail: Compare five countries on four indicators; explain a case where GNI per capita and HDI give different impressions

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand geographical similarities and differences through the study of human geography of regions

lessons.title: The development gap and its causes
objectives: I can explain the physical and human causes of uneven development
I can evaluate strategies to reduce the development gap
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – international development; the use of natural resources
misconceptions: Assuming aid is always the best solution
Thinking a country's development depends only on its physical geography

assessment.detail: Classify causes of uneven development as physical, historical, economic or political; evaluate two strategies with a judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including economic activity and trade links

knowledgeComponents.statement: Development means improvement in the quality of life and standard of living of a population.
GNI per capita is the average income per person in a country.
The Human Development Index combines income, life expectancy and education into one figure between 0 and 1.
An average hides inequality within a country.
Infant mortality and literacy rate are social indicators of development.
Physical causes of uneven development include climate, natural hazards, being landlocked and resource availability.
Human causes include colonial history, conflict, trade rules, debt and governance.
Strategies to reduce the gap include fair trade, debt relief, microfinance, aid and investment.
Small-scale bottom-up projects are often more sustainable than large top-down ones.

lessons.title: Kenya: physical and human geography
objectives: I can describe the physical and human geography of a named African country
I can explain how they interact
lessons.ncRef: Place knowledge – understand geographical similarities, differences and links between places through the study of human and physical geography of a region within Africa
misconceptions: Assuming all of Kenya has the same climate
Treating tourism as an unambiguous good

assessment.detail: Produce a one-page annotated country profile of Kenya covering relief, climate, population, economy and links to the wider world

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand geographical similarities and differences through the study of human and physical geography of a region

knowledgeComponents.statement: Kenya lies on the Equator in East Africa, with a coast on the Indian Ocean.
Kenya's Rift Valley and highlands give it a wide range of climates despite its equatorial location.
Altitude means Nairobi is far cooler than its equatorial latitude alone would suggest.
Kenya's main exports include tea, horticultural products such as cut flowers, and coffee.
Tourism based on wildlife and the coast is a major source of income and employment.
Tourism brings income but can damage habitats and profits may leak abroad.
Nairobi is Kenya's capital and a major regional hub for business and technology.
Mombasa is Kenya's main port, linking East Africa to global trade.

weeks.unit: Regional depth study: change in Kenya

lessons.title: Rural and urban life in Kenya
objectives: I can compare rural and urban life in a named country
I can explain why people migrate from rural to urban areas
lessons.ncRef: Place knowledge – study of a region within Africa; Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation
misconceptions: Assuming migrants are always pulled rather than pushed
Describing informal settlements only as places of poverty

assessment.detail: Compare rural and urban life on five criteria; explain rural-urban migration using push and pull factors

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: types of settlement and land use; economic activity

lessons.title: Kenya's global links and a changing economy
objectives: I can describe how a country is connected to the wider world
I can evaluate the benefits and costs of those connections
lessons.ncRef: Place knowledge – geographical similarities, differences and links between places; Human and physical geography – international development; economic activity
misconceptions: Thinking trade links only benefit the richer partner in every case
Assuming a low-income country has no advanced technology

assessment.detail: Evaluate the benefits and costs of Kenya's cut flower export industry for people and environment; reach a judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including trade links

knowledgeComponents.statement: Push factors drive people away from an area; pull factors attract them to another.
Common rural push factors are limited jobs, poor services and unreliable harvests.
Common urban pull factors are employment, education, healthcare and perceived opportunity.
Rapid urban growth can outpace housing and services, producing informal settlements.
Informal settlements contain strong communities and thriving small businesses as well as hardship.
Interdependence means countries rely on each other through trade, aid, migration and information.
Kenya's cut flower industry supplies European supermarkets and employs tens of thousands of people.
Depending on one export makes an economy vulnerable to price changes, so diversification reduces risk.
Mobile money services such as M-Pesa show technological innovation originating in Kenya.

lessons.title: Comparing an African region with the UK
objectives: I can compare two places systematically
I can explain similarities as well as differences
lessons.ncRef: Place knowledge – understand geographical similarities, differences and links between places through the study of human and physical geography of a region in Africa and a region in Asia
misconceptions: Comparing only differences and missing the similarities
Comparing a whole continent with a single country

assessment.detail: Compare a region of Kenya with a UK region on relief, climate, population, economy and challenges; identify two genuine similarities

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand geographical similarities and differences through the study of human and physical geography of a region of the UK and a region in a European or North/South American country

knowledgeComponents.statement: A systematic comparison uses the same criteria for both places.
Comparisons must be at the same scale: region with region, not continent with country.
Places at different levels of development still share many geographical processes.
Both the UK and Kenya face rural-urban migration, ageing infrastructure and climate pressures.
Comparative statements use connectives such as whereas, in contrast, and similarly.
Data should be quoted with units and sources when comparing places.
Stereotypes are challenged by specific evidence about particular places.
No single place represents a whole continent.

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment: Africa and development
objectives: I can apply locational knowledge and development understanding to unseen material
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge – Africa; Place knowledge; Human and physical geography – international development
misconceptions: Generalising about Africa instead of using a named place

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: African locational knowledge, a development data question, a Kenya case study question and one nine-mark evaluation

lessons.title: Review, retrieval and challenging stereotypes
objectives: I can repair my gaps
I can explain why single-story representations of places are misleading
lessons.ncRef: Purpose of study – geography inspires curiosity and fascination about the world and its people; Place knowledge
misconceptions: Accepting media images as representative of a whole region

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz on weeks 22–32; write a short piece challenging one common representation of Africa using named evidence

knowledgeComponents.statement: Africa contains enormous physical, cultural and economic diversity.
A stereotype is an oversimplified image of a place or group.
Media images are selected, so they represent a viewpoint rather than the whole picture.
Development is multi-dimensional and cannot be captured by income alone.
Uneven development has both physical and human causes acting together.
Desertification results from the interaction of climate and land use.
Every place is connected to others through trade, migration and information.
Naming places and quoting figures is what turns a general answer into a geographical one.

terms.name: Summer 2
terms.focus: Population, urbanisation, resources and a summative fieldwork enquiry. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: World population growth and distribution
objectives: I can describe the pattern of world population growth
I can explain why population is unevenly distributed
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation
misconceptions: Confusing population growth with population size
Thinking a falling birth rate means a falling population immediately

assessment.detail: Interpret a world population growth graph and a density map; explain three factors affecting distribution

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including types of settlement and land use

lessons.title: Population structure and population pyramids
objectives: I can interpret a population pyramid
I can explain the challenges of an ageing and of a youthful population
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation; international development
misconceptions: Reading a pyramid as showing numbers rather than proportions
Assuming a wide base is always a problem

assessment.detail: Interpret four population pyramids; match each to a country and explain two challenges each country faces

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: interpret bar charts and proportions

knowledgeComponents.statement: World population passed 8 billion in November 2022 and is still growing, but more slowly than in the 20th century.
Natural increase is birth rate minus death rate.
Birth rate and death rate are measured per 1000 people per year.
Population is densest where the climate is favourable, land is flat and fertile, and there are jobs and transport links.
Deserts, high mountains, dense rainforest and polar regions are sparsely populated.
A population pyramid shows the proportion of males and females in each age group.
A wide base indicates a youthful population with a high birth rate.
The dependency ratio compares the non-working age population with the working age population.
An ageing population increases pressure on pensions and healthcare; a youthful one on schools and future jobs.

lessons.title: Migration: types, causes and effects
objectives: I can distinguish types of migration
I can explain the effects of migration on source and destination areas
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation; international development
misconceptions: Using 'migrant' and 'refugee' interchangeably
Assuming migration only affects the destination country

assessment.detail: Classify ten migration examples; complete an impacts table for source and destination areas, positive and negative

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: human geography including settlement and economic activity

knowledgeComponents.statement: Migration is the movement of people to live in a new place for a significant period.
Immigration is movement into a country; emigration is movement out of it.
Voluntary migration is a choice; forced migration is not.
A refugee has been forced to leave their country and has been recognised as needing protection.
An asylum seeker has applied for protection and is awaiting a decision.
Remittances are money sent home by migrants and are a major income source for some countries.
Source areas may lose working-age people and skills but gain remittances.
Destination areas may gain labour, skills and cultural diversity, and face pressure on housing and services.

lessons.title: Urbanisation and megacities
objectives: I can define urbanisation and describe global patterns
I can explain why cities grow
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation
misconceptions: Thinking urbanisation means cities getting physically bigger only
Assuming urbanisation is happening equally everywhere

assessment.detail: Locate ten megacities; explain the two causes of urban growth and why urbanisation is fastest in Africa and Asia

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including types of settlement and land use

lessons.title: Urban land use and change in the UK
objectives: I can describe the pattern of land use in a UK city
I can explain how and why urban areas change
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – population and urbanisation; economic activity in the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors
misconceptions: Assuming every city follows the same land use model
Treating regeneration as always beneficial to existing residents

assessment.detail: Annotate a UK city land use map; write a paragraph evaluating one regeneration scheme

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: name and locate cities of the UK and understand how some aspects have changed over time

knowledgeComponents.statement: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of a population living in urban areas.
Over half the world's population now lives in urban areas.
A megacity has a population of over 10 million.
Cities grow through rural-urban migration and through natural increase.
Urbanisation happened earliest in Europe and North America and is now fastest in Africa and Asia.
The central business district has the highest land values and most shops and offices.
Brownfield sites are previously developed land; greenfield sites have not been built on.
Regeneration improves a run-down area, but can raise prices and displace existing residents.
Land use models describe general patterns; every real city departs from them.

lessons.title: Economic sectors and how economies change
objectives: I can classify jobs into the four economic sectors
I can explain how the balance of sectors changes as a country develops
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – economic activity in the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors
misconceptions: Classifying a job by where it happens rather than by what it produces
Thinking manufacturing has disappeared from the UK

assessment.detail: Classify twenty jobs by sector; interpret UK employment structure graphs from 1800 to today and explain the change

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including economic activity including trade links

knowledgeComponents.statement: The primary sector extracts raw materials, such as farming, fishing and mining.
The secondary sector manufactures and processes goods.
The tertiary sector provides services such as retail, health, education and transport.
The quaternary sector involves research, information technology and knowledge-based work.
As a country develops, employment usually shifts from primary to secondary and then to tertiary and quaternary.
Deindustrialisation is the decline of manufacturing employment in a region.
A job is classified by what it produces, not by where the worker sits.
Most UK employment today is in the tertiary sector.

lessons.title: Using and managing natural resources
objectives: I can classify resources as renewable or non-renewable
I can explain what sustainable resource use means
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – the use of natural resources; how human activity relies on the effective functioning of natural systems
misconceptions: Thinking renewable resources cannot be exhausted
Assuming sustainability means never using a resource

assessment.detail: Classify fifteen resources; evaluate two strategies for sustainable water or energy use

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: describe and understand key aspects of human geography including the distribution of natural resources including energy, food, minerals and water

lessons.title: Water and food security
objectives: I can explain the causes of water and food insecurity
I can evaluate strategies to improve security
lessons.ncRef: Human and physical geography – the use of natural resources; international development; how human activity relies on the effective functioning of natural systems
misconceptions: Thinking water scarcity is only about a lack of rain
Assuming there is not enough food globally

assessment.detail: Interpret a global water stress map; evaluate three strategies for improving water security with a judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: distribution of natural resources including energy, food, minerals and water

knowledgeComponents.statement: A renewable resource can be replenished naturally within a human lifetime.
A renewable resource can still be exhausted if it is used faster than it is replenished.
Sustainable use meets present needs without preventing future generations from meeting theirs.
Stewardship is the responsible management of resources for the future.
Water security means reliable access to enough safe water for health and livelihoods.
Water scarcity can be physical (not enough water) or economic (water present but not accessible).
Globally enough food is produced, so food insecurity is largely about distribution, access and waste.
Strategies to improve water security include reservoirs, transfer schemes, desalination and reducing leakage.
Virtual water is the water used to produce a good, which is effectively traded with it.

lessons.title: Planning and carrying out an independent enquiry
objectives: I can design my own geographical enquiry
I can collect appropriate primary and secondary data
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – use fieldwork in contrasting locations to collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data, using multiple sources of increasingly complex information
misconceptions: Choosing a question too broad to answer with available data
Collecting more data than can be analysed

assessment.detail: Design and carry out an enquiry in the local area, with a written methodology justifying each choice

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present human and physical features in the local area

knowledgeComponents.statement: A good enquiry question is specific, answerable with available data and geographical.
A methodology states what was collected, how, where, when and why.
Random, systematic and stratified are the three main sampling strategies.
Combining primary and secondary data strengthens an enquiry.
A risk assessment identifies hazards and control measures before fieldwork.
Data collection must be planned around the question, not the other way round.
Recording the exact time and location of data collection allows later interpretation.
Every methodological choice should be justified in writing.

lessons.title: Presenting, analysing and concluding the enquiry
objectives: I can present my data effectively and analyse it
I can conclude and evaluate my own enquiry
lessons.ncRef: Geographical skills and fieldwork – collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data; communicate geographical information in a variety of ways including through maps, numerical and quantitative skills and writing at length
misconceptions: Presenting data without analysing it
Writing an evaluation that only apologises rather than explaining

assessment.detail: Full written enquiry: question, methodology, presentation, analysis, conclusion and evaluation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: present findings using a range of methods including graphs and digital technologies

lessons.title: End-of-year assessment and Year 8 preview
objectives: I can demonstrate my geographical knowledge from the whole year
I can name the topics Year 8 will build on
lessons.ncRef: Locational knowledge; Place knowledge; Human and physical geography; Geographical skills and fieldwork
misconceptions: Assuming autumn term locational knowledge has been retained without retesting

assessment.detail: 50-minute cumulative paper across all six half terms, plus a Year 8 progression map (Asia, the Middle East, coasts, glaciation, globalisation)

knowledgeComponents.statement: Analysis explains what the data show and why; presentation only displays them.
An evaluation names a specific limitation and a specific improvement.
A conclusion answers the original enquiry question directly.
Year 7 geography covered skills, tectonics, rivers, weather and climate, Africa, and population and resources.
Year 8 extends locational knowledge to Asia, including China and India, and the Middle East.
Physical and human geography always interact; explaining either alone is incomplete.
Locational knowledge needs regular retrieval to be retained.
Geographical writing at length uses named places, data, connectives and a judgement.

subjects.name: History
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: history programmes of study, key stage 3 (DfE, September 2013; statutory from September 2014). Required content: the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509; the development of Church, state and society in Britain 1509-1745; ideas, political power, industry and empire: Britain 1745-1901; challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world 1901 to the present day (including the Holocaust); a local history study; the study of an aspect or theme in British history that consolidates and extends chronological knowledge from before 1066; at least one study of a significant society or issue in world history and its interconnections with other world developments.
subjects.yearShare: Enrichment strand at roughly half the volume of a core subject: 1.5 lessons per week on average. Year 7 covers the pre-1066 thematic study, the whole of Medieval Britain 1066-1509, a local history study, and a world history depth study of the medieval Islamic world, the West African empires and the Mongols. Britain 1509-1745, 1745-1901 and 1901 to the present, including the compulsory Holocaust study, follow in Years 8 and 9.
deferredToY8Y9: Church, state and society in Britain 1509-1745 (Renaissance, Reformation, Civil Wars, Restoration, Act of Union)
Ideas, political power, industry and empire 1745-1901 (Enlightenment, transatlantic slave trade and abolition, industrialisation, Empire, franchise reform)
Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world 1901 to the present, including the compulsory study of the Holocaust
Further world history depth studies such as Mughal India, Qing China, the Russian empires or the USA in the 20th century
priorKnowledgeAssumed: Y3-Y6: develop a chronologically secure knowledge and understanding of British, local and world history, establishing clear narratives within and across periods
Y3-Y6: note connections, contrasts and trends over time and develop the appropriate use of historical terms
Y3-Y6: address and sometimes devise historically valid questions about change, cause, similarity and difference, and significance
Y3-Y6: understand how our knowledge of the past is constructed from a range of sources
Y3-Y6: construct informed responses that involve thoughtful selection and organisation of relevant historical information
Y3-Y6: changes in Britain from the Stone Age to the Iron Age
Y3-Y6: the Roman Empire and its impact on Britain
Y3-Y6: Britain's settlement by Anglo-Saxons and Scots
Y3-Y6: the Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the Kingdom of England to the time of Edward the Confessor
Y3-Y6: a local history study
Y3-Y6: the achievements of the earliest civilizations and a study of one in depth
Y3-Y6: Ancient Greece and its influence on the western world
Y3-Y6: a non-European society that provides contrasts with British history, for example early Islamic civilisation including Baghdad c. AD 900, Mayan civilization c. AD 900, or Benin c. AD 900-1300

terms.name: Autumn 1
terms.focus: What is history? Historical skills, a thematic overview of Britain before 1066 that consolidates and extends KS2 chronology, and the succession crisis of 1066. 12 lessons.

lessons.title: What is history and how do we know about the past?
objectives: I can explain what a historian does
I can distinguish a primary from a secondary source
lessons.ncRef: Aims – pupils should understand the methods of historical enquiry, including how evidence is used rigorously to make historical claims, and discern how and why contrasting arguments and interpretations of the past have been constructed
misconceptions: Thinking primary sources are always more reliable than secondary ones
Believing history is a fixed list of facts rather than an argument from evidence

assessment.detail: Baseline chronology and period-knowledge quiz; classify twelve sources as primary or secondary with reasons

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand how our knowledge of the past is constructed from a range of sources

lessons.title: Chronology: ordering the past
objectives: I can use BC, AD, century and decade correctly
I can place the main periods of British history in order
lessons.ncRef: Aims – know and understand the history of these islands as a coherent, chronological narrative; Key stage 3 – extend and deepen their chronologically secure knowledge and understanding of British, local and world history
misconceptions: Thinking the 15th century means the 1500s
Believing BC dates count forwards

assessment.detail: Build a labelled timeline of British history from the Stone Age to the present; twenty century-and-date conversion questions

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: develop a chronologically secure knowledge and understanding of British, local and world history, establishing clear narratives within and across the periods they study

knowledgeComponents.statement: History is the study of the past using evidence.
A primary source was created at the time being studied; a secondary source was created later.
A primary source is not automatically reliable; it still has a purpose and a point of view.
Archaeology studies the past through physical remains.
AD dates count forwards from year 1; BC dates count backwards.
The years 1400 to 1499 belong to the 15th century.
To find the century, take the first two digits of a year and add one, unless the year ends in 00.
The main periods of British history run: prehistory, Roman, Anglo-Saxon and Viking, medieval, early modern, industrial and modern.

lessons.title: Evaluating sources: usefulness and reliability
objectives: I can evaluate a source for its usefulness to a historian
I can consider provenance when judging a source
lessons.ncRef: Aims – understand the methods of historical enquiry, including how evidence is used rigorously to make historical claims
misconceptions: Dismissing a biased source as useless when its bias is itself evidence
Judging reliability only by whether the source agrees with what is already known

assessment.detail: Evaluate three sources on the same event for usefulness, using nature, origin and purpose

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand how knowledge of the past is constructed from a range of sources; address historically valid questions

knowledgeComponents.statement: Provenance means who made a source, when, where, why and for whom.
A biased source is still useful because it reveals what someone wanted others to believe.
Corroboration is checking a claim against other independent sources.
Usefulness depends on the question being asked, not on the source alone.
A source's purpose may be to record, persuade, justify, entertain or instruct.
Written sources from the medieval period were mostly produced by monks and the powerful, so many voices are missing.
A source's limitations should be stated alongside its uses.
Historians build claims from several sources, not from one.

lessons.title: Prehistoric and Roman Britain: a thematic overview
objectives: I can outline how Britain changed from the Stone Age to the end of Roman rule
I can explain what the Romans changed and what they left behind
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the study of an aspect or theme in British history that consolidates and extends pupils' chronological knowledge from before 1066; for example, Britain's changing landscape from the Iron Age to the present, or the changing nature of political power in Britain traced through case studies
misconceptions: Thinking Roman Britain ended suddenly in a single year
Believing prehistoric people were primitive rather than skilled

assessment.detail: Complete a change-and-continuity chart for Britain from the Neolithic to AD 410; write a paragraph on the most significant Roman change

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: changes in Britain from the Stone Age to the Iron Age; the Roman Empire and its impact on Britain

lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon and Viking Britain
objectives: I can explain how Anglo-Saxon England was ruled
I can describe the impact of Viking settlement
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the study of an aspect or theme in British history that consolidates and extends pupils' chronological knowledge from before 1066
misconceptions: Seeing Vikings only as raiders rather than also as settlers, traders and farmers
Thinking England was a single unified kingdom from the start

assessment.detail: Describe Anglo-Saxon government; assess whether the Vikings changed England more by raiding or by settling

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: Britain's settlement by Anglo-Saxons and Scots; the Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the Kingdom of England to the time of Edward the Confessor

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Romans invaded Britain in AD 43 under the emperor Claudius.
Roman rule brought towns, roads, coinage, writing and later Christianity to Britain.
Roman government of Britain broke down in the early fifth century, around AD 410.
Boudica led a revolt of the Iceni against Roman rule in AD 60 or 61.
Anglo-Saxon England was made up of several kingdoms before it was unified in the tenth century.
The witan was the council of nobles who advised the Anglo-Saxon king and helped choose his successor.
Viking raids on England began in the late eighth century, with Lindisfarne attacked in 793.
The Danelaw was the area of England under Danish law and settlement.
Alfred the Great of Wessex resisted the Vikings and promoted learning and law.

lessons.title: England in 1066 and the death of Edward the Confessor
objectives: I can describe England as it was in January 1066
I can explain why the succession was disputed
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Norman Conquest
misconceptions: Assuming the English crown passed automatically to the eldest son
Thinking 1066 was the start of English history

assessment.detail: Describe the political situation in England in 1066; explain in a paragraph why no claim was clear-cut

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: the Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the Kingdom of England to the time of Edward the Confessor

knowledgeComponents.statement: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without a son.
In Anglo-Saxon England the witan helped choose the next king; succession was not automatic.
England in 1066 was a wealthy, well-governed kingdom with shires, coinage and a strong tax system.
The Godwin family held the most powerful earldoms in England.
A claim to the throne could rest on blood relationship, designation by the previous king, an oath, or force.
England had strong links with both Normandy and Scandinavia before 1066.
Harold Godwinson was crowned the day after Edward's death.
1066 marks a turning point but not the beginning of English history.

lessons.title: The four claimants to the throne
objectives: I can describe the claim of each contender
I can judge which claim was strongest and justify my view
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Norman Conquest
misconceptions: Assuming William's claim was obviously the weakest because he lost the argument at the time
Judging claims by modern rules of inheritance

assessment.detail: Rank the four claims with criteria; write a paragraph justifying the ranking using evidence

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: Anglo-Saxon and Viking England to Edward the Confessor

lessons.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
objectives: I can narrate the events of 1066 in order
I can explain why William won the Battle of Hastings
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Norman Conquest
misconceptions: Believing Harold definitely died from an arrow in the eye
Explaining the outcome by a single cause

assessment.detail: Categorise the causes of William's victory as luck, leadership, tactics and Harold's mistakes; write a full explanation naming the most important

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: chronological narrative; understand how evidence is used

knowledgeComponents.statement: Harold Godwinson claimed Edward had named him on his deathbed and was chosen by the witan.
William of Normandy claimed Edward had promised him the throne in 1051 and that Harold had sworn an oath to support him.
Harald Hardrada of Norway claimed the throne through an earlier agreement between Scandinavian and English kings.
Edgar the Aetheling had the closest blood claim but was a boy of about fourteen.
Harold defeated Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.
The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 and Harold was killed.
Harold's army was tired from the march south and had lost men at Stamford Bridge.
William's use of cavalry, archers and a possible feigned retreat broke the English shield wall.
The Bayeux Tapestry is a Norman source and presents a Norman version of events.

lessons.title: Thinking about causes: categorising and prioritising
objectives: I can group causes into categories
I can explain how causes link together
lessons.ncRef: Aims – gain historical perspective; understand the connections between local, regional, national and international history; Key stage 3 – create their own structured accounts, including written narratives and analyses
misconceptions: Listing causes without ranking or connecting them
Thinking the most immediate cause is always the most important

assessment.detail: Write a structured explanation of why William won in 1066, with categorised causes, links between them and a justified conclusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: address and devise historically valid questions about cause and significance

knowledgeComponents.statement: Long-term causes build up over years; short-term causes act immediately.
A trigger is the event that sets off something already made likely by deeper causes.
Causes are usually connected rather than independent.
Categories of cause include political, military, religious, economic and personal.
A strong causation answer prioritises causes and justifies the ranking.
Historians disagree about the relative weight of causes, which is why interpretations differ.
Each paragraph of a causation essay should end by linking back to the question.
Chance and individual decisions can matter as much as structural causes.

lessons.title: Why do interpretations of 1066 differ?
objectives: I can explain why two historians can reach different conclusions
I can compare two interpretations of the same event
lessons.ncRef: Aims – discern how and why contrasting arguments and interpretations of the past have been constructed; Key stage 3 – understand how different types of historical sources are used rigorously to make historical claims, and discern how and why contrasting arguments and interpretations of the past have been constructed
misconceptions: Thinking one interpretation must simply be wrong
Confusing an interpretation with a source

assessment.detail: Compare two interpretations of the Norman Conquest; explain two reasons why they differ

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand that different versions of past events may exist, giving some reasons for this

lessons.title: Writing history: structuring an analytical paragraph
objectives: I can write a paragraph with a point, evidence and explanation
I can use precise historical vocabulary
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create their own structured accounts, including written narratives and analyses
misconceptions: Narrating events instead of answering the question
Making an assertion with no supporting evidence

assessment.detail: Deconstruct a model paragraph; write two independent paragraphs assessed against a history writing rubric

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English: write well-structured formal explanations

knowledgeComponents.statement: An interpretation is a historian's argument about the past, built from sources.
Interpretations differ because of the evidence available, the questions asked, the emphasis chosen and the historian's own time.
A source is evidence from the past; an interpretation is a later account built from evidence.
Disagreement between historians is normal and productive, not a sign of failure.
A historical paragraph opens with a point that answers the question.
Evidence in history means specific names, dates, places and figures.
Explanation shows how the evidence proves the point.
Narrating events without answering the question cannot reach the higher bands.

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: 1066 and historical skills
objectives: I can apply chronology, source skills and causal explanation to an assessment
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509; historical enquiry and interpretation
misconceptions: Describing sources instead of using them as evidence

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: chronology, a source utility question, a causation essay on 1066 and one interpretation question

lessons.title: Review, retrieval and target setting
objectives: I can identify and repair my gaps
I can recall the key knowledge from this half term
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – extend and deepen chronologically secure knowledge
misconceptions: Reading over notes rather than retrieving from memory

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz on weeks 1–7; rewrite the weakest essay paragraph

knowledgeComponents.statement: Chronology, evidence, causation, significance, change and interpretation are the core historical concepts.
A source utility answer must consider content, provenance and the question asked.
1066 saw three battles: Fulford, Stamford Bridge and Hastings.
William was crowned king on Christmas Day 1066 at Westminster Abbey.
Retrieval from memory strengthens knowledge far more than rereading notes.
Historical writing needs specific evidence rather than general statements.
England before 1066 was already a sophisticated state with shires, sheriffs and taxation.
Turning points are judged by how much changed as a result of them.

terms.name: Autumn 2
terms.focus: The Norman Conquest: how William took control of England and how far the Conquest changed the country. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: Resistance to Norman rule
objectives: I can describe the main rebellions against William
I can explain why they failed
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Norman Conquest
misconceptions: Thinking England accepted Norman rule immediately after Hastings
Believing rebellions were coordinated nationally

assessment.detail: Map and summarise four rebellions between 1067 and 1071; explain two reasons each failed

ks2Prerequisites: Y6: chronological narrative of Anglo-Saxon and Viking England

lessons.title: The Harrying of the North
objectives: I can describe what happened in the north in 1069 to 1070
I can evaluate whether William's actions were justified by the standards of the time
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Norman Conquest; Aims – understand the methods of historical enquiry
misconceptions: Applying only modern moral standards without also considering contemporary ones
Accepting chroniclers' figures uncritically

assessment.detail: Use three contemporary accounts and Domesday evidence to assess the scale of the Harrying and reach a judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand how knowledge of the past is constructed from sources

knowledgeComponents.statement: Rebellions against William broke out in Kent, the south-west, the Welsh borders and the north between 1067 and 1071.
Hereward the Wake led resistance in the Fens around Ely in 1070 to 1071.
Rebellions failed because they were local, uncoordinated and faced Norman castles and cavalry.
The Harrying of the North took place in the winter of 1069 to 1070.
William's forces destroyed crops, livestock and villages, causing famine across Yorkshire and beyond.
Domesday Book records much northern land as 'waste' seventeen years later.
Some contemporaries, including Norman chroniclers, condemned the Harrying as excessive.
Historical judgement considers both the standards of the time and later moral assessment.

lessons.title: Castles as instruments of control
objectives: I can describe the design of motte and bailey and stone keep castles
I can explain how castles helped the Normans control England
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Norman Conquest; the development of art, architecture and literature
misconceptions: Thinking castles were mainly homes rather than military and administrative bases
Assuming stone castles came first

assessment.detail: Label a motte and bailey castle; explain three ways castles secured Norman control; explain why castle design changed over time

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: local history study; the Norman Conquest as a chronological anchor

knowledgeComponents.statement: A motte is a raised earth mound; the bailey is the enclosed courtyard below it.
Early Norman castles were built quickly from earth and timber, then later rebuilt in stone.
The Normans built hundreds of castles across England after 1066.
Castles were placed at river crossings, in towns and on borders to control movement.
A castle was a military base, an administrative centre and a symbol of Norman power.
Building a castle inside a town often meant demolishing existing houses.
Stone keeps such as the White Tower in London were stronger and more permanent.
Castle design changed as siege technology improved.

lessons.title: The feudal system
objectives: I can describe the structure of the feudal system
I can explain how it helped William control England
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: society, economy and culture, for example feudalism
misconceptions: Thinking feudalism was a fixed system designed all at once
Assuming everyone in medieval England fitted neatly into one of four boxes

assessment.detail: Draw and annotate the feudal pyramid; explain how land, loyalty and service were exchanged at each level

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand connections and contrasts within and across periods

lessons.title: How far did landholding change after 1066?
objectives: I can describe the redistribution of land after the Conquest
I can assess how far the ruling class was replaced
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Norman Conquest; society and economy
misconceptions: Thinking all English people lost their land
Believing the Conquest changed everything equally at every level of society

assessment.detail: Analyse figures on English and Norman landholding in 1066 and 1086; write a judgement on how far the elite was replaced

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: interpret proportions and percentages

knowledgeComponents.statement: In the feudal system the king owned all land and granted it in return for service.
Tenants-in-chief were barons and bishops who held land directly from the king.
Barons granted land to knights in return for military service.
Villeins worked the land and owed labour and dues to their lord.
Homage was the ceremony in which a man swore loyalty to his lord.
Feudalism tied loyalty to landholding, making rebellion costly.
By 1086 almost all major landholders in England were Norman or French.
For most peasants, daily work changed far less than it did for the aristocracy.
The word 'feudalism' was invented by later historians to describe the system.

lessons.title: Domesday Book: why it was made and what it tells us
objectives: I can explain why William ordered the Domesday survey
I can use Domesday evidence to answer a question about medieval England
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Norman Conquest; the methods of historical enquiry
misconceptions: Thinking Domesday was a census of people
Assuming it covered the whole of Britain

assessment.detail: Use a Domesday extract for a local settlement to describe its population, land and value; explain what Domesday can and cannot tell us

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand how our knowledge of the past is constructed from a range of sources

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Domesday survey was ordered in 1085 and completed in 1086.
Domesday recorded who held land, how much it was worth and what resources it contained.
William's main motives were to assess tax and to settle disputes over landholding.
Domesday did not cover London, Winchester or most land north of the Tees.
Domesday counted landholders and heads of household, not every individual.
The book was called Domesday because its judgements were final, like the Day of Judgement.
Domesday is the most detailed surviving record of eleventh-century England.
A record made for tax purposes may under-report or omit what did not need taxing.

lessons.title: The Norman Church
objectives: I can describe the changes the Normans made to the English Church
I can explain why controlling the Church mattered
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Christendom, the importance of religion; the development of art and architecture
misconceptions: Thinking the Church was separate from politics
Believing the Normans introduced Christianity to England

assessment.detail: Describe four Norman Church reforms; explain in a paragraph why the Church was central to Norman control

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: Anglo-Saxon Christianity; local history study of a church or cathedral

lessons.title: Language, law and culture after the Conquest
objectives: I can describe how language and law changed after 1066
I can explain which changes lasted
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: society, economy and culture; the development of art, architecture and literature
misconceptions: Thinking English disappeared after 1066
Assuming the Normans replaced all Anglo-Saxon law

assessment.detail: Sort ten features of English life as changed, partly changed or unchanged after 1066, with justification

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English: the history of English and its Norman French vocabulary

knowledgeComponents.statement: William replaced most English bishops and abbots with Norman appointees.
Lanfranc became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1070 and reformed the English Church.
The Normans rebuilt most English cathedrals in the Romanesque style.
The Church controlled education, record-keeping and much of the land, so controlling it was politically essential.
Norman French became the language of the ruling class while English remained the language of most people.
Thousands of French words entered English after 1066, especially in law, government, food and warfare.
The Normans kept much Anglo-Saxon local government, including shires and sheriffs.
Forest law reserved large areas for royal hunting and imposed harsh penalties.
Change and continuity existed side by side after the Conquest.

lessons.title: How significant was the Norman Conquest?
objectives: I can apply criteria for historical significance
I can reach and justify an overall judgement on 1066
lessons.ncRef: Aims – gain historical perspective by placing their growing knowledge into different contexts; Key stage 3 – create their own structured accounts
misconceptions: Assuming an event is significant because it is famous
Judging significance by the drama of the event rather than its consequences

assessment.detail: Write a full essay assessing the significance of the Norman Conquest against stated criteria, with a justified conclusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: devise historically valid questions about significance

knowledgeComponents.statement: Significance can be judged by how many people were affected, how deeply, for how long, and whether it changed later events.
Significance is judged, not fixed, so historians can reasonably disagree about it.
The Conquest replaced the ruling class, reshaped landholding, changed the Church and altered the language.
For most peasants, farming and daily life continued much as before.
1066 tied England more closely to France and continental Europe for centuries.
An essay conclusion must reach a judgement rather than summarise both sides.
A counter-argument strengthens a historical judgement when it is answered.
Significance may change over time as later generations reinterpret an event.

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: the Norman Conquest
objectives: I can demonstrate secure knowledge of Norman England and use it in extended writing
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509
misconceptions: Writing generally about castles or feudalism without specific detail

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: knowledge recall, a Domesday source question and one extended judgement on how William controlled England

lessons.title: Review, retrieval and a Norman local study
objectives: I can repair my gaps
I can find evidence of the Normans in my own local area
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – a local history study, for example a depth study linked to one of the British areas of study listed above
misconceptions: Assuming local history is separate from national history

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz; investigate one local building, place name or Domesday entry and present the findings

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study

knowledgeComponents.statement: William controlled England through military force, castles, land redistribution, the Church and record-keeping.
Evidence of the Normans survives in castles, churches, place names and Domesday entries across England.
Local history illustrates and tests national narratives.
An extended judgement organises factors, weighs them and reaches a conclusion.
Domesday Book, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the Bayeux Tapestry are the three key sources for the Conquest.
William died in 1087 and was succeeded by his son William Rufus.
Norman control was established over about five years of sustained campaigning after 1066.
Place names ending in -ton, -ham and -by reveal Anglo-Saxon and Viking settlement beneath later Norman rule.

terms.name: Spring 1
terms.focus: Church, crown and the growth of political power: religion in medieval life, Becket, the Crusades, Magna Carta and the beginnings of Parliament. 9 lessons.

lessons.title: Religion in everyday medieval life
objectives: I can explain the importance of the Church in medieval life
I can describe the role of parishes, monasteries and abbeys
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Christendom, the importance of religion; society, economy and culture: religion in daily life (parishes, monasteries, abbeys)
misconceptions: Assuming medieval people were simply superstitious rather than holding a coherent worldview
Thinking the Church was only about worship rather than education, welfare and law

assessment.detail: Explain five ways the Church shaped daily life; describe the functions of a monastery

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study; the spread of Christianity in Anglo-Saxon England

lessons.title: Church and crown: the murder of Thomas Becket
objectives: I can explain the causes of the quarrel between Henry II and Becket
I can evaluate who was to blame for Becket's murder
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the struggle between Church and crown
misconceptions: Thinking Henry directly ordered the killing
Reducing the quarrel to a personal falling-out rather than a clash of jurisdictions

assessment.detail: Use four sources to reach a judgement on responsibility for Becket's death in 1170

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand how contrasting accounts of the past are constructed

knowledgeComponents.statement: Christendom means the community of Christian lands in medieval Europe.
A tithe was one tenth of a person's produce or income paid to the Church.
Monasteries provided education, medical care, hospitality and record-keeping as well as prayer.
Most medieval people believed the soul faced judgement, which shaped how they lived.
Pilgrimage to a shrine was believed to bring spiritual benefit and sometimes healing.
Thomas Becket was Archbishop of Canterbury and was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in December 1170.
The quarrel centred on whether clergy accused of crimes should be tried in Church courts or royal courts.
Four knights killed Becket after hearing Henry II's angry words; Henry later did public penance.
Becket was made a saint in 1173 and Canterbury became a major pilgrimage destination.

lessons.title: The Crusades: causes and course
objectives: I can explain why the Crusades were launched
I can outline the main events of the First and Third Crusades
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Christendom, the importance of religion and the Crusades
misconceptions: Thinking the Crusades were only about religion
Treating one side as uniformly civilised and the other as barbaric

assessment.detail: Categorise the causes of the First Crusade; produce a timeline of the First and Third Crusades with five key events each

ks2Prerequisites: Y4–Y6: a non-European society that contrasts with British history, for example early Islamic civilisation

knowledgeComponents.statement: Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095.
Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099 after a siege, killing many of its inhabitants.
Motives for crusading included religious belief, the promise of indulgences, land, wealth and status.
Saladin recaptured Jerusalem for the Muslim world in 1187.
Richard I of England led the Third Crusade from 1189 to 1192 but did not retake Jerusalem.
Richard and Saladin agreed a truce allowing Christian pilgrims access to Jerusalem.
Jerusalem was and is a holy city for Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
The Crusades increased contact and trade between Europe and the Middle East as well as conflict.

lessons.title: What made a medieval king powerful?
objectives: I can identify the sources of medieval royal power
I can compare two kings using the same criteria
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the development of Church, state and society; the changing nature of political power in Britain
misconceptions: Thinking a medieval king could simply do as he liked
Judging kings only by battles won

assessment.detail: Compare Henry II and King John against five criteria of kingship and reach a judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand the changing nature of political power

lessons.title: King John and the road to Magna Carta
objectives: I can explain why the barons rebelled against King John
I can distinguish John's own failings from wider pressures
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament
misconceptions: Accepting the traditional 'bad King John' story uncritically
Thinking the barons were fighting for ordinary people

assessment.detail: Categorise the causes of the baronial rebellion of 1215 and explain the links between them

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: address historically valid questions about cause

knowledgeComponents.statement: Medieval royal power rested on land, wealth, military success, justice, patronage and the support of the Church and barons.
A king who lost the support of his barons could not govern effectively.
Henry II reformed royal justice, laying foundations of English common law.
King John lost Normandy to the French king in 1204.
John raised heavy taxes and scutage to fund attempts to recover his French lands.
John quarrelled with the Pope, and England was placed under interdict from 1208.
The barons rebelled in 1215 because of taxation, military failure, arbitrary justice and John's personal conduct.
Much of what we know about John comes from hostile monastic chroniclers.

lessons.title: Magna Carta: what it said and why it mattered
objectives: I can describe the main terms of Magna Carta
I can evaluate its short-term and long-term significance
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament
misconceptions: Thinking Magna Carta gave rights to everyone
Believing it succeeded immediately

assessment.detail: Analyse five clauses of Magna Carta; assess its significance in 1215 and in the long term

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: significance; the changing nature of political power

knowledgeComponents.statement: Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede in June 1215.
Magna Carta limited the king's power to tax without consent and to imprison without lawful judgement.
Most of Magna Carta's clauses protected the interests of barons and the Church, not ordinary people.
Clause 39 established that no free man should be imprisoned or punished except by lawful judgement of his equals or the law of the land.
The Pope annulled Magna Carta within weeks and civil war followed.
Magna Carta was reissued several times after John's death in 1216 and entered English law.
Magna Carta established the principle that the king is subject to the law.
Magna Carta's long-term significance came from how later generations used and reinterpreted it.

lessons.title: The origins of Parliament
objectives: I can explain how Parliament developed in the thirteenth century
I can describe the role of Simon de Montfort
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament; the changing nature of political power in Britain
misconceptions: Thinking medieval Parliament was democratic
Assuming Parliament was created in a single moment

assessment.detail: Produce an annotated timeline of the growth of Parliament from 1215 to 1300 with an explanation of the direction of change

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand the changing nature of political power in Britain

lessons.title: Wales and Scotland: the expansion of English power
objectives: I can describe English attempts to conquer Wales and Scotland
I can explain how those campaigns affected royal power
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the English campaigns to conquer Wales and Scotland up to 1314
misconceptions: Assuming conquest was inevitable or complete
Treating Scotland and Wales as identical cases

assessment.detail: Compare English campaigns in Wales and Scotland; explain why one succeeded and the other did not

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: chronological knowledge of British history

knowledgeComponents.statement: Parliament grew out of the king's Great Council of barons and bishops.
Kings called Parliament mainly because they needed consent for taxation.
Simon de Montfort summoned a Parliament in 1265 that included knights and townsmen.
Edward I's Parliament of 1295 is known as the Model Parliament.
Medieval Parliament represented landholders and townsmen, not the population as a whole.
Edward I conquered Wales by 1283 and built a ring of great castles to hold it.
The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 placed Wales under English law and administration.
Robert the Bruce defeated the English at Bannockburn in 1314, securing Scottish independence.
War was expensive, so campaigns increased the crown's need to summon Parliament for taxes.

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: Church, crown and power
objectives: I can explain how political and religious power changed between 1066 and 1314
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: Church and crown, Magna Carta, Parliament, campaigns in Wales and Scotland
misconceptions: Describing events without tracing the change over time

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: knowledge recall, a Magna Carta source question and one extended answer on how far royal power changed between 1066 and 1314

knowledgeComponents.statement: Between 1066 and 1314 the king remained powerful but became increasingly bound by law and by the need for consent.
The Church was both a partner and a rival to royal power.
Warfare drove taxation, and taxation drove the growth of Parliament.
Change over time is described by comparing the situation at the start and end of a period.
Key dates: 1170 Becket's murder, 1215 Magna Carta, 1265 de Montfort's Parliament, 1283 conquest of Wales, 1314 Bannockburn.
Continuity as well as change must be assessed in any 'how far did it change' question.
Medieval England was part of a wider Christendom that shaped its politics and culture.
The Crusades connected England to the Middle East through war, trade and ideas.

terms.name: Spring 2
terms.focus: Medieval life: village, town, trade and the Black Death. 8 lessons.

lessons.title: Life in the medieval village
objectives: I can describe the layout and work of a medieval village
I can explain the obligations of a villein to their lord
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: society, economy and culture: for example, farming, housing and everyday life in the countryside
misconceptions: Imagining medieval villagers as passive and unskilled
Thinking peasants owned the land they farmed

assessment.detail: Annotate a manor plan; describe a villein's year of labour obligations and explain the three-field system

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study; understand connections and contrasts within and across periods

lessons.title: Medieval women and the family
objectives: I can describe the range of roles medieval women held
I can explain why evidence about women is limited
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: society, economy and culture; Aims – understand the methods of historical enquiry, including how evidence is used rigorously
misconceptions: Assuming all medieval women had identical experiences regardless of status
Concluding that absence of evidence means absence of activity

assessment.detail: Use four sources on medieval women of different social ranks; write a paragraph on why the record is uneven

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand how our knowledge of the past is constructed from a range of sources

knowledgeComponents.statement: The manor was the basic unit of medieval rural life, controlled by a lord.
Villagers farmed scattered strips in large open fields rather than single enclosed farms.
Under the three-field system, one field was left fallow each year to recover fertility.
A villein was tied to the manor and owed labour service to the lord; a freeman paid rent instead.
The manor court settled local disputes and enforced customary obligations.
Medieval women's experience varied greatly by social rank, marital status and whether they lived in town or countryside.
Women worked in farming, brewing, textiles and trade, and some ran businesses as widows.
An abbess could hold significant authority over land and people.
Records were written mainly by men and about property, so much of women's activity is under-recorded.

lessons.title: Medieval towns, guilds and the wool trade
objectives: I can explain why towns grew in medieval England
I can describe the importance of the wool trade
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: society, economy and culture: for example, trade, the wool trade, and the growth of towns
misconceptions: Thinking medieval towns were the size of modern ones
Assuming everyone in a town was free and wealthy

assessment.detail: Explain three reasons towns grew; map the medieval wool trade routes from England to Flanders and Italy

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study; economic activity and trade links

knowledgeComponents.statement: A borough was a town with a royal charter granting rights such as holding a market.
Towns grew where trade routes, rivers, bridges or castles created opportunity.
A villein who lived in a town for a year and a day could gain freedom.
Guilds regulated quality, prices and training in a trade.
The stages of a craft career were apprentice, journeyman and master.
English wool was the country's most valuable export in the medieval period.
Wool was exported to Flanders and Italy, where it was woven into cloth.
Taxes on wool exports were a major source of royal income.

lessons.title: The Black Death: arrival, spread and beliefs about its causes
objectives: I can describe how the plague reached and spread through England
I can explain what people at the time believed caused it
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Black Death and its social and economic impact
misconceptions: Thinking medieval people had no explanations at all
Assuming everyone died or that recovery was impossible

assessment.detail: Analyse four contemporary explanations of the plague; explain what they reveal about medieval beliefs

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: chronological knowledge; how sources are used

lessons.title: Consequences of the Black Death
objectives: I can explain the social and economic consequences of the Black Death
I can distinguish short-term from long-term consequences
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Black Death and its social and economic impact
misconceptions: Thinking the plague only caused suffering with no other consequences
Assuming wages rose immediately and without resistance

assessment.detail: Classify consequences as social, economic and political, and as short or long term; write an explanation of the most important

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: address historically valid questions about change and consequence

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Black Death reached England in 1348 and spread rapidly through 1349.
Estimates suggest between a third and a half of England's population died.
The plague spread along trade routes from Asia through the Mediterranean into Europe.
Contemporary explanations included God's punishment, bad air or miasma, planetary alignments and, wrongly and violently, blame directed at Jewish communities.
Some communities used quarantine and isolation, which had a real effect even without understanding the cause.
The population fall created a severe labour shortage.
Surviving peasants could demand higher wages and better terms.
The Statute of Labourers of 1351 tried to fix wages at pre-plague levels.
Over the following century serfdom declined and many villages were abandoned.

lessons.title: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381
objectives: I can explain the causes of the Peasants' Revolt
I can assess whether the revolt succeeded
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Peasants' Revolt
misconceptions: Thinking the rebels wanted to overthrow the king
Judging the revolt a total failure because its leaders were killed

assessment.detail: Categorise the causes of the revolt; write an evaluation of how far it achieved anything, short and long term

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: address historically valid questions about cause and significance

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Peasants' Revolt broke out in Essex and Kent in May and June 1381.
The immediate trigger was the third poll tax, charged at the same rate regardless of wealth.
Longer-term causes included resentment at the Statute of Labourers, war taxation and continued serfdom.
Wat Tyler led the rebels and the priest John Ball preached social equality.
The rebels blamed the king's advisers rather than the fourteen-year-old Richard II himself.
Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield and Richard's promises to the rebels were then revoked.
The revolt was suppressed, but no further poll tax of that kind was attempted for centuries.
Serfdom continued to decline after 1381 for economic reasons as much as political ones.

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: medieval society and the Black Death
objectives: I can explain how medieval society changed across the fourteenth century
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: society, economy and culture; the Black Death; the Peasants' Revolt
misconceptions: Describing the Black Death without explaining its consequences

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: knowledge recall, a source question on plague beliefs and one extended answer on the consequences of the Black Death

lessons.title: Review, retrieval and a medieval local study
objectives: I can repair my gaps
I can investigate medieval evidence in my own area
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – a local history study; extend and deepen chronologically secure knowledge
misconceptions: Assuming there is no medieval evidence in a modern area

assessment.detail: 30-item retrieval quiz on weeks 16–25; investigate a local medieval church, field pattern or market charter and present the findings

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Black Death is one of the clearest examples of demographic change reshaping a society.
Economic pressure, not only rebellion, ended serfdom in England.
Key dates: 1348 plague arrives, 1351 Statute of Labourers, 1381 Peasants' Revolt.
Medieval evidence survives locally in parish churches, field boundaries, place names and manorial records.
Ridge and furrow field patterns are visible traces of medieval open field farming.
A consequence question must distinguish immediate effects from long-term change.
Ordinary people's lives can be reconstructed from indirect evidence such as court rolls and archaeology.
Towns, trade and the wool trade linked medieval England to the wider European economy.

terms.name: Summer 1
terms.focus: War, crisis and the end of the Middle Ages: the Hundred Years War, the Wars of the Roses, Henry VII, and a local history study. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: Causes and course of the Hundred Years War
objectives: I can explain why England and France went to war in 1337
I can outline the main phases of the war
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Hundred Years War
misconceptions: Thinking the war lasted continuously for a hundred years
Assuming English victories meant England was winning overall

assessment.detail: Categorise the causes of the war; produce a timeline of six turning points from 1337 to 1453

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: chronologically secure knowledge; cause and consequence

lessons.title: Warfare and society: technology and the longbow
objectives: I can explain how military technology changed during the war
I can assess the impact of war on ordinary people
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Hundred Years War; society, economy and culture
misconceptions: Thinking the longbow alone explains English victories
Assuming war only affected soldiers

assessment.detail: Explain three military changes and their effects; write a paragraph on how war affected people who never fought

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand connections and contrasts within and across periods

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Hundred Years War ran from 1337 to 1453, with long truces between periods of fighting.
Causes included Edward III's claim to the French throne, disputes over Gascony, and the wool trade with Flanders.
England won major victories at Crecy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356 and Agincourt in 1415.
France, aided by Joan of Arc from 1429, eventually drove the English out; only Calais remained by 1453.
The English longbow could be fired rapidly and at long range by trained archers.
Gunpowder artillery became decisive in sieges by the fifteenth century.
Chevauchee raids destroyed crops and villages to damage the enemy's economy and morale.
War required heavy taxation, which strengthened Parliament's bargaining position.

lessons.title: Causes of the Wars of the Roses
objectives: I can explain why civil war broke out in 1455
I can identify the rival houses and their claims
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Wars of the Roses
misconceptions: Thinking the whole country was constantly at war for thirty years
Assuming the wars were between the north and south of England

assessment.detail: Build a family tree of the rival claims; categorise the causes of the wars and explain the links between them

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: chronologically secure knowledge of British history

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Wars of the Roses were fought between the houses of Lancaster and York from 1455 to 1487.
Both houses descended from Edward III, which is why both had a claim.
Henry VI's weak rule and periods of mental illness created a power vacuum.
Defeat in the Hundred Years War discredited the Lancastrian government and left trained soldiers at home.
Over-mighty subjects were nobles with private armies who could challenge the crown.
The fighting consisted of short campaigns and battles rather than continuous war.
The rose emblems became widely associated with the two houses largely after the wars ended.
Most ordinary people's lives continued with little direct disruption for most of the period.

lessons.title: Bosworth and the end of the wars
objectives: I can narrate the key events from 1483 to 1485
I can explain why Henry Tudor won at Bosworth
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Wars of the Roses; Henry VII's attempts to restore stability
misconceptions: Accepting the Tudor portrayal of Richard III uncritically
Assuming Bosworth was inevitable

assessment.detail: Explain why Henry Tudor won at Bosworth; compare a Tudor and a modern interpretation of Richard III

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: discern how and why contrasting interpretations are constructed

lessons.title: Henry VII and the restoration of stability
objectives: I can describe how Henry VII secured his throne
I can assess how successful he was
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Wars of the Roses and Henry VII's attempts to restore stability
misconceptions: Thinking Bosworth ended all opposition immediately
Assuming stability was achieved only through force

assessment.detail: Classify Henry VII's methods as dynastic, financial, legal and diplomatic; write a judgement on his success by 1509

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: change and significance

knowledgeComponents.statement: Richard III took the throne in 1483 after the disappearance of his nephews, the Princes in the Tower.
Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard III at Bosworth on 22 August 1485.
The Stanleys' decision to switch sides was decisive at Bosworth.
Much of Richard III's reputation comes from Tudor writers with an interest in blackening it.
Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486, uniting the two houses.
Henry VII defeated the pretenders Lambert Simnel in 1487 and Perkin Warbeck in the 1490s.
Henry VII used bonds and recognisances to control the nobility financially.
Henry VII left a solvent treasury and a secure succession in 1509.
1485 is a conventional dividing line between the medieval and early modern periods, but the division is a historian's choice.

lessons.title: Medieval art, architecture and literature
objectives: I can describe medieval achievements in building, art and writing
I can explain what cathedrals reveal about medieval society
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the development of English art, architecture and literature
misconceptions: Thinking the Middle Ages were culturally backward
Assuming everything was written in Latin

assessment.detail: Compare Romanesque and Gothic architecture; explain what a cathedral reveals about medieval wealth, faith and technology

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study, often a church; English: the history of English

knowledgeComponents.statement: Romanesque architecture used round arches and thick walls; Gothic used pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses.
Gothic engineering allowed taller buildings with much larger windows.
Stained glass and wall paintings taught biblical stories to a largely non-reading population.
Illuminated manuscripts were hand-copied and decorated, mostly in monasteries.
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in Middle English in the late fourteenth century.
