Writing in the vernacular rather than Latin widened who could read a text.
Cathedrals took decades or centuries to build and consumed enormous resources.
William Caxton set up England's first printing press in 1476.

lessons.title: Planning a local history enquiry
objectives: I can frame a local historical question
I can identify the sources available to answer it
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – a local history study: for example, a depth study linked to one of the British areas of study listed above; a study over time testing how far sites in their locality reflect aspects of national history
misconceptions: Assuming local history has fewer sources than national history
Choosing a question too broad for the sources available

assessment.detail: Frame a local enquiry question and list at least five sources, primary and secondary, that could answer it

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: a local history study; address and devise historically valid questions

lessons.title: Carrying out the local history enquiry
objectives: I can use local sources to build a historical argument
I can link local evidence to national developments
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – a local history study; Aims – understand the connections between local, regional, national and international history
misconceptions: Describing what was found without arguing from it
Treating the local case as typical without checking

assessment.detail: Produce a written enquiry using at least four local sources, explicitly linking findings to national developments studied this year

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: construct informed responses that involve thoughtful selection and organisation of historical information

knowledgeComponents.statement: Local sources include maps, census returns, parish registers, photographs, buildings and place names.
Map regression compares maps of the same place at different dates to reveal change.
County record offices and online archives hold most surviving local documents.
A good local enquiry question is narrow enough that the available sources can answer it.
Local evidence can confirm, qualify or challenge a national narrative.
One locality is not automatically typical of the country as a whole.
Buildings are themselves primary sources about the society that built them.
An enquiry ends with an argued answer to the original question, not a list of findings.

lessons.title: How much did England change between 1066 and 1509?
objectives: I can trace change and continuity across four centuries
I can identify the turning points that mattered most
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Medieval Britain 1066-1509; the changing nature of political power in Britain traced through selective case studies
misconceptions: Assuming change was steady and continuous
Ignoring continuity in a question about change

assessment.detail: Write an essay tracing change and continuity in one strand (power, religion, or society and economy) from 1066 to 1509

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: note connections, contrasts and trends over time

knowledgeComponents.statement: Change over time is uneven: some periods change rapidly and others hardly at all.
A turning point is a moment after which the direction of change is clearly different.
Between 1066 and 1509 royal power became more bound by law and by consent to taxation.
The Church remained central to life throughout the period, though its relationship with the crown shifted.
Serfdom largely disappeared in England during the fifteenth century.
Towns, trade and the use of English all grew across the period.
A change-over-time essay must address continuity as well as change.
Selecting a strand keeps a long-period essay focused.

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment: the end of the Middle Ages
objectives: I can demonstrate secure knowledge of 1337 to 1509 and use it in an argued answer
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509: the Hundred Years War, the Wars of the Roses, Henry VII
misconceptions: Retelling the narrative instead of arguing a case

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: knowledge recall, an interpretation question on Richard III and one extended judgement on Henry VII's success

knowledgeComponents.statement: Key dates: 1337 to 1453 Hundred Years War, 1455 to 1487 Wars of the Roses, 1485 Bosworth, 1509 death of Henry VII.
Foreign war, dynastic weakness and over-mighty nobles combined to produce civil war.
Interpretations of Richard III differ because of Tudor propaganda, later fiction and modern archaeology.
An interpretation question asks why an account says what it does, not whether it is true.
Henry VII secured his dynasty through marriage, finance, law and the suppression of pretenders.
Historical judgements should be supported by specific dates, names and figures.
Period labels such as medieval and early modern are tools historians use, not facts about the past.
An argued answer states its case in the first sentence and proves it thereafter.

terms.name: Summer 2
terms.focus: The wider medieval world: a depth study of a significant world society and its interconnections, covering the Islamic world, the empires of West Africa and the Mongols. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: The rise and reach of the Islamic world
objectives: I can describe the growth of the Islamic world to about 900
I can locate its major cities and trade routes
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – at least one study of a significant society or issue in world history and its interconnections with other world developments; Aims – understand the connections between local, regional, national and international history
misconceptions: Treating the Islamic world as a single unchanging place
Assuming medieval Europe and the Islamic world were isolated from one another

assessment.detail: Map the extent of the Islamic world in 750 and 900; produce a timeline of six key developments

ks2Prerequisites: Y4–Y6: a non-European society that provides contrast with British history, for example early Islamic civilisation including a study of Baghdad c. AD 900

lessons.title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
objectives: I can describe Baghdad around 900 and explain why it flourished
I can give examples of scholarship and its transmission
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – at least one study of a significant society or issue in world history and its interconnections with other world developments
misconceptions: Thinking Islamic scholars only preserved Greek learning rather than extending it
Assuming Europe was the only source of later scientific advance

assessment.detail: Describe three achievements of Baghdad scholarship; explain how they reached Europe and why that mattered

ks2Prerequisites: Y4–Y6: early Islamic civilisation, including a study of Baghdad c. AD 900

knowledgeComponents.statement: Islam began in Arabia in the seventh century and spread rapidly across the Middle East, North Africa and into Spain.
A caliphate was a state ruled by a caliph, regarded as the successor to political leadership of the Muslim community.
The Abbasid caliphate founded Baghdad in 762 as its capital.
Baghdad and Cordoba were among the largest and wealthiest cities in the world around 900.
The House of Wisdom in Baghdad gathered and translated works from Greek, Persian and Indian sources.
Al-Khwarizmi's work gave us the words algebra and algorithm.
Ibn Sina's medical writings were used in European universities for centuries.
Papermaking reached the Islamic world from China and then spread to Europe.
Scholars in the Islamic world extended as well as preserved earlier learning.

lessons.title: The empire of Mali and Mansa Musa
objectives: I can describe the wealth and organisation of the Mali empire
I can explain the importance of the trans-Saharan trade
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – at least one study of a significant society or issue in world history and its interconnections with other world developments
misconceptions: Assuming pre-colonial Africa had no large states or written scholarship
Thinking African history begins with European contact

assessment.detail: Map the trans-Saharan trade routes; use the Catalan Atlas and Arabic accounts to explain Mali's reputation

ks2Prerequisites: Y4–Y6: a non-European society that provides contrasts with British history, for example Benin c. AD 900-1300

knowledgeComponents.statement: The Mali empire dominated West Africa from the thirteenth to the fifteenth century.
Mali's wealth came from control of gold production and the trans-Saharan trade routes.
Salt was traded south across the Sahara and gold traded north.
Mansa Musa ruled Mali from about 1312 and made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324.
Accounts of Mansa Musa's spending in Cairo spread Mali's reputation for wealth across Europe and the Middle East.
Timbuktu became a centre of trade and Islamic scholarship, with universities and large manuscript libraries.
The Catalan Atlas of 1375 depicts Mansa Musa holding a gold nugget, showing European awareness of Mali.
West Africa had extensive written records and long-distance trade centuries before European colonisation.

lessons.title: The Mongol empire: conquest and connection
objectives: I can explain how the Mongols built the largest land empire in history
I can assess the positive and negative consequences of Mongol rule
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – at least one study of a significant society or issue in world history and its interconnections with other world developments
misconceptions: Seeing the Mongols only as destroyers
Assuming the empire remained united after Genghis Khan

assessment.detail: Complete a consequences table with destruction and connection; write a judgement on the overall impact of the Mongol empire

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand the connections between world developments

lessons.title: Connected worlds: how the medieval world was linked
objectives: I can describe the networks connecting Europe, Africa and Asia
I can explain how goods, ideas and disease travelled along them
lessons.ncRef: Aims – understand the connections between local, regional, national and international history; Key stage 3 – a study of a significant society in world history and its interconnections with other world developments
misconceptions: Thinking the medieval world was made of isolated regions
Assuming only goods travelled along trade routes

assessment.detail: Map the main Afro-Eurasian trade networks; explain three things that travelled along them, including the plague

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand connections and contrasts between periods and societies

knowledgeComponents.statement: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and began decades of conquest.
At its height the Mongol empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history.
Mongol success rested on mobile cavalry, discipline, adaptable tactics and the use of terror.
The Pax Mongolica made long-distance travel and trade across Asia safer for around a century.
The Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate there.
The empire fragmented into separate khanates after Genghis Khan's death.
The Silk Road and Indian Ocean routes connected Europe, Africa and Asia by land and sea.
Goods, technologies, religions, scholarship and disease all travelled along trade networks.
The Black Death spread to Europe along the same routes that carried trade.

lessons.title: Comparing medieval England with a wider world society
objectives: I can compare two societies systematically
I can challenge the assumption that medieval Europe was the most advanced region
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – at least one study of a significant society in world history and its interconnections; Aims – gain historical perspective by placing knowledge into different contexts
misconceptions: Judging all societies by European standards
Assuming 'advanced' means the same thing in every context

assessment.detail: Compare medieval England with Abbasid Baghdad or Mali on government, cities, trade, learning and religion; reach a judgement

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: understand connections and contrasts between societies studied

knowledgeComponents.statement: A systematic comparison uses the same criteria for both societies.
Eurocentric history judges other societies by European standards and timelines.
Around 900, Baghdad and Cordoba were far larger and wealthier than London or Paris.
Different societies developed strengths in different fields at different times.
Comparison must be of like with like: city with city, state with state.
Medieval societies were connected by trade, scholarship, religion and conflict.
Historical perspective means understanding a society on its own terms as well as comparatively.
Comparative claims need evidence, not assertion.

lessons.title: Planning an independent historical enquiry
objectives: I can frame my own historical question
I can select sources that will answer it
lessons.ncRef: Aims – understand the methods of historical enquiry; Key stage 3 – pursue historically valid enquiries including some they have framed themselves, and create relevant, structured and evidentially supported accounts
misconceptions: Choosing a topic rather than a question
Selecting sources that only support a predetermined answer

assessment.detail: Frame an enquiry question on any topic studied this year and select six sources with a justification for each

ks2Prerequisites: Y3–Y6: address and sometimes devise historically valid questions

lessons.title: Writing the enquiry
objectives: I can write an evidentially supported historical account
I can reach a conclusion that answers my own question
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create relevant, structured and evidentially supported accounts; Aims – create their own structured accounts including written narratives and analyses
misconceptions: Writing a narrative rather than an argument
Omitting evidence that complicates the argument

assessment.detail: 1000-word researched enquiry with a clear argument, cited evidence and a conclusion

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 English: write well-structured formal expository essays

knowledgeComponents.statement: A historical enquiry question must be answerable from evidence and narrow enough in scope.
Sources should be selected to test an argument, not only to support it.
A hypothesis is a provisional answer to be tested against the evidence.
An evidentially supported account cites where each claim comes from.
Evidence that complicates the argument should be addressed, not omitted.
A historical conclusion answers the question and acknowledges the limits of the evidence.
Structure in a historical account is organised by argument, not chronology alone.
Referencing allows a reader to check a claim.

lessons.title: End-of-year assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate my knowledge and skills across the whole of Year 7
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – Medieval Britain 1066-1509; a local history study; a pre-1066 thematic study; a world history depth study
misconceptions: Revising only the most recent unit

assessment.detail: 60-minute cumulative paper: chronology, source utility, interpretations, a causation question and one extended judgement drawn from any unit

knowledgeComponents.statement: The core Year 7 chronology runs from prehistory and Rome, through Anglo-Saxon and Viking England, to 1066 and the medieval period ending in 1509.
Source utility depends on content, provenance and the question asked.
Interpretations differ because of evidence, emphasis, purpose and the historian's own context.
Causation answers categorise, link and prioritise causes.
Significance is judged against stated criteria and can change over time.
Medieval England was part of a connected Afro-Eurasian world.
Every historical claim in an assessment needs specific supporting detail.
Cumulative assessment tests retention as well as recent learning.

lessons.title: Whole-year retrieval and gap repair
objectives: I can retrieve knowledge from every unit of Year 7
I can repair my remaining gaps
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – extend and deepen chronologically secure knowledge and understanding of British, local and world history
misconceptions: Assuming earlier units are secure without testing them

assessment.detail: 60-item quiz sampling all 39 weeks; weak components re-queued at short spacing

lessons.title: Looking ahead: what Year 8 builds on
objectives: I can explain how Year 8 continues the chronological narrative
I can identify the themes that run across periods
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – the development of Church, state and society in Britain 1509-1745; know and understand the history of these islands as a coherent, chronological narrative
misconceptions: Treating each year of history as a separate subject

assessment.detail: Map how Year 7 themes of power, religion, society and world connections continue into the Year 8 study of 1509 to 1745; set three personal targets

knowledgeComponents.statement: Year 8 continues the narrative with the Renaissance, Reformation and Britain 1509 to 1745.
The themes of power, religion, society, economy and world connections run across every period.
The Reformation transformed the relationship between Church and crown established in the medieval period.
Parliament's growth in the medieval period sets up the constitutional conflicts of the seventeenth century.
Chronological knowledge must be retrieved regularly to stay secure.
Historical skills of enquiry, causation, significance and interpretation transfer to every period.
Year 7 covered before 1066, the Norman Conquest, Church and crown, medieval society, the end of the Middle Ages and the wider medieval world.
A coherent narrative connects periods rather than treating them as separate topics.

subjects.name: Computing
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: computing programmes of study, key stage 3 (DfE, September 2013; statutory from September 2014). Pupils should be taught to: design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model the state and behaviour of real-world problems and physical systems; understand several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking (for example, sorting and searching) and use logical reasoning to compare alternative algorithms; use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve computational problems; design and develop modular programs that use procedures or functions and make appropriate use of data structures; understand simple Boolean logic and its uses in circuits and programming; understand how numbers can be represented in binary and carry out simple operations on binary numbers; understand the hardware and software components of computer systems and how they communicate; understand how instructions are stored and executed, and how text, sound and images are represented digitally; undertake creative projects combining multiple applications to meet the needs of known users; create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability; understand a range of ways to use technology safely, respectfully, responsibly and securely, including protecting online identity and privacy, recognising inappropriate content, contact and conduct, and knowing how to report concerns.
subjects.yearShare: Enrichment strand at roughly half the volume of a core subject: 1.5 lessons per week on average. Year 7 covers every one of the eleven KS3 computing statements at an introductory level, including both required programming languages (Scratch, block-based, and Python, textual). Years 8 and 9 revisit each strand at greater depth.
deferredToY8Y9: More complex data structures, two-dimensional lists and file handling
Advanced algorithms including merge sort and recursion
Databases and SQL
Hexadecimal and two's complement
Networking topologies and protocols in depth
Cyber security threats and defences in depth
Artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts
priorKnowledgeAssumed: Y5-Y6: design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems; solve problems by decomposing them into smaller parts
Y5-Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition in programs; work with variables and various forms of input and output
Y5-Y6: use logical reasoning to explain how some simple algorithms work and to detect and correct errors in algorithms and programs
Y5-Y6: understand computer networks including the internet; how they can provide multiple services such as the world wide web
Y5-Y6: use search technologies effectively, appreciate how results are selected and ranked, and be discerning in evaluating digital content

Y5-Y6: select, use and combine a variety of software on a range of digital devices to design and create a range of programs, systems and content that accomplish given goals, including collecting, analysing, evaluating and presenting data and information
Y5-Y6: use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; recognise acceptable and unacceptable behaviour; identify a range of ways to report concerns about content and contact

terms.name: Autumn 1
terms.focus: Computer systems, networks and safe, responsible use of technology. 12 lessons.

lessons.title: What is a computer? Input, process, output, storage
objectives: I can describe a computer system as input, process, output and storage
I can identify these stages in an everyday device
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand the hardware and software components that make up computer systems, and how they communicate with one another and with other systems
misconceptions: Thinking a computer is only a desktop machine
Confusing storage with memory

assessment.detail: Baseline computing quiz; classify twenty components as input, process, output or storage; analyse three everyday devices as systems

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: select, use and combine a variety of software on a range of digital devices

lessons.title: Hardware: inside the computer
objectives: I can name the main internal components of a computer
I can explain the role of the CPU, RAM and secondary storage
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand the hardware and software components that make up computer systems, and how they communicate with one another and with other systems; understand how instructions are stored and executed within a computer system
misconceptions: Thinking more storage makes a computer faster
Believing RAM keeps data when the power is off

assessment.detail: Label the internal components of a computer; explain the difference between RAM and secondary storage with an example

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand computer networks including the internet

knowledgeComponents.statement: A computer system takes an input, processes it, produces an output and can store data.
An input device sends data into the computer; an output device presents data to the user.
An embedded system is a computer built into another device, such as a washing machine.
The CPU, or central processing unit, executes the instructions of a program.
RAM is volatile working memory: its contents are lost when the power is switched off.
Secondary storage such as a hard drive or SSD keeps data permanently.
ROM is read-only memory that holds the start-up instructions.
A program must be loaded from storage into RAM before the CPU can run it.

lessons.title: Software: system and application
objectives: I can distinguish system software from application software
I can explain what an operating system does
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand the hardware and software components that make up computer systems, and how they communicate with one another and with other systems
misconceptions: Thinking the operating system is the same as the computer
Believing all software is an app the user opens

assessment.detail: Classify fifteen items of software; explain four jobs an operating system does

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: select, use and combine software on a range of digital devices

knowledgeComponents.statement: Hardware is the physical parts; software is the set of instructions that runs on it.
System software manages the computer; application software does a task for the user.
An operating system manages hardware, files, memory, users and running programs.
Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are operating systems.
A device driver lets the operating system communicate with a piece of hardware.
A user interface is how a person interacts with a computer.
Utility software carries out maintenance tasks such as backup and compression.
The operating system runs whenever the computer is on, whether or not the user opens anything.

lessons.title: Computer networks: LANs, WANs and topologies
objectives: I can explain what a computer network is and why we use them
I can distinguish a LAN from a WAN
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand the hardware and software components that make up computer systems, and how they communicate with one another and with other systems
misconceptions: Thinking the internet and the world wide web are the same thing
Believing wireless means no physical infrastructure

assessment.detail: Draw a home network diagram; explain three advantages and two risks of networking computers

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand computer networks, including the internet; how they can provide multiple services, such as the world wide web

lessons.title: How the internet works
objectives: I can explain how data travels across the internet
I can describe what happens when a web page is requested
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand the hardware and software components that make up computer systems, and how they communicate with one another and with other systems
misconceptions: Thinking data travels as one continuous stream
Believing the internet is stored in the cloud rather than on physical servers

assessment.detail: Order the eight steps from typing a URL to a page appearing; explain the role of packets and DNS

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand computer networks including the internet; how they can provide multiple services such as the world wide web

knowledgeComponents.statement: A network is two or more computers connected together to share data and resources.
A LAN covers a small area such as a home or school; a WAN covers a wide geographical area.
A router connects networks together and directs traffic between them.
A server provides a service or resource to client computers.
The internet is a global network of networks; the world wide web is one service that runs on it.
Data is broken into packets which travel separately and are reassembled at the destination.
An IP address uniquely identifies a device on a network.
DNS translates a human-readable domain name into an IP address.
A protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication between devices.
HTTPS encrypts the data sent between a browser and a website.

lessons.title: Protecting your online identity and privacy
objectives: I can explain what a digital footprint is
I can take practical steps to protect my privacy online
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand a range of ways to use technology safely, respectfully, responsibly and securely, including protecting their online identity and privacy
misconceptions: Believing deleted content is gone forever
Thinking a private account makes content unshareable

assessment.detail: Audit the privacy settings of a service; produce a personal action plan with five specific steps

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; recognise acceptable and unacceptable behaviour

knowledgeComponents.statement: A digital footprint is the trail of data left by online activity.
Content shared online can be copied and may persist even after it is deleted.
Personal data includes name, address, date of birth, school, photographs and location.
Photographs can carry metadata including the time and place they were taken.
Privacy settings should be checked when an account is created and after every app update.
Location sharing should be turned off unless there is a specific reason for it.
Sharing another person's image or information requires their agreement.
A private account limits who sees content but does not prevent it being screenshotted and shared.

lessons.title: Passwords, security and staying safe from scams
objectives: I can create and manage strong passwords
I can recognise phishing and other online scams
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand a range of ways to use technology safely, respectfully, responsibly and securely, including protecting their online identity and privacy
misconceptions: Thinking a complicated short password is stronger than a long simple one
Believing a message from a known name is automatically genuine

assessment.detail: Test password strength; identify eight messages as genuine or phishing with reasons

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; identify a range of ways to report concerns

lessons.title: Recognising inappropriate content, contact and conduct, and reporting concerns
objectives: I can recognise inappropriate content, contact and conduct online
I can explain how and where to report a concern
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – recognise inappropriate content, contact and conduct and know how to report concerns
misconceptions: Thinking a problem must be serious before it is worth reporting
Believing that reporting always makes things worse

assessment.detail: Respond to six scenarios stating the category of risk, the immediate action and who to report to

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: identify a range of ways to report concerns about content and contact

knowledgeComponents.statement: Password length matters more than complexity, so a long passphrase is very strong.
A password should never be reused across different accounts.
Two-factor authentication adds a second check, so a stolen password is not enough.
Phishing is a message designed to trick someone into revealing information or clicking a harmful link.
Signs of phishing include urgency, unexpected requests, odd addresses and spelling errors.
The three categories of online risk are content, contact and conduct.
Evidence should be kept, for example by screenshot, before blocking or deleting.
Concerns can be reported to a trusted adult, the platform's report function, or a service such as CEOP.
An upstander supports someone being targeted rather than staying silent.

lessons.title: Searching effectively and evaluating what you find
objectives: I can use search techniques to find better results
I can judge the trustworthiness of an online source
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability; understand a range of ways to use technology safely and responsibly
misconceptions: Believing the top result is the most reliable
Thinking a professional-looking website is automatically accurate

assessment.detail: Answer one research question using three sources; score each for trustworthiness against stated criteria

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use search technologies effectively, appreciate how results are selected and ranked, and be discerning in evaluating digital content

knowledgeComponents.statement: Search engines rank results by relevance and popularity, not by accuracy.
Quotation marks search for an exact phrase.
The site: operator restricts a search to one website or domain.
Trustworthiness is judged by author, date, purpose, evidence and whether other sources agree.
Sponsored results are advertisements, not ranked results.
Misinformation is false information spread without intent to deceive; disinformation is spread deliberately.
Cross-checking a claim against an independent source is the strongest single test.
Design quality of a website is no guide to the accuracy of its content.

lessons.title: Copyright, licensing and using others' work
objectives: I can explain what copyright protects
I can find and correctly credit openly licensed material
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability; use technology responsibly
misconceptions: Thinking anything found online is free to use
Believing crediting the source removes the need for a licence

assessment.detail: Source five openly licensed images and audio clips; write correct attributions for each

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use technology responsibly; select, use and combine software

lessons.title: Data, the law and how organisations use your information
objectives: I can explain why data protection law exists
I can describe how organisations collect and use personal data
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand a range of ways to use technology safely, respectfully, responsibly and securely, including protecting their online identity and privacy
misconceptions: Thinking free services have no cost
Believing accepting cookies is always required to use a site

assessment.detail: Analyse a real privacy policy; list what data is collected, why, and what rights the user has

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use technology safely and responsibly

knowledgeComponents.statement: Copyright automatically protects original creative work from being copied without permission.
A licence sets out what others may do with a work.
Creative Commons licences allow reuse under stated conditions, usually including attribution.
Public domain work is free of copyright and may be used without permission.
An attribution names the creator, the work, the source and the licence.
Data protection law gives individuals rights over how their personal data is used.
A cookie is a small file that lets a website remember a user between visits.
Many free online services are funded by collecting data and selling targeted advertising.
Users have the right to see, correct and request deletion of their personal data.

lessons.title: Autumn 1 assessment: systems, networks and safe use
objectives: I can demonstrate my knowledge of computer systems, networks and online safety
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – hardware and software components; safe, respectful, responsible and secure use of technology
misconceptions: Naming a component without explaining its function

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: hardware and software, a network diagram question, a scenario-based online safety response and one extended explanation of how a web page is loaded

knowledgeComponents.statement: Every computer system follows the input, process, output and storage model.
The CPU executes instructions held in RAM, which are loaded from secondary storage.
Data crosses the internet as packets, routed by IP address and resolved by DNS.
Online risk is categorised as content, contact and conduct.
Strong, unique passwords plus two-factor authentication are the core of account security.
Trustworthiness of a source is judged by author, date, purpose, evidence and corroboration.
Copyright applies online exactly as it does offline.
Explaining a component means saying what it does and why the system needs it.

terms.name: Autumn 2
terms.focus: Computational thinking, algorithms and computational abstraction. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: The four pillars of computational thinking
objectives: I can define decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms
I can apply them to a non-computing problem
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model the state and behaviour of real-world problems and physical systems; understand several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking
misconceptions: Thinking computational thinking only applies to programming
Confusing abstraction with simply leaving things out at random

assessment.detail: Apply all four pillars to a real problem such as planning a journey; annotate each stage

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use logical reasoning to explain how some simple algorithms work

lessons.title: Abstraction and modelling a real system
objectives: I can identify what to include and exclude when modelling a system
I can design an abstraction of a real-world system
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model the state and behaviour of real-world problems and physical systems
misconceptions: Believing a model must contain every detail to be useful
Thinking abstraction is the same as decomposition

assessment.detail: Design an abstraction for a system such as a vending machine or a library: list its states, behaviours and the details deliberately excluded

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems

knowledgeComponents.statement: Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller sub-problems.
Pattern recognition finds similarities that let one solution serve several problems.
Abstraction removes detail that is not relevant to the problem being solved.
An algorithm is a precise sequence of steps that solves a problem.
Computational thinking applies to any problem, not only to problems solved by computers.
A model represents the state and behaviour of a system.
State is the current condition of a system; behaviour is how it changes state.
A map of the London Underground is an abstraction: it keeps connections and drops geography.
A good abstraction keeps what matters for the purpose and removes everything else.

lessons.title: Writing algorithms: flowcharts and pseudocode
objectives: I can express an algorithm as a flowchart using correct symbols
I can express an algorithm as pseudocode
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking; use logical reasoning to compare the utility of alternative algorithms for the same problem
misconceptions: Using the wrong flowchart symbol for a decision
Writing pseudocode that is actual code in a particular language

assessment.detail: Express three algorithms both as a flowchart and as pseudocode, including one with a decision and one with a loop

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition in programs; use logical reasoning to explain how some simple algorithms work

knowledgeComponents.statement: A flowchart uses an oval for start and stop, a rectangle for a process, a parallelogram for input or output and a diamond for a decision.
Every decision diamond has exactly two labelled outputs in a standard flowchart.
Pseudocode expresses an algorithm in structured English, independent of any programming language.
Sequence means steps carried out one after another in order.
Selection means choosing between paths based on a condition.
Iteration means repeating a set of steps.
An algorithm must be unambiguous, finite and produce a result.
An algorithm is designed before code is written.

lessons.title: Linear and binary search
objectives: I can describe how linear search and binary search work
I can explain why binary search is faster and when it can be used
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking (for example, ones for sorting and searching); use logical reasoning to compare the utility of alternative algorithms for the same problem
misconceptions: Trying to apply binary search to unsorted data
Thinking binary search is always fewer steps for very small lists

assessment.detail: Trace both searches on a given list; count comparisons; explain which is better for 1000 items and why

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use logical reasoning to explain how some simple algorithms work

lessons.title: Comparing algorithms for efficiency
objectives: I can compare two algorithms for the same problem
I can explain what makes an algorithm efficient
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use logical reasoning to compare the utility of alternative algorithms for the same problem
misconceptions: Judging efficiency by how short the code looks
Ignoring how performance changes as data grows

assessment.detail: Complete a table of comparisons for both searches at list sizes 10, 100 and 1000; explain the pattern

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: powers of 2; halving; interpret patterns in data

knowledgeComponents.statement: Linear search checks each item in turn from the start until it finds the target.
Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list by comparing with the middle item.
Binary search only works on data that is already sorted.
Linear search on n items takes up to n comparisons in the worst case.
Binary search on 1000 items takes at most about 10 comparisons.
Efficiency is measured by how the number of steps grows as the input grows.
Algorithms can trade memory use against speed.
The advantage of a more efficient algorithm grows with the size of the data.

lessons.title: Bubble sort and insertion sort
objectives: I can describe how bubble sort and insertion sort work
I can trace each algorithm on a small list
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking (for example, ones for sorting and searching)
misconceptions: Stopping bubble sort after a single pass
Confusing the two algorithms' strategies

assessment.detail: Trace both sorts on the same six-item list, showing every pass; count the swaps and comparisons

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use logical reasoning to explain how some simple algorithms work

knowledgeComponents.statement: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
After each pass of bubble sort, the largest remaining item is in its final position.
Bubble sort is finished when a pass makes no swaps.
Insertion sort builds a sorted section by inserting each new item into its correct place.
Insertion sort is efficient on lists that are already nearly sorted.
Tracing an algorithm means recording the state of the data after each step.
Both bubble sort and insertion sort become slow as list size grows.
Sorting data first can make later searching far faster.

lessons.title: Finding errors in algorithms
objectives: I can trace an algorithm to find where it goes wrong
I can use a trace table to check a program's logic
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use logical reasoning to compare the utility of alternative algorithms for the same problem; Aims – can evaluate and apply information technology analytically to solve problems
misconceptions: Assuming a program is correct because it runs without an error message
Testing only with typical values

assessment.detail: Use a trace table to find the fault in three faulty algorithms; design test data including normal, boundary and invalid cases

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use logical reasoning to detect and correct errors in algorithms and programs

lessons.title: Designing test data
objectives: I can design test data that covers normal, boundary and erroneous cases
I can record test results systematically
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design, use and evaluate computational abstractions; Aims – can evaluate and apply information technology analytically
misconceptions: Writing a test plan after finishing rather than before
Recording only whether a test passed and not the actual output

assessment.detail: Produce a test plan for a given algorithm with at least six tests covering all three categories

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: detect and correct errors in algorithms and programs

knowledgeComponents.statement: A syntax error breaks the language's rules and stops the program running.
A logic error lets the program run but produces the wrong result.
A trace table records the value of each variable after every step.
A dry run means working through an algorithm by hand without a computer.
Normal test data is typical and should be accepted.
Boundary test data sits at the edge of what is acceptable.
Erroneous test data should be rejected by the program.
A test plan states the test, the data, the expected output and the actual output.
Testing should be planned before the program is written.

lessons.title: Solving a problem end to end
objectives: I can take a problem from decomposition through to a tested algorithm
I can justify my design decisions
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model the state and behaviour of real-world problems; understand several key algorithms
misconceptions: Jumping to a solution before analysing the problem
Not evaluating whether the solution actually met the requirement

assessment.detail: Take one problem from decomposition to a tested, evaluated flowchart and pseudocode solution, with justification

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: solve problems by decomposing them into smaller parts

knowledgeComponents.statement: Problem solving runs from understanding the problem, to design, to implementation, to testing, to evaluation.
Requirements state what the solution must do before any design begins.
Design decisions should be justified against the requirements.
An evaluation compares the finished solution with the original requirements.
Refining a solution after testing is part of the process, not a sign of failure.
The same problem can have several valid algorithmic solutions.
Decomposition makes a large problem tractable by producing smaller solvable parts.
A solution that works but does not meet the requirement is not a solution.

lessons.title: Autumn 2 assessment: computational thinking and algorithms
objectives: I can apply computational thinking, design algorithms and compare their efficiency
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – computational abstractions; key algorithms including sorting and searching; comparing alternative algorithms
misconceptions: Describing an algorithm rather than tracing it accurately

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: define the four pillars, trace a sort and a search, design a flowchart and compare two algorithms for efficiency

lessons.title: Unplugged algorithms challenge
objectives: I can apply algorithmic thinking away from a computer
I can explain my reasoning to someone else
lessons.ncRef: Aims – can understand and apply the fundamental principles and concepts of computer science, including abstraction, logic, algorithms and data representation
misconceptions: Believing computing only happens on a computer

assessment.detail: Solve three unplugged algorithm puzzles (card sorting, network routing, binary guessing game) and explain the strategy used for each

knowledgeComponents.statement: The four pillars are decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design.
Linear search works on any list; binary search requires a sorted list.
Bubble sort and insertion sort both produce a sorted list but by different strategies.
A trace table is the reliable way to check what an algorithm actually does.
Efficiency comparisons depend on the size of the data.
Algorithms exist independently of any programming language.
Explaining an algorithm to another person exposes gaps in your own understanding.
A guessing game that halves the range each time is binary search in disguise.

terms.name: Spring 1
terms.focus: Programming 1: block-based programming in Scratch, the first of two required languages. 9 lessons.

lessons.title: Sequence: making things happen in order
objectives: I can write a program that runs a sequence of instructions
I can predict what a sequence of blocks will do before running it
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve a variety of computational problems
misconceptions: Thinking blocks run in the order they were dragged rather than the order they are joined
Expecting instant visual feedback without a wait or animation

assessment.detail: Build an animation using at least eight sequenced blocks; predict then verify the output

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals; use sequence in programs

lessons.title: Variables and input
objectives: I can create and use a variable
I can take input from the user and store it
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages; make appropriate use of data structures
misconceptions: Thinking a variable holds all its previous values
Forgetting to initialise a variable before using it

assessment.detail: Build a program that asks the user two questions, stores the answers and uses them in an output

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: work with variables and various forms of input and output

knowledgeComponents.statement: A sprite is an object in Scratch that can be given its own scripts.
Blocks run from top to bottom in the order they are joined.
An event block such as 'when green flag clicked' starts a script.
The Scratch stage uses x and y coordinates with (0, 0) at the centre.
A variable is a named store that holds one value at a time.
Assigning a new value to a variable replaces the old one.
A variable should be initialised to a known starting value before it is used.
Variable names should describe what the variable holds.
In Scratch, the ask block stores the user's response in the 'answer' variable.

lessons.title: Selection: if and if-else
objectives: I can use an if block to make a decision
I can use if-else to choose between two outcomes
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages to solve a variety of computational problems; understand simple Boolean logic
misconceptions: Using = when a comparison is required in a condition
Nesting ifs when an if-else would be clearer

assessment.detail: Build a quiz that responds differently to correct and incorrect answers, using if-else

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition in programs

knowledgeComponents.statement: Selection chooses which instructions to run based on a condition.
A condition evaluates to either true or false.
An if block runs its contents only when the condition is true.
An if-else block runs one branch when true and the other when false.
Comparison operators include greater than, less than and equals.
Conditions can be combined with AND, OR and NOT.
Exactly one branch of an if-else runs each time it is reached.
Nested selection places one if inside another to test a further condition.

lessons.title: Iteration: count-controlled and condition-controlled loops
objectives: I can use a repeat loop a fixed number of times
I can use a repeat-until loop that runs based on a condition
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages to solve a variety of computational problems
misconceptions: Creating an infinite loop by never changing the condition variable
Confusing repeat 10 with repeat until

assessment.detail: Draw regular polygons with a count-controlled loop; build a guessing game with a condition-controlled loop

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition in programs

lessons.title: Combining sequence, selection and iteration
objectives: I can combine all three programming constructs in one program
I can trace a program containing a loop and a decision
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages to solve a variety of computational problems
misconceptions: Placing a decision outside a loop when it needs to run each iteration
Losing track of variable values across iterations

assessment.detail: Build a scoring game combining all three constructs; produce a trace table for three iterations

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition; work with variables

knowledgeComponents.statement: Iteration repeats a set of instructions.
A count-controlled loop repeats a fixed number of times.
A condition-controlled loop repeats until a condition becomes true.
An infinite loop never ends because its condition never becomes true.
To draw a regular polygon with n sides, repeat n times: move forward, then turn 360 divided by n degrees.
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.
Sequence, selection and iteration are the three fundamental programming constructs.
Flow of control is the order in which a program's instructions actually execute.
A counter variable must be updated inside the loop for a condition-controlled loop to end.

lessons.title: Lists: storing many values
objectives: I can create a list and add items to it
I can access an item by its position in a list
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – make appropriate use of data structures (for example, lists, tables or arrays)
misconceptions: Confusing an item's index with its value
Assuming lists always start at index 0 in every language

assessment.detail: Build a program that stores user inputs in a list and reports the length, first and last items

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: work with variables and various forms of input and output

knowledgeComponents.statement: A list is a data structure that holds many values under one name.
Each item in a list has a position, called its index.
Scratch lists are indexed from 1; Python lists are indexed from 0.
A list can be searched by looping through each index in turn.
Using a list avoids creating many separate variables for related values.
The length of a list is the number of items it currently holds.
An index outside the list's range causes an error.
Data structures let a program handle a quantity of data unknown at the time of writing.

lessons.title: Subroutines and modular design
objectives: I can create a custom block to reuse code
I can explain why breaking a program into parts helps
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design and develop modular programs that use procedures or functions; make appropriate use of data structures
misconceptions: Copying and pasting code instead of writing a subroutine
Thinking a subroutine must always return a value

assessment.detail: Refactor a working program to use at least two custom blocks, one with a parameter

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: solve problems by decomposing them into smaller parts

lessons.title: Scratch project: design, build and test
objectives: I can plan, build and test a program against a requirement
I can debug my own program systematically
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages to solve a variety of computational problems; undertake creative projects; design and develop modular programs
misconceptions: Building before planning
Fixing symptoms rather than finding the cause of a bug

assessment.detail: Design, build and test a Scratch game or simulation against a written requirement, with a test plan and evaluation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems

knowledgeComponents.statement: A subroutine is a named block of code that can be called from elsewhere in a program.
Subroutines avoid repetition, so a change need only be made in one place.
A parameter passes a value into a subroutine so it can behave differently each time.
Modular design breaks a program into independent, testable parts.
A program should be tested against its written requirements.
Systematic debugging isolates the fault by testing one part at a time.
An evaluation states what works, what does not and what could be improved.
Programs are developed iteratively: build a little, test, then extend.

lessons.title: Spring 1 assessment: block-based programming
objectives: I can demonstrate my programming knowledge and build a working solution
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages; design and develop modular programs; make appropriate use of data structures
misconceptions: Producing a program that runs but does not meet the stated requirement

assessment.detail: Written section on constructs and tracing, plus a timed practical task building a program to a given specification

knowledgeComponents.statement: Sequence, selection and iteration together can express any algorithm.
Variables store single values; lists store many.
Subroutines make programs shorter, clearer and easier to change.
A trace table proves what a program does rather than what it was meant to do.
A specification defines exactly what a program must do.
Block-based and text-based languages express the same constructs differently.
Testing with boundary and invalid data finds faults that normal data hides.
Meaningful variable and subroutine names are part of writing good code.

terms.name: Spring 2
terms.focus: Data representation: binary numbers, binary arithmetic, representing text, images and sound, and Boolean logic. 8 lessons.

lessons.title: Why computers use binary
objectives: I can explain why computers represent data in binary
I can convert between binary and denary up to 8 bits
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand how numbers can be represented in binary, and be able to carry out simple operations on binary numbers (for example, binary addition, and conversion between binary and decimal)
misconceptions: Reading binary 10 as ten
Thinking binary is a code that has to be memorised rather than a place value system

assessment.detail: Twenty conversions in each direction between 8-bit binary and denary, timed for fluency

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: place value; powers of 10; understand that our number system is positional

lessons.title: Binary addition and units of storage
objectives: I can add two binary numbers
I can order and convert units of data storage
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – be able to carry out simple operations on binary numbers, for example binary addition, and conversion between binary and decimal
misconceptions: Forgetting to carry when 1 plus 1 is added
Thinking a kilobyte is exactly 1000 bytes in every context

assessment.detail: Ten binary additions including one that overflows 8 bits; ten storage unit conversions

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: column addition with carrying; multiplication and division by powers of 10

knowledgeComponents.statement: Computers use binary because electronic circuits have two reliable states: on and off.
A bit is a single binary digit, 0 or 1.
A byte is 8 bits.
The place values of an 8-bit binary number are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
To convert binary to denary, add the place values wherever there is a 1.
An 8-bit number can represent 256 different values, from 0 to 255.
In binary addition, 1 + 1 = 10, which means write 0 and carry 1.
Overflow occurs when a result needs more bits than are available.
Storage units in order are bit, nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte.
A nibble is 4 bits, or half a byte.

lessons.title: Representing text: ASCII and Unicode
objectives: I can explain how characters are stored as binary
I can compare ASCII and Unicode
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand how data of various types (including text, sounds and pictures) can be represented and manipulated digitally, in the form of binary digits
misconceptions: Thinking the character '5' is stored as the number 5
Believing every language fits into ASCII

assessment.detail: Encode and decode short messages using an ASCII table; calculate the storage needed for a given text in ASCII and in Unicode

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: place value and number bases as an extension

knowledgeComponents.statement: A character set maps each character to a unique binary code.
ASCII uses 7 bits and represents 128 characters, usually stored in one byte.
In ASCII, capital A is 65 and lower case a is 97.
ASCII codes for letters run in alphabetical order, so B is one more than A.
The character '5' has ASCII code 53, which is not the number five.
Unicode uses more bits and can represent characters from every writing system, plus emoji.
Text stored in ASCII takes one byte per character.
A shared standard is what allows different systems to exchange text correctly.

lessons.title: Representing images: pixels, resolution and colour depth
objectives: I can explain how an image is stored as binary
I can calculate the file size of a bitmap image
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand how data of various types (including text, sounds and pictures) can be represented and manipulated digitally, in the form of binary digits
misconceptions: Thinking a pixel has a fixed physical size
Confusing resolution with colour depth

assessment.detail: Create a small bitmap by hand from binary; calculate file sizes for three images with different resolutions and colour depths

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: select, use and combine software including for images; Y6 maths: multiplication and unit conversion

lessons.title: Representing sound: sampling
objectives: I can explain how sound is converted into binary
I can describe how sample rate and bit depth affect quality and file size
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand how data of various types (including text, sounds and pictures) can be represented and manipulated digitally, in the form of binary digits
misconceptions: Thinking a digital recording is an exact copy of the original sound wave
Assuming higher quality has no cost

assessment.detail: Explain sampling with an annotated waveform; calculate the file size of a sound clip from sample rate, bit depth and duration

ks2Prerequisites: Y4 science: sound as vibrations; Y6 maths: multiplication and units

knowledgeComponents.statement: A bitmap image is made of pixels, each stored as a binary colour value.
Resolution is the number of pixels in an image, usually width by height.
Colour depth is the number of bits used per pixel.
A colour depth of n bits gives 2 to the power n possible colours.
Image file size in bits = width x height x colour depth.
Metadata stored with an image includes dimensions, colour depth, date and sometimes location.
Sampling measures the amplitude of a sound wave at regular intervals.
Sample rate is the number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz.
Sound file size in bits = sample rate x bit depth x duration in seconds.
Higher sample rate and bit depth give better quality but larger files.

lessons.title: Boolean logic: AND, OR and NOT
objectives: I can complete a truth table for AND, OR and NOT
I can apply Boolean logic to searches and to conditions in programs
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand simple Boolean logic (for example, AND, OR and NOT) and some of its uses in circuits and programming
misconceptions: Reading OR as exclusive, so both being true makes it false
Confusing everyday 'and' with logical AND in a search

assessment.detail: Complete truth tables for the three gates and two combined circuits; write three program conditions using AND, OR and NOT

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use logical reasoning; use search technologies effectively

lessons.title: Logic circuits and how instructions are executed
objectives: I can interpret a simple logic circuit diagram
I can describe how instructions are stored and executed in a computer
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – understand simple Boolean logic and some of its uses in circuits and programming; understand how instructions are stored and executed within a computer system
misconceptions: Thinking the CPU understands program code directly rather than binary instructions
Believing fetch-decode-execute happens once per program

assessment.detail: Complete truth tables for two combined logic circuits; explain the fetch-decode-execute cycle in your own words

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 science: simple electrical circuits and switches

knowledgeComponents.statement: A Boolean value is either true or false.
AND is true only when both inputs are true.
OR is true when at least one input is true.
NOT inverts its input: true becomes false and false becomes true.
A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and the resulting output.
A search using AND narrows the results; using OR widens them.
A logic gate is an electronic circuit that implements a Boolean operation.
The CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction, decodes it and executes it.
Both program instructions and data are stored in memory as binary.
Each memory location has an address so the CPU can find it.

lessons.title: Spring 2 assessment: data representation and logic
objectives: I can convert and calculate with binary and apply Boolean logic
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – binary representation and operations; representation of text, sound and images; simple Boolean logic
misconceptions: Making place value errors under time pressure

assessment.detail: 45-minute paper: binary conversion and addition, ASCII, image and sound file size calculations, truth tables and one extended explanation

knowledgeComponents.statement: All data in a computer, of every type, is stored as binary digits.
The meaning of a binary pattern depends on how the computer has been told to interpret it.
Binary place values double from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.
File size calculations should be converted from bits to bytes by dividing by 8.
More bits always means more possible values and a larger file.
Boolean logic underlies both program conditions and hardware circuits.
Compression reduces file size by removing redundancy or, in lossy formats, some detail.
Showing working in a conversion allows a place value error to be identified.

terms.name: Summer 1
terms.focus: Programming 2: text-based programming in Python, the required textual language. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: First Python programs: output and syntax
objectives: I can write and run a Python program that produces output
I can recognise and fix common syntax errors
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve a variety of computational problems
misconceptions: Forgetting quotation marks around a string
Thinking Python ignores capitalisation

assessment.detail: Write five short programs producing formatted output; debug five programs containing deliberate syntax errors

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design, write and debug programs; use logical reasoning to detect and correct errors

lessons.title: Variables, input and data types
objectives: I can store user input in a variable
I can convert between data types with casting
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual; make appropriate use of data structures
misconceptions: Trying to do arithmetic on the string returned by input()
Confusing concatenation with addition

assessment.detail: Write a program that takes two numbers as input, casts them and outputs their sum, difference and product

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: work with variables and various forms of input and output

knowledgeComponents.statement: print() displays output in Python.
A string is text and must be enclosed in matching quotation marks.
Python is case sensitive, so Print and print are different.
A syntax error stops the program running and Python reports the line number.
input() reads text typed by the user and always returns a string.
int() converts a string to a whole number; float() converts it to a decimal number.
The main Python data types are string, integer, float and Boolean.
The plus operator adds numbers but joins strings, which is called concatenation.
A variable is assigned with a single equals sign.

lessons.title: if, elif and else
objectives: I can write a program that makes decisions
I can use elif to handle several cases
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual; understand simple Boolean logic and some of its uses in programming
misconceptions: Using = instead of == in a condition
Getting indentation wrong so a statement falls outside the if block

assessment.detail: Write a grade calculator using if, elif and else; test with normal, boundary and invalid data

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition in programs

knowledgeComponents.statement: In Python, == tests equality and = assigns a value.
An if statement ends with a colon and its block is indented.
Indentation defines code blocks in Python; it is not decoration.
elif tests a further condition only if the previous ones were false.
else runs when every preceding condition was false.
Comparison operators in Python are ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=.
Conditions can be combined with and, or and not.
The order of elif branches matters when the ranges overlap.

lessons.title: for loops and while loops
objectives: I can use a for loop to repeat a fixed number of times
I can use a while loop to repeat until a condition changes
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve a variety of computational problems
misconceptions: Assuming range(5) produces 1 to 5
Writing a while loop whose condition never becomes false

assessment.detail: Write four programs using loops, including a times table generator and an input validation loop

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: use sequence, selection and repetition in programs

lessons.title: Combining constructs and validating input
objectives: I can combine loops and selection in one program
I can validate user input before using it
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages to solve a variety of computational problems; design and develop modular programs
misconceptions: Assuming users always enter valid data
Validating after using the value rather than before

assessment.detail: Write a program that repeatedly asks for a number between 1 and 10 until valid input is given, then uses it

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design, write and debug programs; work with variables and input

knowledgeComponents.statement: A for loop repeats a known number of times.
range(5) produces the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
range(1, 11) produces 1 to 10 inclusive of 1 and exclusive of 11.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains true.
A while loop needs something inside it that can eventually make the condition false.
Validation checks that input is acceptable before the program uses it.
A range check confirms a value lies between stated limits.
A validation loop reprompts the user until acceptable input is entered.
A robust program does not crash when given unexpected input.

lessons.title: Lists and iterating over them
objectives: I can create a Python list and access its items
I can loop through a list to process every item
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – make appropriate use of data structures (for example, lists, tables or arrays)
misconceptions: Forgetting that Python lists start at index 0
Trying to access an index equal to the list length

assessment.detail: Write programs that build a list from input, find the largest item, and calculate the mean of the list

ks2Prerequisites: Y6 maths: mean; Y5–Y6 computing: variables and input

knowledgeComponents.statement: A Python list is written in square brackets with items separated by commas.
Python lists are zero-indexed, so the first item is at index 0.
len() returns the number of items in a list.
append() adds an item to the end of a list.
The last item of a list of length n is at index n minus 1.
A for loop can iterate directly over the items of a list.
To find the largest item, keep a running maximum updated as the list is traversed.
An index error occurs when a program accesses a position that does not exist.

lessons.title: Writing and calling functions
objectives: I can define and call a function
I can use parameters and return values
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design and develop modular programs that use procedures or functions
misconceptions: Confusing printing a value with returning one
Expecting a variable defined inside a function to be available outside it

assessment.detail: Write three functions with parameters and return values; refactor an earlier program to use them

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: solve problems by decomposing them into smaller parts

lessons.title: Modular program design
objectives: I can design a program as a set of functions
I can explain why modular programs are easier to maintain
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design and develop modular programs that use procedures or functions; design, use and evaluate computational abstractions
misconceptions: Writing one very long function that does everything
Creating functions so small they add confusion

assessment.detail: Draw a structure chart for a program with at least four functions, then implement and test it

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: decompose problems into smaller parts

knowledgeComponents.statement: A function is defined with def, a name, brackets and a colon.
A parameter is named in the definition; an argument is the value passed in when the function is called.
return sends a value back to the code that called the function.
Printing shows a value to the user; returning gives it back to the program.
A variable created inside a function is local to it.
A function must be defined before it is called.
Each function should do one clearly defined job.
Modular programs are easier to test, debug, reuse and change.
A structure chart shows how a program is broken into modules.

lessons.title: Python project: design and build
objectives: I can design a program to meet a written specification
I can implement it in Python using all the constructs I know
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve a variety of computational problems; design and develop modular programs; make appropriate use of data structures
misconceptions: Coding before designing
Adding features not in the specification instead of finishing those that are

assessment.detail: Design and build a Python program such as a quiz with score tracking, using functions, a list, selection, iteration and validation

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals

knowledgeComponents.statement: A specification lists exactly what the program must do before any code is written.
Pseudocode design comes before implementation.
A quiz program needs a list of questions, a loop, a comparison and a score variable.
Building incrementally and testing each part is faster than writing everything then debugging.
Comments explain why code does something, not what it obviously does.
Meaningful identifier names make code readable without comments.
A score counter must be initialised before the loop that updates it.
Every requirement in the specification should be checked against the finished program.

lessons.title: Summer 1 assessment: text-based programming
objectives: I can demonstrate Python knowledge and build a working program
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual; design and develop modular programs; make appropriate use of data structures
misconceptions: Reading code carelessly and missing an indentation level

assessment.detail: Written section tracing Python code and identifying errors, plus a timed practical build to a specification

lessons.title: Comparing Scratch and Python
objectives: I can compare a block-based and a text-based language
I can explain that the same constructs appear in both
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – use 2 or more programming languages, at least one of which is textual, to solve a variety of computational problems
misconceptions: Thinking Scratch is not real programming
Believing skills learned in one language do not transfer

assessment.detail: Write the same algorithm in both languages side by side; write a paragraph comparing their strengths

knowledgeComponents.statement: Sequence, selection and iteration appear in both Scratch and Python.
Block-based languages remove syntax errors; text-based languages give more power and precision.
Programming concepts transfer between languages even though the syntax differs.
Tracing Python code means recording each variable's value line by line.
Indentation errors are among the most common faults in Python.
input() returns a string, so numeric input must be cast before arithmetic.
Functions, lists and validation make a program modular and robust.
Reading an error message carefully usually identifies the line and the type of fault.

terms.name: Summer 2
terms.focus: Creative digital projects: data modelling with spreadsheets, web technologies, and a digital artefact built for a known user. 11 lessons.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets: formulae, functions and cell referencing
objectives: I can build a spreadsheet using formulae and functions
I can use absolute and relative cell references correctly
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – undertake creative projects that involve selecting, using, and combining multiple applications, preferably across a range of devices, to achieve challenging goals, including collecting and analysing data
misconceptions: Typing a calculated answer instead of a formula
Not understanding why a reference changes when a formula is copied

assessment.detail: Build a working budget spreadsheet using at least five different functions, including an IF and one absolute reference

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: select, use and combine a variety of software to design and create content including collecting, analysing, evaluating and presenting data

lessons.title: Modelling and 'what if' analysis
objectives: I can build a computational model of a real situation
I can use a model to answer 'what if' questions
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model the state and behaviour of real-world problems and physical systems; collect and analyse data
misconceptions: Treating a model's output as certain fact
Forgetting that a model's assumptions determine its results

assessment.detail: Build a model such as a fundraising or trip-cost forecast; run three 'what if' scenarios; state the model's assumptions and limitations

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: collect, analyse, evaluate and present data and information

knowledgeComponents.statement: A spreadsheet formula begins with an equals sign.
SUM adds a range, AVERAGE finds the mean and COUNT counts the entries.
A relative reference changes when a formula is copied to another cell.
An absolute reference, written with dollar signs, stays fixed when copied.
An IF function returns one value when a condition is true and another when it is false.
A model is a simplified representation used to explore how a system behaves.
Changing an input to see the effect on the output is called what-if analysis.
Every model rests on assumptions that should be stated explicitly.
A model's output is only as good as its assumptions and its data.

lessons.title: Analysing and presenting data honestly
objectives: I can choose an appropriate chart for a data set
I can recognise when a chart is misleading
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – undertake creative projects that involve collecting and analysing data and meeting the needs of known users; create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability
misconceptions: Choosing a chart type for appearance rather than for the data
Not noticing a truncated vertical axis exaggerating a difference

assessment.detail: Produce three charts from one data set; critique two deliberately misleading charts and explain the distortion

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: collect, analyse, evaluate and present data; Y6 maths: bar charts, line graphs and pie charts

knowledgeComponents.statement: Bar charts suit categorical data; line graphs suit continuous data over time.
Pie charts show parts of a whole and should be used only when the parts sum to 100 per cent.
Every chart needs a title, labelled axes and units.
A vertical axis that does not start at zero exaggerates differences.
Data cleaning removes duplicates and errors before analysis.
A chart should make the pattern in the data easier to see, not harder.
Presenting data honestly is an ethical responsibility, not only a technical choice.
Three-dimensional effects on charts distort the reader's perception of values.

lessons.title: How web pages are built: HTML
