objectives: I can write basic HTML to structure a page
I can explain the role of tags and elements
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability; undertake creative projects
misconceptions: Forgetting to close a tag
Thinking HTML controls how a page looks rather than its structure

assessment.detail: Build a two-page HTML site with headings, paragraphs, a list, an image and a working link

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: understand how the world wide web works; select, use and combine software to create content

lessons.title: Styling and usability: CSS and design for a user
objectives: I can apply CSS to change the appearance of a page
I can design a page for a specified user's needs
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability
misconceptions: Styling each element individually rather than using a stylesheet
Treating accessibility as optional

assessment.detail: Style the site with an external stylesheet; run an accessibility check covering contrast, alt text and heading order

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: design and create content for a given audience

knowledgeComponents.statement: HTML describes the structure and content of a web page.
Most HTML elements have an opening tag and a matching closing tag.
Headings run from h1 to h6 and should be used in order.
An attribute provides extra information inside an opening tag, such as the src of an image.
CSS controls the presentation of a page: colour, layout, spacing and fonts.
A CSS rule has a selector, then properties and values inside braces.
An external stylesheet lets one change update every page of a site.
Alt text describes an image for screen reader users and when an image fails to load.
Sufficient colour contrast is required for text to be readable by everyone.
Usability means a user can achieve their goal quickly and without confusion.

lessons.title: Planning a digital artefact for a known user
objectives: I can identify a user's needs and turn them into requirements
I can plan a project that combines several applications
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – undertake creative projects that involve selecting, using, and combining multiple applications, preferably across a range of devices, to achieve challenging goals, including collecting and analysing data and meeting the needs of known users
misconceptions: Designing for oneself rather than for the stated user
Writing success criteria too vague to test

assessment.detail: Interview a real user; write a brief with at least six testable success criteria and a plan naming the applications to be combined

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: select, use and combine a variety of software to design and create content that accomplishes given goals

knowledgeComponents.statement: A known user is a real person whose needs the artefact must meet.
Requirements state what the product must do, in terms that can be tested.
Success criteria are specific, measurable statements agreed before building begins.
Asking the user questions is more reliable than assuming what they want.
A prototype is an early version built to test ideas before full development.
Combining applications means choosing each tool for what it does best.
A project plan sequences tasks and estimates how long each will take.
Designing for a user other than yourself is the core discipline of digital design.

lessons.title: Building the digital artefact
objectives: I can combine multiple applications to build my artefact
I can reuse and repurpose existing material legally and with attribution
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability; undertake creative projects combining multiple applications
misconceptions: Using material without checking its licence
Failing to keep versions so that a change cannot be undone

assessment.detail: Build the artefact combining at least three applications; keep a build log with versions and an attribution list

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: select, use and combine software on a range of digital devices

lessons.title: Testing with the user and refining
objectives: I can test my artefact with the real user
I can act on feedback to improve it
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for a given audience, with attention to trustworthiness, design and usability
misconceptions: Asking the user whether they like it rather than watching them use it
Explaining how to use it instead of observing whether they can

assessment.detail: Run a user test observing task completion; record three issues and the changes made in response

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: evaluate and present digital content

knowledgeComponents.statement: File formats determine what a file can hold and which applications can open it.
Exporting converts a file into a format another application can use.
Reused material must be licensed for that use and correctly attributed.
Keeping numbered versions allows a change to be undone.
User testing means watching a user attempt a task, not asking their opinion.
A usability issue is anything that stops the user completing their task easily.
If the user needs the designer to explain it, the design has a problem.
Refinement should be evidenced by the specific feedback that prompted it.

lessons.title: Evaluating the project against its success criteria
objectives: I can evaluate my artefact against the agreed success criteria
I can identify what I would do differently
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – undertake creative projects that meet the needs of known users; Aims – can evaluate and apply information technology analytically to solve problems
misconceptions: Evaluating by describing what was made rather than judging it
Claiming a criterion was met without evidence

assessment.detail: Evaluate the artefact against every success criterion with evidence, plus three specific improvements

ks2Prerequisites: Y5–Y6: evaluate digital content

knowledgeComponents.statement: An evaluation judges the product against the criteria agreed at the start.
Each judgement must be supported by evidence from testing.
A limitation is something the product cannot do, stated honestly.
Improvements should be specific and achievable, not general wishes.
Reflection on process is as valuable as evaluation of the product.
An unmet criterion is useful information, not a failure to hide.
Trustworthiness, design and usability are the three qualities a digital artefact is judged on.
An evaluation written for the user is more useful than one written for the marker.

lessons.title: End-of-year assessment
objectives: I can demonstrate my computing knowledge from the whole year
lessons.ncRef: Key stage 3 – computer systems, networks, computational thinking, algorithms, programming, data representation, Boolean logic, creative projects and safe use
misconceptions: Revising only the programming units

assessment.detail: 60-minute cumulative paper covering systems, networks, safety, algorithms, binary, Boolean logic and programming

lessons.title: Computing in the world and looking ahead to Year 8
objectives: I can describe how computing is used in different careers
I can name the topics Year 8 will build on
lessons.ncRef: Aims – are responsible, competent, confident and creative users of information and communication technology; Key stage 3 – progression across the key stage
misconceptions: Thinking computing careers are only about writing code

assessment.detail: Research three computing-related careers; map Year 7 topics onto their Year 8 successors and set three personal targets

knowledgeComponents.statement: Year 7 computing covered systems and networks, online safety, computational thinking, algorithms, two programming languages, data representation, Boolean logic and a creative project.
Abstraction, logic, algorithms and data representation are the fundamental principles of computer science.
Computing skills apply across science, medicine, design, finance, media and the arts.
Year 8 extends programming with more complex data structures and file handling.
Cyber security, artificial intelligence and data science are growing areas of computing.
Ethical questions about data, privacy and automation are part of computing, not separate from it.
Programming skills are maintained by regular practice, not by revision alone.
Being a responsible user of technology is a stated aim of the computing curriculum alongside technical skill.
